bundle.domain: Diabetes diagnostic criteria and prediabetes / intermediate hyperglycaemia (non-pregnant adults)

findings.assertion: ADA diagnoses diabetes at a fasting plasma glucose at or above 7.0 mmol/L, with fasting defined as no caloric intake for at least 8 hours.
findings.value: FPG >=126 mg/dL (>=7.0 mmol/L)
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 2, Table 2.1 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S27-S49; doi 10.2337/dc26-S002)
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
findings.quote: FPG >=126 mg/dL (>=7.0 mmol/L). Fasting is defined as no caloric intake for at least 8 h.
findings.notes: Fetched from the free PMC mirror (PMC12690183). The publisher page (diabetesjournals.org/care/article/49/Supplement_1/S27/163926) and its PDF both returned HTTP 403 (Cloudflare) to every fetch attempt, so the ADA-domain copy was NOT read directly.

findings.assertion: ADA diagnoses diabetes at a 2-hour plasma glucose at or above 11.1 mmol/L during a 75-g OGTT performed as described by WHO.
findings.value: 2-h PG >=200 mg/dL (>=11.1 mmol/L) during 75-g OGTT
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 2, Table 2.1
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
findings.quote: 2-h PG >=200 mg/dL (>=11.1 mmol/L) during OGTT. The test should be performed as described by the WHO, using a glucose load containing the equivalent of 75 g anhydrous glucose dissolved in water.
findings.notes: ADA recommendation 2.14 adds a pre-test condition: adequate carbohydrate intake (at least 150 g/day) should be assured for 3 days prior to OGTT.

findings.assertion: ADA diagnoses diabetes at an A1C at or above 6.5%, measured by an NGSP-certified, DCCT-standardised laboratory method.
findings.value: A1C >=6.5% (>=48 mmol/mol IFCC)
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 2, Table 2.1
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
findings.quote: A1C >=6.5% (>=48 mmol/mol). The test should be performed in a laboratory using a method that is NGSP certified and standardized to the DCCT assay.
findings.notes: Recommendation 2.2b restricts point-of-care A1C for screening/diagnosis to FDA-approved devices in CLIA-certified laboratories of moderate complexity or higher. A1C has no mg/dL or mmol/L equivalent; the two unit systems are NGSP % and IFCC mmol/mol.

findings.assertion: ADA permits diagnosis of diabetes from a single random plasma glucose at or above 11.1 mmol/L only when the person has classic symptoms of hyperglycaemia or is in hyperglycaemic crisis.
findings.value: Random PG >=200 mg/dL (>=11.1 mmol/L) PLUS classic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, unexplained weight loss) or hyperglycaemic crisis (DKA and/or HHS)
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 2, Table 2.1
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
findings.quote: In an individual with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis, a random plasma glucose >=200 mg/dL (>=11.1 mmol/L). Random is any time of the day without regard to time since previous meal.
findings.notes: The symptom list is given in the body text: 'random glucose accompanied by classic symptoms of hyperglycemia (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss) or hyperglycemic crises (i.e., diabetic ketoacidosis [DKA] and/or hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state [HHS])'. This is the ONLY route to a single-sample diagnosis under ADA.

findings.assertion: ADA requires two abnormal results to diagnose diabetes when hyperglycaemia is not unequivocal, and explicitly allows the two results to come from two different tests drawn at the SAME time.
findings.value: Two abnormal results required; may be two different tests at the same time (e.g., A1C + FPG) or the same test at two different time points
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 2, Table 2.1 footnote and Recommendation 2.1b
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
findings.quote: In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia, diagnosis requires two abnormal results from different tests, which may be obtained at the same time (e.g., A1C and FPG), or the same test at two different time points.
findings.notes: Recommendation 2.1b (grade B): 'In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia (e.g., hyperglycemic crises), diagnosis requires confirmatory testing.' This same-sample allowance is the key divergence from WHO — see conflicts.

findings.assertion: ADA specifies how to resolve discordant confirmatory tests: repeat the test whose result was above the diagnostic cut point, and diagnose on the confirmatory test even if the other test is normal.
findings.value: Discordant results -> repeat the abnormal test; two A1C results >=6.5% (>=48 mmol/mol) confirm diabetes even if FPG <126 mg/dL (<7.0 mmol/L)
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 2, 'Confirming the Diagnosis'
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
findings.quote: if an individual has discordant results from two different tests, then the test result that is above the diagnostic cut point should be repeated, with careful consideration of factors that may affect measured A1C or glucose levels. The diagnosis is made based on the confirmatory screening test. For example, if an individual meets the diagnostic criterion for A1C (two results >=6.5% [>=48 mmol/mol]) but not FPG (<126 mg/dL [<7.0 mmol/L]), that person should nevertheless be considered to have diabetes.
findings.notes: The same paragraph gives a worked example of a valid repeat: 'if the A1C is 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) and a repeat result is 6.8% (51 mmol/mol), the diagnosis of diabetes is confirmed' — i.e. the repeat need not itself exceed the cut point by the same margin, only be in range.

findings.assertion: ADA defines the prediabetes A1C band as 5.7-6.4%.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 2, Table 2.2
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
findings.notes: Table 2.2 is titled 'Criteria defining prediabetes in nonpregnant individuals'. No SI glucose equivalent applies to A1C. WHO does not endorse this band — see conflicts.

findings.assertion: ADA defines impaired fasting glucose (IFG) as a fasting plasma glucose of 5.6-6.9 mmol/L, on the FPG value alone.
findings.value: FPG 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) to 125 mg/dL (6.9 mmol/L)
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 2, Table 2.2
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
findings.quote: FPG 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) to 125 mg/dL (6.9 mmol/L) (IFG)
findings.notes: This is the disputed definition. ADA's IFG imposes no condition on the 2-h PG; WHO/IDF IFG requires 2-h PG <7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL) if measured. Lower bound differs from WHO/IDF (5.6 vs 6.1 mmol/L) — see conflicts.

findings.assertion: ADA defines impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) as a 2-hour plasma glucose of 7.8-11.0 mmol/L on a 75-g OGTT.
findings.value: 2-h PG 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) to 199 mg/dL (11.0 mmol/L)
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 2, Table 2.2
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
findings.quote: 2-h PG during 75-g OGTT 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) to 199 mg/dL (11.0 mmol/L) (IGT)
findings.notes: Numerically the same band as WHO/IDF IGT, but ADA states it as a standalone 2-h PG range while WHO/IDF additionally require FPG <7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL). Table 2.2 footnote: 'For all three tests, risk is continuous, extending below the lower limit of the range and becoming disproportionately greater at the higher end of the range.'

findings.assertion: ADA directs that plasma glucose criteria, not A1C, be used to diagnose diabetes where the A1C-glycaemia relationship is altered — a caveat that matters heavily in African settings (haemoglobinopathy, G6PD deficiency, HIV, altered red-cell turnover).
findings.value: Use plasma glucose criteria (FPG >=126 mg/dL / >=7.0 mmol/L or 2-h PG >=200 mg/dL / >=11.1 mmol/L) instead of A1C in these conditions
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026, Section 2, Recommendation 2.4 (grade B)
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026
findings.quote: 2.4 In conditions associated with an altered relationship between A1C and glycemia, such as some hemoglobin variants, pregnancy, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, HIV, and conditions that may alter red blood cell turnover, plasma glucose criteria should be used to diagnose diabetes.
findings.notes: Flagged for CSO review because of direct relevance to the Ugandan patient population (sickle cell trait/disease, malaria-related anaemia, high HIV prevalence). ADA also quantifies: G6PD G202A, 'carried by 11% of Black individuals in the U.S., is associated with a decrease in A1C of about 0.8% in homozygous men and 0.7% in homozygous women'. ADA further notes 'an A1C assay without interference from hemoglobin variants should be used in individuals with sickle cell trait'.

findings.assertion: ADA's patient-facing guidance states each diagnostic test usually needs repeating on a second day, with an exception for very high glucose or classic symptoms.
findings.value: FPG: normal <100 mg/dL, prediabetes 100-125 mg/dL, diabetes >=126 mg/dL; 2-h OGTT: normal <140, prediabetes 140-199, diabetes >=200 mg/dL; A1C: normal <5.7%, prediabetes 5.7-6.4%, diabetes >=6.5%
findings.standardVersion: diabetes.org consumer/clinical education page, accessed 2026-09-05 (undated on page)
findings.sourceTitle: Diabetes Diagnosis & Tests | ADA
findings.quote: Each way usually needs to be repeated on a second day to diagnose diabetes.
findings.notes: ADA-owned but patient-facing, NOT the Standards of Care. It gives only mg/dL, no SI units. Its 'repeat on a second day' framing is looser than Table 2.1's footnote, which explicitly permits two different tests from the same draw. Where they differ, the Standards of Care governs. Included only as ADA-domain corroboration since the Standards themselves could not be read on ADA's domain.

findings.assertion: WHO's current classification document states four diagnostic tests and their thresholds, including HbA1c and a random blood glucose with signs and symptoms.
findings.value: FPG >=7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL); 2-h post-load PG >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL); HbA1c >=6.5% (48 mmol/mol); or random blood glucose >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) with signs and symptoms
findings.standardVersion: Classification of diabetes mellitus, WHO, 2019 (Section 1, 'Diabetes: Definition and diagnosis'; IRIS handle 10665/325182)
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019)
findings.quote: People with fasting plasma glucose values of >= 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dl), 2-h post-load plasma glucose >= 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dl) (5), HbA1c >= 6.5% (48 mmol/mol); or a random blood glucose >= 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dl) in the presence of signs and symptoms are considered to have diabetes (6).
findings.notes: PDF fetched directly from WHO IRIS (canonical landing page: https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/325182). Note the wording is 'random BLOOD glucose', not 'random plasma glucose' as in ADA/IDF — WHO's own Recommendation 5 (2006) says venous plasma glucose should be the standard measurement, so this is most likely loose drafting rather than an intended capillary/whole-blood criterion, but it is not clarified in the 2019 text.

findings.assertion: WHO requires a repeat test on a SUBSEQUENT DAY, preferably the same test, to confirm diabetes in asymptomatic people.
findings.value: Repeat testing, preferably with the same test, on a subsequent day
findings.standardVersion: Classification of diabetes mellitus, WHO, 2019, Section 1
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019)
findings.quote: If elevated values are detected in asymptomatic people, repeat testing, preferably with the same test, is recommended as soon as practicable on a subsequent day to confirm the diagnosis (6).
findings.notes: Flagged: this is materially stricter than ADA, which allows both confirmatory results from a single draw. A decision-support rule that follows ADA would diagnose some patients on one visit whom WHO would require to return. Uganda follows WHO-aligned practice, so the CSO should decide which rule the tool encodes.

findings.assertion: WHO/IDF define impaired fasting glucose (IFG) as fasting plasma glucose 6.1-6.9 mmol/L AND, if measured, a 2-hour plasma glucose below 7.8 mmol/L.
findings.value: FPG 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L (110 mg/dL to 125 mg/dL) AND (if measured) 2-h PG <7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL)
findings.standardVersion: Definition and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and intermediate hyperglycaemia: report of a WHO/IDF consultation, 2006 (summary table; IRIS handle 10665/43588)
findings.sourceTitle: Definition and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and intermediate hyperglycaemia: report of a WHO/IDF consultation
findings.quote: Impaired fasting Glucose (IfG) / Fasting plasma glucose 6.1 to 6.9mmol/l (110mg/dl to 125mg/dl) and (if measured) 2-h plasma glucose <7.8mmol/l (140mg/dl)
findings.notes: This is the canonical WHO/IDF IFG definition and it is still current — the WHO 2019 classification did not revisit it. Table footnotes: '* Venous plasma glucose 2-h after ingestion of 75g oral glucose load' and '* If 2-h plasma glucose is not measured, status is uncertain as diabetes or IGT cannot be excluded.' Direct conflict with ADA's 5.6 mmol/L lower bound.

findings.assertion: WHO/IDF define impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) as fasting plasma glucose below 7.0 mmol/L AND a 2-hour plasma glucose of 7.8 to below 11.1 mmol/L.
findings.value: FPG <7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) AND 2-h PG >=7.8 and <11.1 mmol/L (140 mg/dL and 200 mg/dL)
findings.standardVersion: Definition and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and intermediate hyperglycaemia: WHO/IDF consultation, 2006 (summary table)
findings.sourceTitle: Definition and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and intermediate hyperglycaemia: report of a WHO/IDF consultation
findings.quote: Impaired Glucose tolerance (IGt) / Fasting plasma glucose <7.0mmol/l (126mg/dl) and 2-h plasma glucose >=7.8 and <11.1mmol/l (140mg/dl and 200mg/dl)
findings.notes: Both criteria must be met ('BOTH of the following'). Numerically the 2-h band matches ADA, but WHO makes the FPG condition part of the definition, so a person with FPG 7.2 mmol/L and 2-h PG 9.0 mmol/L is diabetes (not IGT) under WHO, whereas ADA's Table 2.2 wording would also label the 2-h value as IGT.

findings.assertion: WHO explicitly considered and REJECTED lowering the IFG cut-point to the ADA's 5.6 mmol/L, keeping it at 6.1 mmol/L.
findings.value: IFG fasting cut-point remains 6.1 mmol/L (110 mg/dL); the alternative considered and rejected was 5.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL)
findings.standardVersion: WHO/IDF consultation 2006, Recommendation 4
findings.sourceTitle: Definition and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and intermediate hyperglycaemia: report of a WHO/IDF consultation
findings.quote: The fasting plasma glucose cut-point for Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) should remain at 6.1mmol/l. This decision was based on concerns about the significant increase in IFG prevalence which would occur with lowering the cut-point and the impact on individuals and health systems. There is a lack of evidence of any benefit in terms of reducing adverse outcomes or progression to diabetes and people identified by a lower cut-point eg 5.6mmol/l (100mg/dl) have a more favourable cardiovascular risk profile and only half the risk of developing diabetes compared with those above the current WHO cut-point.
findings.notes: Important for a resource-constrained setting: WHO's stated reason is health-system burden and absence of outcome benefit. The 2006 report also records the origin of the divergence: 'in 2003, the ADA reviewed its diagnostic criteria... the ADA recommended lowering the threshold for Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) from 6.1mmol/l (110mg/dl) to 5.6mmol/l (100mg/dl)'.

findings.assertion: WHO recommends performing an OGTT in anyone whose fasting plasma glucose falls in the IFG band, because FPG alone misses about 30% of undiagnosed diabetes.
findings.value: Perform 75-g OGTT when FPG is 6.1-6.9 mmol/L (110-125 mg/dL)
findings.standardVersion: WHO/IDF consultation 2006, Recommendation 6
findings.sourceTitle: Definition and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and intermediate hyperglycaemia: report of a WHO/IDF consultation
findings.quote: An OGTT should be used in individuals with fasting plasma glucose 6.1-6.9mmol/l (110-125mg/dl) to determine glucose tolerance status.
findings.notes: Rationale given in the same recommendation: 'fasting plasma glucose alone fails to diagnose approximately 30% of cases of previously undiagnosed diabetes' and 'an OGTT is the only means of identifying people with IGT'. This is an actionable follow-up rule for a triage/clerkship engine.

findings.assertion: WHO accepts HbA1c 6.5% as the diabetes diagnostic cut-point, but states a value below 6.5% does not exclude diabetes diagnosed by glucose testing.
findings.value: HbA1c >=6.5% for diagnosis; HbA1c <6.5% does NOT rule out diabetes
findings.standardVersion: Use of glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus: abbreviated report of a WHO consultation, 2011 (IRIS handle 10665/70523)
findings.sourceTitle: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus - WHO 2011 (NCBI Bookshelf full text NBK304271)
findings.quote: HbA1c can be used as a diagnostic test for diabetes providing that stringent quality assurance tests are in place and assays are standardised to criteria aligned to the international reference values, and there are no conditions present which preclude its accurate measurement. An HbA1c of 6.5% is recommended as the cut point for diagnosing diabetes. A value of less than 6.5% does not exclude diabetes diagnosed using glucose tests.
findings.notes: Read via the NCBI Bookshelf full text of the WHO report, NOT the WHO IRIS PDF (IRIS handle 10665/70523 located but its PDF not downloaded). WHO grades this recommendation: 'Quality of evidence assessed by GRADE: moderate. Strength of recommendation based on GRADE criteria: conditional.' The 2011 report states the cut-point in % only; the 48 mmol/mol equivalent comes from WHO 2019 and IDF 2025.

findings.assertion: WHO declines to define any HbA1c prediabetes / intermediate-hyperglycaemia band, concluding the evidence is insufficient.
findings.value: No WHO HbA1c band below 6.5% (48 mmol/mol); WHO makes no recommendation on interpreting HbA1c <6.5%
findings.standardVersion: WHO 2011 HbA1c consultation report
findings.sourceTitle: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus - WHO 2011 (NCBI Bookshelf full text NBK304271)
findings.quote: The consultation concluded that there is insufficient evidence to make any formal recommendation on the interpretation of HbA1c levels below 6.5%.
findings.notes: The same report notes the competing proposals it declined to adopt: 'Levels of HbA1c just below 6.5% may indicate the presence of intermediate hyperglycaemia. The precise lower cut-off point for this has yet to be defined, although the ADA has suggested 5.7 - 6.4% as the high risk range' and that the International Expert Committee proposed 6.0-6.5%. A tool must not present ADA's 5.7-6.4% band as a WHO position.

findings.assertion: WHO's confirmatory rule for asymptomatic people: never diagnose on a single abnormal value, and if only one of two concurrently measured tests is abnormal, repeat that test using the SAME method.
findings.value: At least one additional HbA1c or plasma glucose result in the diabetic range is required; if only one of glucose/HbA1c is abnormal, a further abnormal result using the same method is required
findings.standardVersion: WHO 2011 HbA1c consultation report, 'Recommendations for diagnostic practice' section
findings.sourceTitle: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus - WHO 2011 (NCBI Bookshelf full text NBK304271)
findings.quote: The diagnosis of diabetes in an asymptomatic person should not be made on the basis of a single abnormal plasma glucose or HbA1c value. At least one additional HbA1c or plasma glucose test result with a value in the diabetic range is required... It is advisable to use one test or the other but if both glucose and HbA1c are measured and both are "diagnostic" then the diagnosis is made. If one only is abnormal then a further abnormal test result, using the same method, is required to confirm the diagnosis.
findings.notes: WHO does accept two concurrently diagnostic tests (glucose AND HbA1c both diagnostic) as confirming — narrowing but not eliminating the gap with ADA. The residual conflict is the discordant case: ADA repeats the abnormal test and diagnoses on it; WHO also requires a repeat by the same method, and adds 'If such tests fail to confirm the diagnosis of diabetes, it will usually be advisable to maintain surveillance with periodic re-testing until the glycaemic status becomes clear.'

findings.assertion: IDF's current Diabetes Atlas states the diabetes diagnostic thresholds, requiring one or more criteria to be met.
findings.value: FPG >=7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) OR 2-h PG >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) after 75-g OGTT OR random PG >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) with symptoms of hyperglycaemia OR HbA1c >=48 mmol/mol (equivalent to 6.5%)
findings.standardVersion: IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th Edition, 2025, Figure 1.1 'Diagnostic criteria for diabetes'
findings.sourceTitle: IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th Edition 2025
findings.quote: Diabetes / Should be diagnosed if ONE OR MORE of the following criteria are met ... Fasting plasma glucose 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) ... Two-hour plasma glucose after a 75g oral glucose load (oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)) 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) ... Random plasma glucose in the presence of symptoms of hyperglycaemia 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) ... HbA1c 48 mmol/L (equivalent to 6.5%)
findings.notes: Fetched as PDF (8.3 MB), Figure 1.1 on p.15/p.20 of PDF. TYPOGRAPHICAL ERROR IN THE SOURCE: the figure labels the HbA1c value '48 mmol/L' where it must be 48 mmol/mol (IFCC). Do not propagate the units as printed. Figure 1.1 note: 'Fasting is defined as no caloric intake for at least eight hours' and the HbA1c must be NGSP-certified and DCCT-standardised. IDF cites its own 'Clinical Practice Recommendations for Managing Type 2 Diabetes in Primary Care' as the figure's source.

findings.assertion: IDF defines impaired fasting glucose identically to WHO 2006, at 6.1-6.9 mmol/L with 2-hour PG below 7.8 mmol/L if measured.
findings.value: FPG 6.1-6.9 mmol/L (110-125 mg/dL) AND (if measured) 2-h PG <7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL)
findings.standardVersion: IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th Edition, 2025, Figure 1.1
findings.sourceTitle: IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th Edition 2025
findings.quote: Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) / Should be diagnosed if THE FIRST OR BOTH of the following are met ... 6.1-6.9 mmol/L (110 - 125 mg/dL) ... < 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL)
findings.notes: IDF sides with WHO, not ADA, on the IFG lower bound. IDF's phrasing 'THE FIRST OR BOTH' is slightly looser than WHO 2006's 'and (if measured)' but is materially the same rule.

findings.assertion: IDF defines impaired glucose tolerance identically to WHO 2006, requiring both a fasting PG below 7.0 mmol/L and a 2-hour PG of 7.8 to below 11.1 mmol/L.
findings.value: FPG <7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) AND 2-h PG >=7.8 and <11.1 mmol/L (140-199 mg/dL)
findings.standardVersion: IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th Edition, 2025, Figure 1.1
findings.sourceTitle: IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th Edition 2025
findings.quote: Impaired Glucose Tolerance / Should be diagnosed if BOTH of the following criteria are met ... < 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) ... 7.8 and < 11.1 mmol/L (140-199 mg/dL)
findings.notes: Note IDF prints the conventional-unit band as 140-199 mg/dL whereas WHO 2006 printed '140mg/dl and 200mg/dl' for the same >=7.8 and <11.1 mmol/L interval; ADA prints 140-199 mg/dL (7.8-11.0 mmol/L). All three describe the same interval.

findings.assertion: IDF requires two abnormal tests to diagnose diabetes in the absence of symptoms, but accepts a single random plasma glucose at or above 11.1 mmol/L with classic symptoms.
findings.value: Two abnormal tests required if asymptomatic; single random PG >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) with polyuria, polydipsia and unexplained weight loss is sufficient
findings.standardVersion: IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th Edition, 2025, Figure 1.1 note and Section 1.4
findings.sourceTitle: IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th Edition 2025
findings.quote: In the absence of symptoms of hyperglycaemia, two abnormal tests are required for the diagnosis of diabetes. ... For type 2 diabetes, if a single random plasma glucose concentration is >= 11.1 mmol/l in the presence of symptoms such as polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss, the diagnosis can be made without a second abnormal measurement.
findings.notes: IDF does not specify whether the two abnormal tests may come from the same draw, so it does not adjudicate the ADA/WHO same-sample question.

findings.assertion: IDF states explicitly that WHO supports HbA1c >=6.5% for diagnosing diabetes but NOT for defining intermediate hyperglycaemia, citing global availability of quality-assured assays.
findings.value: HbA1c >=6.5% (48 mmol/mol) for diabetes diagnosis only; no HbA1c-based intermediate hyperglycaemia category under WHO/IDF
findings.standardVersion: IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th Edition, 2025, Section 1.4 'Diagnostic criteria for diabetes'
findings.sourceTitle: IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th Edition 2025
findings.quote: WHO supports the use of HbA1c >=6.5% for diabetes diagnosis but not for intermediate hyperglycaemia, partly on the grounds that quality-assured HbA1c measurement is not available on a global scale.
findings.notes: Directly relevant to Mulago/Uganda deployment: the stated reason for WHO/IDF rejecting an HbA1c prediabetes band is assay availability and quality assurance in exactly this kind of setting. IDF also reproduces ADA's competing definitions in the Figure 1.1 footnote rather than adopting them: 'The American Diabetes Association (ADA) recommends diagnosing "prediabetes" with a fasting plasma glucose between 5.6 and 6.9 mmol/L (100mg/dL to 125mg/dL: impaired fasting glucose), a 2-h plasma glucose >=7.8 and <11.1 mmol/L (140-200 mg/dl: impaired glucose tolerance) or HbA1c values between 39 and 47 mmol/mol (5.7-6.4%).'

findings.assertion: IDF and WHO both currently recommend the 75-g OGTT with measurement of BOTH fasting and 2-hour plasma glucose to detect IGT, IFG and diabetes.
findings.value: 75-g OGTT with both fasting and 2-h plasma glucose
findings.standardVersion: IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th Edition, 2025, Section 1.4
findings.sourceTitle: IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th Edition 2025
findings.quote: Currently, IDF and WHO recommend the use of the 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) with measurement of both fasting and two-hour plasma glucose to detect IGT, IFG and diabetes. However, there is literature favouring the use of the one-hour 75-gram OGTT, which may be a more sensitive method of identifying intermediate hyperglycaemia.
findings.notes: The 1-hour OGTT is flagged by IDF as emerging, not adopted in Figure 1.1. IDF has a separate 2024 position statement on the 1-h post-load PG which I could NOT retrieve (paywalled) — see unverifiable.

conflicts.assertion: Lower threshold for impaired fasting glucose (IFG)
positions: ADA (Standards of Care 2026, Table 2.2): FPG 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) to 125 mg/dL (6.9 mmol/L)
WHO (WHO/IDF consultation 2006, Recommendation 4 and summary table): FPG 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L (110 to 125 mg/dL) — WHO reviewed the 5.6 mmol/L cut-point in 2005 and explicitly declined to adopt it
IDF (Diabetes Atlas 11th ed., 2025, Figure 1.1): FPG 6.1-6.9 mmol/L (110-125 mg/dL), aligned with WHO
conflicts.recommendation: Do NOT hard-code a single IFG band. Store both and label the standard on the face of any output, e.g. 'IFG (WHO/IDF): FPG 6.1-6.9 mmol/L' vs 'IFG (ADA): FPG 5.6-6.9 mmol/L'. For a Mulago/Uganda deployment the WHO/IDF 6.1 mmol/L cut-point is the appropriate default, since Ugandan practice is WHO-aligned and WHO's stated rationale for rejecting 5.6 was health-system burden without demonstrated outcome benefit. Escalate to the CSO before shipping: choosing ADA's band would roughly double the population labelled prediabetic. Upper bound (6.9 mmol/L / 125 mg/dL) is agreed by all three and is safe to treat as fixed.

conflicts.assertion: Whether IFG requires a normal 2-hour plasma glucose
positions: ADA (Table 2.2): IFG is defined on the FPG value alone; no OGTT condition attached

WHO (2006 summary table): 'Fasting plasma glucose 6.1 to 6.9mmol/l ... and (if measured) 2-h plasma glucose <7.8mmol/l (140mg/dl)', with the footnote 'If 2-h plasma glucose is not measured, status is uncertain as diabetes or IGT cannot be excluded'
IDF (Figure 1.1): 'Should be diagnosed if THE FIRST OR BOTH of the following are met' — FPG 6.1-6.9 mmol/L and 2-h PG <7.8 mmol/L
conflicts.recommendation: Encode the WHO/IDF conditional: when a 2-hour PG is available it must be <7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL) for the label 'IFG' to be correct, and when it is not available the tool should state that glucose-tolerance status is undetermined rather than asserting isolated IFG. WHO 2006 Recommendation 6 gives the actionable follow-up: perform a 75-g OGTT in anyone with FPG 6.1-6.9 mmol/L, because FPG alone misses roughly 30% of undiagnosed diabetes. This matters clinically — a patient labelled 'IFG' on FPG alone may in fact have diabetes on OGTT.

conflicts.assertion: Whether an HbA1c band defines prediabetes / intermediate hyperglycaemia
positions: ADA (Table 2.2): A1C 5.7-6.4% (39-47 mmol/mol) defines prediabetes

WHO (2011 HbA1c consultation): 'there is insufficient evidence to make any formal recommendation on the interpretation of HbA1c levels below 6.5%' — no WHO band exists; the report records ADA's 5.7-6.4% and the International Expert Committee's 6.0-6.5% as proposals it did not adopt

IDF (Atlas 11th ed., 2025, s1.4): 'WHO supports the use of HbA1c >=6.5% for diabetes diagnosis but not for intermediate hyperglycaemia, partly on the grounds that quality-assured HbA1c measurement is not available on a global scale'
conflicts.recommendation: Never present 5.7-6.4% as a consensus or WHO-endorsed band. If the tool surfaces an HbA1c-based prediabetes flag at all, it must be attributed to ADA on screen. Given that WHO's stated reason for rejecting the band is assay quality assurance in low-resource settings — precisely the MedSync deployment context — the safer default is to base intermediate-hyperglycaemia detection on FPG and OGTT, and treat an A1C of 5.7-6.4% as a risk signal prompting glucose testing rather than as a diagnosis. CSO decision required.

conflicts.assertion: Whether the two confirmatory results may come from a single blood draw
positions: ADA (Table 2.1 footnote): 'diagnosis requires two abnormal results from different tests, which may be obtained at the same time (e.g., A1C and FPG), or the same test at two different time points' — same-visit diagnosis is explicitly permitted

WHO (Classification of diabetes mellitus 2019): 'repeat testing, preferably with the same test, is recommended as soon as practicable on a subsequent day to confirm the diagnosis' — a second day is specified

WHO (2011 HbA1c report): accepts concurrent confirmation only when both tests are diagnostic — 'if both glucose and HbA1c are measured and both are "diagnostic" then the diagnosis is made. If one only is abnormal then a further abnormal test result, using the same method, is required'
IDF (Atlas 11th ed., Figure 1.1 note): 'In the absence of symptoms of hyperglycaemia, two abnormal tests are required' — silent on timing, so it does not adjudicate
conflicts.recommendation: Treat this as an unresolved workflow conflict and default to the stricter WHO position for asymptomatic patients: require a repeat on a subsequent day, preferably by the same method. Note the two WHO documents are not fully consistent with each other either — the 2011 report allows a same-time diagnosis when BOTH glucose and HbA1c are diagnostic, while the 2019 text asks for a subsequent-day repeat. The one point of full agreement across ADA, WHO and IDF is the symptomatic exception: a random plasma glucose >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) with classic symptoms or hyperglycaemic crisis needs no second sample. Encode that exception confidently and route everything else through a confirm-on-a-second-day rule pending CSO sign-off.

conflicts.assertion: Whether the fasting PG condition forms part of the IGT definition
positions: ADA (Table 2.2): IGT stated as the 2-h PG band alone, 140-199 mg/dL (7.8-11.0 mmol/L), with no fasting condition
WHO (2006 summary table): 'Should be diagnosed if BOTH ... Fasting plasma glucose <7.0mmol/l (126mg/dl) and 2-h plasma glucose >=7.8 and <11.1mmol/l'
IDF (Figure 1.1): 'Should be diagnosed if BOTH of the following criteria are met' — FPG <7.0 mmol/L and 2-h PG 7.8 to <11.1 mmol/L
conflicts.recommendation: The numeric 2-hour band (7.8 to <11.1 mmol/L; 140-199 mg/dL) is agreed by all three and can be treated as settled. The divergence is structural: under WHO/IDF a patient with FPG >=7.0 mmol/L cannot be classified as IGT — they already meet the diabetes criterion. Implement WHO/IDF precedence logic (diabetes criteria evaluated first, intermediate categories only if no diabetes criterion is met) so the engine cannot emit a reassuring 'IGT' label for someone whose fasting glucose is already diagnostic.

conflicts.assertion: Specimen type for the random/casual glucose criterion
positions: ADA (Table 2.1): 'a random plasma glucose >=200 mg/dL (>=11.1 mmol/L)'
WHO (Classification of diabetes mellitus 2019): 'a random blood glucose >= 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dl) in the presence of signs and symptoms' — says blood, not plasma
IDF (Figure 1.1): 'Random plasma glucose in the presence of symptoms of hyperglycaemia ... 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL)'
conflicts.recommendation: Treat this as loose drafting in the WHO 2019 text rather than a genuine whole-blood criterion: WHO's own 2006 Recommendation 5 states 'Venous plasma glucose should be the standard method for measuring and reporting glucose concentrations in blood', and both ADA and IDF specify plasma. Encode the threshold as venous PLASMA glucose >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL). This matters at the bedside in Uganda because capillary glucometer readings are the common point-of-care measurement and are not interchangeable with venous plasma for diagnosis — the tool should require laboratory confirmation and should never diagnose from a meter reading. I did NOT find a WHO document that resolves the 2019 wording explicitly; flag to the CSO.

unverifiable: ADA Standards of Care 2026 could not be read on ADA's own domain. Both https://diabetesjournals.org/care/article/49/Supplement_1/S27/163926/2-Diagnosis-and-Classification-of-Diabetes and its PDF (dc26s002.pdf) returned HTTP 403 to every attempt (WebFetch and curl with browser headers). Every ADA value above was read from the free PMC mirror, PMC12690183, which carries the suggested citation 'Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S27-S49' and doi 10.2337/dc26-S002. The mirror is authoritative in practice but a CSO signing this off may want the publisher copy checked by a human with journal access.

Whether a WHO guideline newer than the 2019 'Classification of diabetes mellitus' supersedes the 2006 IFG/IGT definitions or the 2011 HbA1c report. I searched but did not positively confirm the absence of a 2020-2026 WHO update, and WHO IRIS was queried only by keyword. The 2006 thresholds are being treated as current on the strength of IDF's 2025 Atlas still reproducing them, which is indirect evidence, not a WHO statement of currency.

The IDF 2024 position statement 'International Diabetes Federation Position Statement on the 1-hour post-load plasma glucose for the diagnosis of intermediate hyperglycaemia and type 2 diabetes' (Diabetes Res Clin Pract 2024; doi 10.1016/j.diabres.2024.111589; PMID 38458916) is paywalled and NOT open access on Europe PMC. I could not retrieve it, so I have recorded NO 1-hour OGTT thresholds. IDF's Atlas acknowledges the 1-hour approach as promising but does not put it in Figure 1.1. If the product wants 1-hour criteria, someone must obtain this paper.

IDF's underlying source document for Figure 1.1 — 'IDF Clinical Practice Recommendations for Managing Type 2 Diabetes in Primary Care' — was cited as reference 1 of Atlas chapter 1 but was not fetched. The Figure 1.1 values are verified from the Atlas itself, not from that upstream document, and its edition/year is unconfirmed.

The IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th edition prints the HbA1c diagnostic value in Figure 1.1 as '48 mmol/L', which is a units error in the published source (it must be 48 mmol/mol, IFCC). I read this verbatim and am reporting it as printed; I could not find an IDF erratum. Do not propagate the printed units.

WHO's 2011 HbA1c report was read via the NCBI Bookshelf full text (NBK304271), not from WHO IRIS. I located the IRIS handle (10665/70523) but did not download that PDF, so I have not confirmed the Bookshelf text is byte-identical to WHO's own copy.

The 48 mmol/mol IFCC equivalent of HbA1c 6.5% is verified from WHO 2019 and IDF 2025, but the WHO 2011 consultation report itself states the cut-point in NGSP % only. The 39-47 mmol/mol equivalents for ADA's 5.7-6.4% band are verified from ADA 2026 Table 2.2.

Capillary versus venous plasma glucose conversion values. WHO 2006 Recommendation 5 states that conversion values for capillary plasma glucose are provided for post-load values and that fasting venous and capillary values are identical, but I did not extract the conversion table itself. This is a real gap for a Ugandan deployment where point-of-care capillary testing predominates.

Whether the 2026 ADA edition changed any threshold relative to 2025. I did not fetch the 'Summary of Revisions: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026' article, so I cannot state which criteria are new or unchanged this cycle.

Alignment with Uganda Ministry of Health / Uganda Clinical Guidelines national diabetes criteria was not checked at all. Before this data drives decision support at Mulago, someone must confirm which of the WHO and ADA positions Ugandan national guidance adopts, particularly for the IFG cut-point.

Gestational diabetes and hyperglycaemia in pregnancy were out of scope and are NOT covered. I incidentally read WHO 2019's GDM line ('fasting plasma glucose 5.1-6.9 mmol/L or 1-hour post-load plasma glucose >= 10.0 mmol/L or 2-hour post-load plasma glucose 8.5-11.0 mmol/L') but did not cross-verify it against the WHO 2013 hyperglycaemia-in-pregnancy document, and ADA's pregnancy criteria were not extracted. Do not use anything here for pregnant patients.

Paediatric and adolescent diagnostic thresholds were not separately verified. ADA's Tables 2.1 and 2.2 are titled 'in nonpregnant individuals' and I did not confirm whether any threshold differs for children.

Diagnostic criteria for type 1 versus type 2 classification (islet autoantibody testing, C-peptide) were outside the requested scope and are not captured, though ADA 2026 Section 2 contains recommendations on them.

audit.assertion: ADA (Standards of Care 2026, Table 2.1): diabetes at FPG >=7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL), fasting = no caloric intake for >=8 h
audit.reason: Independently downloaded PMC12690183 and extracted the raw text. Table 2.1 reads verbatim: 'FPG >=126 mg/dL (>=7.0 mmol/L). Fasting is defined as no caloric intake for at least 8 h.' Citation line in the article itself confirms 'Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S27-S49' and the PMC header confirms 'doi: 10.2337/dc26-S002'. Table title is 'Criteria for the diagnosis of diabetes in nonpregnant individuals'. Both units present. URL resolves (HTTP 200) and contains the claim.

audit.assertion: ADA (2026, Table 2.1): 2-h PG >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) during 75-g OGTT performed as described by WHO
audit.reason: Verbatim from the fetched Table 2.1: '2-h PG >=200 mg/dL (>=11.1 mmol/L) during OGTT. The test should be performed as described by the WHO, using a glucose load containing the equivalent of 75 g anhydrous glucose dissolved in water.' Value, units and attribution all correct.

audit.assertion: ADA (2026, Table 2.1): A1C >=6.5% (48 mmol/mol) by NGSP-certified, DCCT-standardised method
audit.reason: Verbatim from the fetched Table 2.1: 'A1C >=6.5% (>=48 mmol/mol). The test should be performed in a laboratory using a method that is NGSP certified and standardized to the DCCT assay.' Corroborated by Recommendation 2.2a in the same document. The finding's parenthetical '(IFCC)' is an added gloss - the table prints 'mmol/mol' without naming IFCC - but the unit is the IFCC unit, so this is not an error of substance.

audit.assertion: ADA (2026, Table 2.1): single random PG >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) diagnostic only with classic symptoms or hyperglycaemic crisis
audit.reason: Table 2.1 verbatim: 'In an individual with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis, a random plasma glucose >=200 mg/dL (>=11.1 mmol/L).' The parenthetical expansions are also verbatim elsewhere in Section 2: 'classic symptoms of hyperglycemia (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss) or hyperglycemic crises (i.e., diabetic ketoacidosis [DKA] and/or hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state [HHS])'.

audit.assertion: ADA (2026, Table 2.1 footnote + Rec 2.1b): two abnormal results required absent unequivocal hyperglycaemia; the two may be different tests drawn at the same time
audit.reason: Table 2.1 footnote verbatim: '*In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia, diagnosis requires two abnormal results from different tests, which may be obtained at the same time (e.g., A1C and FPG), or the same test at two different time points.' Recommendation 2.1b verbatim: 'In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia (e.g., hyperglycemic crises), diagnosis requires confirmatory testing (Table 2.1). B'. Both cited locators exist and carry the claim.

audit.assertion: ADA (2026, 'Confirming the Diagnosis'): discordant tests -> repeat the abnormal test; two A1C >=6.5% confirm diabetes even if FPG <126 mg/dL
audit.reason: Section heading 'Confirming the Diagnosis' exists (h3 in the article). Verbatim: 'if an individual has discordant results from two different tests, then the test result that is above the diagnostic cut point should be repeated, with careful consideration of factors that may affect measured A1C or glucose levels. The diagnosis is made based on the confirmatory screening test. For example, if an individual meets the diagnostic criterion for A1C (two results >=6.5% [>=48 mmol/mol]) but not FPG (<126 mg/dL [<7.0 mmol/L]), that person should nevertheless be considered to have diabetes.' Exact match including both unit systems.

audit.assertion: ADA (2026, Table 2.2): prediabetes A1C band 5.7-6.4% (39-47 mmol/mol)
audit.reason: Table 2.2 ('Criteria defining prediabetes in nonpregnant individuals') verbatim: 'A1C 5.7-6.4% (39-47 mmol/mol)'. Corroborated twice more in the Prediabetes narrative of the same section.

audit.assertion: ADA (2026, Table 2.2): IFG = FPG 5.6-6.9 mmol/L (100-125 mg/dL) on FPG alone
audit.reason: Table 2.2 verbatim: 'FPG 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) to 125 mg/dL (6.9 mmol/L) (IFG)'. The table lists this as a standalone OR-criterion, so the 'on the FPG value alone' gloss is accurate. Both units present.

audit.assertion: ADA (2026, Table 2.2): IGT = 2-h PG 7.8-11.0 mmol/L (140-199 mg/dL) on 75-g OGTT
audit.reason: Table 2.2 verbatim: '2-h PG during 75-g OGTT 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) to 199 mg/dL (11.0 mmol/L) (IGT)'. Note the ADA table's upper bound is printed as 199 mg/dL = 11.0 mmol/L; the finding's SI range '7.8-11.0 mmol/L' matches the source exactly.

audit.assertion: ADA (2026, Rec 2.4, grade B): use plasma glucose criteria not A1C where the A1C-glycaemia relationship is altered
audit.reason: Recommendation 2.4 verbatim, with grade B: 'In conditions associated with an altered relationship between A1C and glycemia, such as some hemoglobin variants, pregnancy, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, HIV, and conditions that may alter red blood cell turnover, plasma glucose criteria should be used to diagnose diabetes. B'. Number and grade both correct. Two minor wording drifts, neither material: the ADA says 'some hemoglobin variants' (the finding says 'haemoglobinopathy'), and the finding silently drops pregnancy from the list. The African-setting relevance is the sourcing agent's own gloss, not a source claim.

audit.assertion: ADA consumer page (diabetes.org/about-diabetes/diagnosis): FPG normal <100 / prediabetes 100-125 / diabetes >=126 mg/dL; OGTT <140 / 140-199 / >=200; A1C <5.7 / 5.7-6.4 / >=6.5; each test usually repeated on a second day
audit.reason: URL fetched directly (HTTP 200, no redirect). Page carries all nine values verbatim in three result tables, plus the random PG '>=200 mg/dL'. Confirmatory clause verbatim: 'Each way usually needs to be repeated on a second day to diagnose diabetes... If your doctor determines that your blood glucose (blood sugar) level is very high, or if you have classic symptoms of high blood glucose in addition to one positive test, your doctor may not require a second test.' The 'undated' claim also checks out - no publication or review date appears on the page. (Worth noting for downstream use: this consumer page is mg/dL-only, so it cannot itself support any SI value.)

audit.assertion: WHO (Classification of diabetes mellitus, 2019, Section 1): four diagnostic tests - FPG >=7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL); 2-h PG >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL); HbA1c >=6.5% (48 mmol/mol); random glucose >=11.1 mmol/L with signs and symptoms
audit.reason: Downloaded the IRIS bitstream (the given URL 500s on HEAD but returns a valid 27-page-linearised, 40-page PDF on GET) and extracted text: 'Four diagnostic tests for diabetes are currently recommended... People with fasting plasma glucose values of >= 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dl), 2-h post-load plasma glucose >= 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dl) (5), HbA1c >= 6.5% (48 mmol/mol); or a random blood glucose >= 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dl) in the presence of signs and symptoms are considered to have diabetes (6).' Document identity verified (ISBN 978-92-4-151570-2, WHO 2019). Section heading '1. Diabetes: Definition and diagnosis' exists as cited. IRIS handle 10665/325182 independently resolved via the IRIS discover API to 'Classification of diabetes mellitus'.

audit.assertion: WHO (2019, Section 1): repeat testing on a subsequent day, preferably the same test, to confirm diabetes in asymptomatic people
audit.reason: Verbatim from the fetched PDF: 'If elevated values are detected in asymptomatic people, repeat testing, preferably with the same test, is recommended as soon as practicable on a subsequent day to confirm the diagnosis (6).' One wording caution: WHO says the repeat 'is recommended', while the finding says WHO 'requires' it - a small strengthening of modality. Substance (subsequent day, preferably same test, asymptomatic people) is exact.

audit.assertion: WHO/IDF 2006: IFG = FPG 6.1-6.9 mmol/L (110-125 mg/dL) AND, if measured, 2-h PG <7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL)
audit.reason: Downloaded the IRIS bitstream; PDF is 'Definition and diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and intermediate hyperglycemia: Report of a WHO/IDF Consultation', ISBN 92 4 159493 4, WHO 2006. Summary table verbatim: 'Impaired fasting Glucose (IFG) / Fasting plasma glucose 6.1 to 6.9mmol/l (110mg/dl to 125mg/dl) and (if measured) 2-h plasma glucose <7.8mmol/l (140mg/dl)'. IRIS handle 10665/43588 independently resolved to the correct title.

audit.assertion: WHO/IDF 2006: IGT = FPG <7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) AND 2-h PG >=7.8 and <11.1 mmol/L (140-200 mg/dL)
audit.reason: Summary table verbatim: 'Impaired Glucose tolerance (IGT) / Fasting plasma glucose <7.0mmol/l (126mg/dl) and 2-h plasma glucose >=7.8 and <11.1mmol/l (140mg/dl and 200mg/dl)'. Both the conjunction (AND) and the open upper bound are correctly rendered.

audit.assertion: WHO/IDF 2006, Recommendation 4: IFG fasting cut-point remains 6.1 mmol/L (110 mg/dL); the 5.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) alternative was considered and rejected
audit.reason: Recommendation 4 verbatim: 'The fasting plasma glucose cut-point for Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) should remain at 6.1mmol/l. This decision was based on concerns about the significant increase in IFG prevalence which would occur with lowering the cut-point... people identified by a lower cut-point eg 5.6mmol/l (100mg/dl) have a more favourable cardiovascular risk profile and only half the risk of developing diabetes compared with those above the current WHO cut-point.' Recommendation number, value and the rejected alternative all correct.

audit.assertion: WHO/IDF 2006, Recommendation 6: perform a 75-g OGTT when FPG is 6.1-6.9 mmol/L (110-125 mg/dL); FPG alone misses ~30% of undiagnosed diabetes
audit.reason: Recommendation 6 verbatim: 'fasting plasma glucose alone fails to diagnose approximately 30% of cases of previously undiagnosed diabetes' and 'An OGTT should be used in individuals with fasting plasma glucose 6.1-6.9mmol/l (110-125mg/dl) to determine glucose tolerance status.' Recommendation number correct.

audit.assertion: WHO 2011 HbA1c consultation: HbA1c >=6.5% is the diabetes cut point; a value <6.5% does not exclude diabetes diagnosed by glucose testing
audit.reason: Fetched the cited NCBI Bookshelf page (NBK304271, HTTP 200) - it is chapter 2 of 'Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus: Abbreviated Report of a WHO Consultation. Geneva: WHO; 2011'. Boxed Recommendation verbatim: 'An HbA1c of 6.5% is recommended as the cut point for diagnosing diabetes. A value of less than 6.5% does not exclude diabetes diagnosed using glucose tests.' Cross-checked against the original WHO PDF (WHO/NMH/CHP/CPM/11.1) pulled from IRIS, where the Executive Summary carries the same sentence. IRIS handle 10665/70523 independently resolved to the correct title.

audit.assertion: WHO 2011: no HbA1c prediabetes / intermediate-hyperglycaemia band; evidence judged insufficient
audit.reason: Verbatim in both the NCBI chapter and the original WHO PDF: 'The consultation concluded that there is insufficient evidence to make any formal recommendation on the interpretation of HbA1c levels below 6.5%.' The Executive Summary repeats it. Correctly characterised as a refusal to define a band rather than a band set to zero.

audit.assertion: WHO 2011, 'Recommendations for diagnostic practice' section: never diagnose on a single abnormal value; if only one of two concurrently measured tests is abnormal, repeat using the SAME method
audit.reason: The VALUE is fully correct and present at the cited URL, verbatim: 'The diagnosis of diabetes in an asymptomatic person should not be made on the basis of a single abnormal plasma glucose or HbA1c value. At least one additional HbA1c or plasma glucose test result with a value in the diabetic range is required... It is advisable to use one test or the other but if both glucose and HbA1c are measured and both are "diagnostic" then the diagnosis is made. If one only is abnormal then a further abnormal test result, using the same method, is required to confirm the diagnosis.' However the cited LOCATOR does not exist: there is no section titled 'Recommendations for diagnostic practice' anywhere in the report. I checked the NCBI chapter's heading tree (only 'Recommendation', 'Figure 1-2', 'Table 1-4') and grepped the original WHO PDF (WHO/NMH/CHP/CPM/11.1, 25 pp.) for 'practice' - the sole hit is 'clinical practice (14)' in unrelated prose. The passage sits in unheaded closing paragraphs of chapter 2. Body, year and numbers are right; the section name appears to have been invented, so the citation should be corrected rather than trusted as-is.
audit.correctedSource: WHO, Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus: Abbreviated Report of a WHO Consultation, 2011 (WHO/NMH/CHP/CPM/11.1; IRIS handle 10665/70523), Chapter 2 'Glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) for the diagnosis of diabetes', closing paragraphs - no section titled 'Recommendations for diagnostic practice' exists

audit.assertion: IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th Edition (2025), Figure 1.1: diabetes if ONE OR MORE of FPG >=7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL), 2-h PG >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL), random PG >=11.1 mmol/L with symptoms, HbA1c >=48 mmol/mol (6.5%)
audit.reason: Downloaded the exact URL (HTTP 200, 8.3 MB, 131-page PDF, InDesign creation date 2025-10-09) and extracted page 20. Figure caption verbatim: 'Figure 1.1 Diagnostic criteria for diabetes.' Panel verbatim: 'Diabetes / Should be diagnosed if ONE OR MORE of the following criteria are met' with '7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL)', '11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL)' for the 2-h OGTT value, '11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL)' for random plasma glucose 'in the presence of symptoms of hyperglycaemia', and '48 mmol/L [sic - printed unit] (equivalent to 6.5%)' for HbA1c. Running footer confirms 'IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th Edition - 2025 | diabetesatlas.org'. Caveat worth carrying forward: the Atlas's HbA1c panel prints the unit as 'mmol/L' rather than 'mmol/mol' - a typo in the source; the finding silently corrects it to mmol/mol, which is clinically right but is not literally what the page says.

audit.assertion: IDF Atlas 11th Ed. (2025), Figure 1.1: IFG = FPG 6.1-6.9 mmol/L (110-125 mg/dL) AND, if measured, 2-h PG <7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL)
audit.reason: Figure 1.1 verbatim: 'Impaired Fasting Glucose (IFG) / Should be diagnosed if THE FIRST OR BOTH of the following are met / 6.1-6.9 mmol/L (110-125 mg/dL) ... < 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL)' with the connector 'and if measured'. Values and units match, and the claimed identity with WHO 2006 holds (I compared against the WHO 2006 summary table fetched above). Minor: IDF's framing is 'THE FIRST OR BOTH', WHO's is 'and (if measured)' - logically equivalent, so the finding's 'identically to WHO 2006' is fair.

audit.assertion: IDF Atlas 11th Ed. (2025), Figure 1.1: IGT = FPG <7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) AND 2-h PG >=7.8 and <11.1 mmol/L (140-199 mg/dL)
audit.reason: Figure 1.1 verbatim: 'Impaired Glucose Tolerance / Should be diagnosed if BOTH of the following criteria are met / < 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) ... 7.8 and < 11.1 mmol/L (140-199 mg/dL)'. Conjunction, bounds and both unit systems all match the source and match WHO 2006.

audit.assertion: IDF Atlas 11th Ed. (2025): two abnormal tests required if asymptomatic; single random PG >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) with polyuria, polydipsia and unexplained weight loss suffices
audit.reason: Figure 1.1 note verbatim: 'In the absence of symptoms of hyperglycaemia, two abnormal tests are required for the diagnosis of diabetes.' Section 1.4 verbatim: 'For type 2 diabetes, if a single random plasma glucose concentration is >= 11.1 mmol/l in the presence of symptoms such as polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss, the diagnosis can be made without a second abnormal measurement.' Both cited locators exist. One nuance the finding drops: the Atlas scopes the single-random-glucose shortcut to type 2 diabetes specifically.

audit.assertion: IDF Atlas 11th Ed. (2025), Section 1.4: WHO supports HbA1c >=6.5% for diabetes diagnosis but not for intermediate hyperglycaemia, citing global availability of quality-assured assays
audit.reason: Section 1.4 verbatim: 'WHO supports the use of HbA1c >=6.5% for diabetes diagnosis but not for intermediate hyperglycaemia, partly on the grounds that quality-assured HbA1c measurement is not available on a global scale.' Exact match including the stated rationale. Independently consistent with the WHO 2011 report I fetched (finding 19).

audit.assertion: IDF Atlas 11th Ed. (2025), Section 1.4: IDF and WHO recommend the 75-g OGTT with measurement of both fasting and 2-hour plasma glucose to detect IGT, IFG and diabetes
audit.reason: Section 1.4 verbatim: 'Currently, IDF and WHO recommend the use of the 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) with measurement of both fasting and two-hour plasma glucose to detect IGT, IFG and diabetes.' Exact match. The source adds a qualifier the finding omits (that literature favours the one-hour 75-g OGTT as possibly more sensitive for intermediate hyperglycaemia) - not an error, but relevant context if this is used for decision support.

bundle.domain: Diabetes — (a) aetiological classification (WHO 2019 / ADA Standards of Care) and (b) conditions under which HbA1c is unreliable

findings.assertion: WHO 2019 defines the top-level aetiological types of diabetes as: type 1; type 2; hybrid forms (slowly evolving immune-mediated diabetes of adults; ketosis-prone type 2); other specific types; unclassified diabetes; and hyperglycaemia first detected during pregnancy.
findings.value: 6 top-level categories (not a numeric threshold). Sub-lists: 'Other specific types' = monogenic diabetes (defects of β-cell function / of insulin action), diseases of the exocrine pancreas, endocrine disorders, drug- or chemical-induced, infections, uncommon specific forms of immune-mediated diabetes, other genetic syndromes.
findings.standardVersion: Classification of diabetes mellitus, 2019 (ISBN 978-92-4-151570-2); Table 1 (p.4) and Table 2 (p.13)
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2019
findings.quote: Type 1 diabetes / Type 2 diabetes / Hybrid forms of diabetes / Slowly evolving immune-mediated diabetes of adults / Ketosis prone type 2 diabetes / Other specific types (see Tables) / Monogenic diabetes - Monogenic defects of β-cell function - Monogenic defects in insulin action / Diseases of the exocrine pancreas / Endocrine disorders / Drug- or chemical-induced / Infections / Uncommon specific forms of immune-mediated diabetes / Other genetic syndromes sometimes associated with diabetes / Unclassified diabetes / Hyperglyacemia first detected during pregnancy / Diabetes mellitus in pregnancy / Gestational diabetes mellitus
findings.notes: Retrieved the WHO PDF by curl (HTTP 200) after WebFetch returned 403, then decoded the embedded font ToUnicode CMaps to recover text. Note WHO 2019 explicitly removed type 1 and type 2 SUB-classes: 'this classification does not recognize subtypes of type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes and includes new types of diabetes ("hybrid types of diabetes" and "unclassified diabetes")'. 'Hyperglyacemia' typo is verbatim in the WHO table.

findings.assertion: WHO 2019 states its classification deliberately prioritises clinical parameters over laboratory aetiology precisely because antibody/C-peptide testing is not globally available.
findings.value: Not numeric — design principle. Prerequisites stated: 'internationally applicable and using easy and readily available clinical parameters and resources; being reliable and equitable; and feasible to implement'.
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019), §2.4 WHO classification of diabetes 2019
findings.quote: The only classification system which could currently go some way towards achieving this is one based on clinical parameters to identify diabetes subtypes. Some countries and clinical or research centres can supplement this approach with specific additional investigations, but these are not universally available and a classification system which relied on these measures would have limited global applicability.
findings.notes: This is the single most load-bearing statement for a low-resource deployment: WHO's classification is designed to be assignable WITHOUT antibodies or C-peptide.

findings.assertion: WHO 2019 gives an explicit 5-step clinical subtyping procedure for a newly diagnosed patient, in which diagnostic tests are the LAST step and explicitly conditional on availability.
findings.value: Steps: (1) Confirm diagnosis of diabetes in an asymptomatic individual; (2) Exclude secondary causes of diabetes; (3) Consider age at diagnosis, family history, physical findings especially obesity, presence of features of metabolic syndrome; (4) Note presence or absence of ketosis or ketoacidosis; (5) Perform diagnostic tests if available (β-cell autoantibodies, C-peptide).
findings.standardVersion: 2019, §3 Assigning diabetes type in clinical settings (p.24)
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019), §3
findings.quote: With the limited access in most countries throughout the world to laboratory investigations which might assist with the classification of an individual, the Expert group opted for providing guidance on identifying clinical subtypes, while recognizing the limitations of this approach. […] Steps in clinical subtyping an individual first diagnosed with diabetes: 1. Confirm diagnosis of diabetes in an asymptomatic individual 1. Exclude secondary causes of diabetes 1. Consider the following which may assist in differentiating subtypes: age at diagnosis, family history, physical findings, especially presence of obesity, presence of features of metabolic syndrome 1. Note presence or absence of ketosis or ketoacidosis 1. Perform diagnostic tests if available (β-cell autoantibodies, C-peptide)
findings.notes: The repeated '1.' numbering is a PDF list-rendering artefact in the source; the steps are sequential 1–5. Directly answers 'what does WHO say to do when those tests are UNAVAILABLE'.

findings.assertion: WHO 2019 states the decision to start insulin must be driven by clinical need, NOT by autoantibody results — the key safety instruction when antibody testing is unavailable.
findings.value: Not numeric — decision rule. Also: 'While measuring islet autoantibodies has limited value in clinical practice, in classical T1DM it may have a role when there is uncertainty as to whether a person has T1DM or T2DM.'
findings.standardVersion: 2019, §2.4.1 Type 1 diabetes (p.14)
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019), §2.4.1
findings.quote: However, the decision to use insulin should not rely on the presence of such markers, but rather on the clinical need.
findings.notes: This should be encoded as a hard guardrail in any decision-support logic: absence of (or inability to obtain) autoantibodies must never gate insulin initiation.

findings.assertion: WHO 2019 'unclassified diabetes' is a temporary holding category for use when the type cannot be determined, explicitly justified by the global unavailability of C-peptide and autoantibody testing.
findings.value: Not numeric — category definition. WHO Table 1 description: 'Used to describe diabetes that does not clearly fit into other categories. This category should be used temporarily when there is not a clear diagnostic category especially close to the time of diagnosis'.
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019), §2.4.5 Unclassified diabetes
findings.quote: While further investigation may help – including measurement of C-peptide and T1DM-associated autoantibodies, and the monitoring of the course of endogenous insulin secretion with time – these investigations are not widely available throughout the world. Until there is a definite diagnosis of the type of diabetes, a classification of "unclassified" should be used and attempts to classify the type of diabetes should continue to support appropriate management decisions.
findings.notes: Pairs with WHO's instruction that classification 'should be regularly reviewed' — i.e. the type field must be revisable over time, not write-once.

findings.assertion: WHO 2019 requires that an assigned diabetes type be re-reviewed over time rather than fixed at diagnosis.
findings.value: Not numeric — process requirement.
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019), §3
findings.quote: It may not be possible to definitively subtype an individual at the time of presentation and classification may only become possible over time when, for example, the longer term insulin requirement to manage glycaemia has been established. Consequently, the individual should be monitored and the appropriateness of the assigned diabetes classification should be regularly reviewed, especially in individuals without the classical features of diabetes subtypes.
findings.notes: Relevant to the append-only clinical record model — the type assignment needs a revision history, not overwriting.

findings.assertion: WHO 2019: 70–90% of people with type 1 diabetes have detectable β-cell autoantibodies at diagnosis (GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8, insulin), and C-peptide is low or undetectable at classical presentation.
findings.value: 70–90% autoantibody-positive at diagnosis; C-peptide 'low or undetectable' (no numeric cut-off given by WHO)
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019), §2.4.1 Type 1 diabetes
findings.quote: At the time of classical clinical presentation with T1DM, there is little or no insulin secretion as manifested by low or undetectable levels of C-peptide in blood or urine (32). […] Between 70% and 90% of people with T1DM at diagnosis have evidence of an immune-mediated process with β-cell autoantibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65), islet antigen-2 (IA-2), ZnT8 transporter or insulin, and associations with genes controlling immune responses (33).
findings.notes: Corollary: 10–30% of genuine T1DM is antibody-negative, so a negative antibody panel does not exclude T1DM. WHO gives NO numeric C-peptide cut-off; only ADA does (see separate finding).

findings.assertion: WHO 2019 renamed LADA to 'slowly evolving immune-mediated diabetes of adults' and places it in the new 'hybrid forms' category (not under type 1), with three commonly used criteria.
findings.value: Three criteria commonly used: (1) positivity for GAD autoantibodies; (2) age older than 35 years at diagnosis; (3) no need for insulin therapy in the first 6–12 months after diagnosis. Prevalence of GAD autoantibodies among clinically diagnosed T2DM: 5–14% (Europe, North America, Asia); of those antibody-positive, 90% have GAD and 18–24% have IA-2 or ZnT8.
findings.standardVersion: 2019, §2.4.3 Hybrid forms of diabetes (pp.15–16)
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019), §2.4.3
findings.quote: There are no universally agreed criteria for this subtype of diabetes, but three criteria are often used: positivity for GAD autoantibodies, age older than 35 years at diagnosis, and no need for insulin therapy in the first 6–12 months after diagnosis. Among individuals with clinically diagnosed T2DM, the prevalence of autoantibodies to GAD differs between regions and ethnic groups, with 5–14% in Europe, North America, and Asia having autoantibodies
findings.notes: WHO itself flags 'There are no universally agreed criteria'. WHO Table 1 distinguishing features vs T1DM: 'more often has features of the metabolic syndrome, a single GAD autoantibody and retains greater β-cell function'. Also: 'In some regions of the world this form of diabetes is more common than classic, rapid-onset T1DM.' Conflicts with ADA — see conflicts.

findings.assertion: WHO 2019 recognises ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes as a distinct hybrid form: presents with ketoacidosis and severe insulin deficiency but subsequently does not require insulin; non-immune, no genetic markers.
findings.value: ~90% have further ketotic episodes within 10 years. WHO Table 1 description: 'Presents with ketosis and insulin deficiency but later does not require insulin; common episodes of ketosis, not immune-mediated'.
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019), §2.4.3 Ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes
findings.quote: Typically, those affected present with ketosis and evidence of severe insulin deficiency but later go into remission and do not require insulin treatment. Reports suggest that further ketotic episodes occur in 90% of these people within 10 years. […] Subsequently similar phenotypes were described in populations in sub-Saharan African (68). […] Ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes is observed in all populations, but it is least common in populations of European origin. […] No genetic markers or evidence of auto-immunity have been identified.
findings.notes: Directly relevant to a Ugandan/sub-Saharan cohort: WHO notes the sub-Saharan African phenotype and that in low-income countries it has been observed in LEAN individuals (unlike the obese-male pattern in high-income countries). This is a common DKA-presentation confounder for type-assignment logic.

findings.assertion: WHO 2019 lists the monogenic (MODY/neonatal) genes under 'other specific types', with gene-then-syndrome naming.
findings.value: Monogenic defects of β-cell function: GCK MODY, HNF1A MODY, HNF4A MODY, HNF1B RCAD, mtDNA 3243 MIDD, KCNJ11 PNDM, KCNJ11 DEND, 6q24 TNDM, ABCC8 MODY, INS PNDM, WFS1 Wolfram syndrome, FOXP3 IPEX syndrome, EIF2AK3 Wolcott-Rallison syndrome. Monogenic defects in insulin action: INSR Type A insulin resistance, INSR Leprechaunism, INSR Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome, LMNA FPLD, PPARG FPLD, AGPAT2 CGL, BSCL2 CGL.
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019), Table 3: Other specific types of diabetes
findings.quote: Monogenic defects of β-cell function (mutated gene followed by clinical syndrome) […] GCK MODY / HNF1A MODY / HNF4A MODY / HNF1B RCAD / mtDNA 3243 MIDD / KCNJ11 PNDM / KCNJ11 DEND / 6q24 TNDM / ABCC8 MODY / INS PNDM / WFS1 Wolfram syndrome / FOXP3 IPEX syndrome / EIF2AK3 Wolcott-Rallison syndrome … Abbreviations: MODY = maturity-onset diabetes of the young; RCAD = renal cysts and diabetes; MIDD = maternally inherited diabetes and deafness; PNDM = permanent neonatal diabetes; TNDM = transient neonatal diabetes; DEND = developmental delay epilepsy and neonatal diabetes.
findings.notes: WHO footnotes Table 3: '*This is a list of the most common types in each category but is not exhaustive'. WHO also cites the Exeter clinical prediction models at www.diabetesgenes.org for discriminating monogenic from T1DM/T2DM in those diagnosed aged 1–35.

findings.assertion: WHO 2019 places fibrocalculous pancreatopathy under 'Diseases of the exocrine pancreas' — it does NOT restore a malnutrition-related diabetes category.
findings.value: Diseases of the exocrine pancreas listed: Fibrocalculous pancreatopathy, Pancreatitis, Trauma/pancreatectomy, Neoplasia, Cystic fibrosis, Haemochromatosis, Others. Epidemiology quoted: diabetes following pancreatic disease incidence 2.59 per 100,000 person-years vs T1DM 1.64 per 100,000 person-years; 87.8% misclassified by clinicians as T2DM, only 2.7% as diabetes of the exocrine pancreas; insulin use within 5 years 4.1% (T2DM), 20.9% (post-acute pancreatitis), 45.8% (post-chronic pancreatic disease).
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019), §2.4.4 Diseases of the exocrine pancreas
findings.quote: Fibrocalculous pancreatopathy may be accompanied by abdominal pain and pancreatic calcification on X-ray or ultrasound and ductal dilatation (101). Pancreatic fibrosis and calcified stones in the exocrine ducts are found at autopsy. Diabetes following pancreatic disease (incidence 2.59 per 100 000 person-years) has been reported to be more common than T1DM (incidence 1.64 per 100 000 person-years). The majority of diabetes following pancreatic disease is classified by clinicians as T2DM (87.8%) and uncommonly as diabetes of the exocrine pancreas (2.7%).
findings.notes: The 87.8%/2.7% misclassification figure is the strongest argument for an explicit 'diseases of the exocrine pancreas' option in the UI rather than defaulting to T2DM. The near-50% insulin requirement after chronic pancreatic disease is clinically decisive.

findings.assertion: WHO withdrew 'malnutrition-related diabetes mellitus' (MRDM) in 1999 for lack of supporting evidence, and the 2019 classification does not reinstate it.
findings.value: MRDM introduced in the WHO 1985 report; dropped in the WHO 1999 classification; absent from WHO 2019.
findings.standardVersion: 2019, §2.2 Previous WHO classifications of diabetes (pp.9–10)
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019), §2.2
findings.quote: The 1985 report omitted the terms "type 1" and "type 2", but retained the classes IDDM and NIDDM, and introduced a class of malnutrition-related diabetes mellitus (MRDM) (22). […] In 1999, WHO reintroduced the terms type 1 and type 2 diabetes and dropped MRDM because of lack of evidence to support its existence
findings.notes: This is the direct counterpoint to the IDF 2025 'type 5 diabetes' recognition — see conflicts. I verified by grep that the string 'malnutrition' appears in WHO 2019 only in this historical passage and in a T2DM risk-factor sentence ('fetal malnutrition').

findings.assertion: WHO 2019 gives an age-at-diagnosis heuristic for subtyping when laboratory tests are unavailable, and lists the clinical features favouring T2DM over T1DM.
findings.value: Age <6 months: monogenic neonatal diabetes (T1DM extremely rare); 6 months–<10 years: T1DM most common; 10–<25 years: T1DM, T2DM, monogenic (monogenic peak 15–20 years); 25–50 years: T2DM, slowly evolving immune-mediated, T1DM; >50 years: same as 25–50 but T1DM less common. Highest-misclassification-risk group: young adults aged 20–40 years. T1DM accounts for ~5% of diabetes diagnosed between ages 31 and 60. Features favouring T2DM: overweight or obesity; age above 10 years; strong family history of T2DM; acanthosis nigricans; undetectable islet autoantibodies (if measured); elevated or normal C-peptide (if assessed). Features favouring T1DM in adults: ketosis, rapid weight loss, age of onset below 50 years, BMI below 25 kg/m2, or personal/family history of autoimmune disease.
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019), §3.1 Age at diagnosis as a guide to subtyping diabetes
findings.quote: Features favouring a diagnosis of T2DM rather than T1DM at diagnosis include: Overweight or obesity / Age above 10 years / Strong family history of T2DM / Acanthosis nigricans / Undetectable islet autoantibodies (if measured) / Elevated or normal C-peptide (if assessed) […] T1DM should be especially considered on clinical grounds in adults presenting with one or more of the following: ketosis, rapid weight loss, age of onset below 50 years, BMI below 25kg/m2, or personal and/or family history of autoimmune disease (127).
findings.notes: Note the parenthetical '(if measured)' / '(if assessed)' — WHO frames antibodies and C-peptide as optional adjuncts to a clinical rule, not required inputs. The 20–40y window is flagged by WHO as the highest-heterogeneity, highest-misclassification group.

findings.assertion: WHO 2019 diagnostic thresholds for diabetes (unchanged from prior WHO criteria).
findings.value: Fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L (≥126 mg/dL); OR 2-h post-load plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (≥200 mg/dL) after 75 g OGTT; OR HbA1c ≥6.5% (≥48 mmol/mol); OR random blood glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (≥200 mg/dL) in the presence of signs and symptoms.
findings.standardVersion: 2019, §1 Diabetes: Definition and diagnosis (p.6); criteria carried from WHO 2006/2011
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019), §1
findings.quote: People with fasting plasma glucose values of ≥ 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dl), 2-h post-load plasma glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dl) (5), HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (48 mmol/mol); or a random blood glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dl) in the presence of signs and symptoms are considered to have diabetes (6). If elevated values are detected in asymptomatic people, repeat testing, preferably with the same test, is recommended as soon as practicable on a subsequent day to confirm the diagnosis (6).
findings.notes: Both units are given verbatim in the WHO source. Identical thresholds to ADA (see ADA Table 2.1 finding).

findings.assertion: WHO 2019 gestational diabetes diagnostic criteria (2013 WHO criteria) — given in SI units only in the source.
findings.value: GDM: fasting plasma glucose 5.1–6.9 mmol/L (92–125 mg/dL) OR 1-hour post-load plasma glucose ≥10.0 mmol/L (≥180 mg/dL) OR 2-hour post-load plasma glucose 8.5–11.0 mmol/L (153–198 mg/dL). 'Diabetes mellitus in pregnancy' is diagnosed by the same criteria as in non-pregnant persons.
findings.standardVersion: 2019 Table 1 (p.4), restating WHO 2013 criteria; §2.4.6 (p.23)
findings.sourceTitle: Classification of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2019), Table 1 and §2.4.6
findings.quote: Diagnostic criteria for gestational diabetes: fasting plasma glucose 5.1–6.9 mmol/L or 1-hour post-load plasma glucose ≥ 10.0 mmol/L or 2-hour post-load plasma glucose 8.5–11.0 mmol/L
findings.notes: IMPORTANT: the mg/dL values above are MY arithmetic conversion (×18.0), not present in the WHO document, which states SI only. WHO also states: 'This classification of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy has not been revisited for this document.'

findings.assertion: ADA 2026 classifies diabetes into four conventional clinical categories — it has no 'hybrid forms' or 'unclassified' category.
findings.value: (1) Type 1 diabetes (autoimmune β-cell destruction, usually leading to absolute insulin deficiency, including LADA); (2) Type 2 diabetes (nonautoimmune progressive loss of adequate β-cell insulin secretion, frequently on a background of insulin resistance); (3) Specific types of diabetes due to other causes (monogenic diabetes syndromes, diseases of the exocrine pancreas, drug- or chemical-induced); (4) Gestational diabetes mellitus.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S27–S49; doi 10.2337/dc26-S002)
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Diabetes is classified conventionally into several clinical categories, although these are being reconsidered based on genetic, metabolomic, and other characteristics and pathophysiology (1): 1. Type 1 diabetes (due to autoimmune β-cell destruction, usually leading to absolute insulin deficiency, including latent autoimmune diabetes in adults) 2. Type 2 diabetes (due to a nonautoimmune progressive loss of adequate β-cell insulin secretion, frequently on the background of insulin resistance) 3. Specific types of diabetes due to other causes, e.g., monogenic diabetes syndromes, diseases of the exocrine pancreas, and drug- or chemical-induced diabetes 4. Gestational diabetes mellitus
findings.notes: diabetesjournals.org returned 403; retrieved the identical article via its PubMed Central deposit (PMC12690183, PMID 41358893, confirmed via Europe PMC DOI lookup for 10.2337/dc26-S002). Structural mismatch with WHO — see conflicts.

findings.assertion: ADA 2026 states misdiagnosis occurs in up to 40% of adults with new type 1 diabetes, and gives the AABBCC heuristic plus the clinical features most useful for identifying type 1.
findings.value: Misdiagnosis in up to 40% of adults with new type 1 diabetes. Features most useful for type 1: younger age at diagnosis (<35 years), lower BMI (<25 kg/m2), unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, and plasma glucose >360 mg/dL (>20 mmol/L) at presentation. AABBCC = Age, Autoimmunity, Body habitus, Background, Control, Comorbidities.
