findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: The features most useful in determination of type 1 diabetes include younger age at diagnosis (<35 years), lower BMI (<25 kg/m2), unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, and plasma glucose >360 mg/dL (>20 mmol/L) at presentation (32) (Fig. 2.1). […] It is important for health care professionals to realize that classification of diabetes type is not always straightforward at presentation and that misdiagnosis can occur in up to 40% of adults with new type 1 diabetes […] Although not prospectively validated, the AABBCC approach is a useful tool to help distinguish type 1 from type 2 diabetes
findings.notes: ADA itself labels AABBCC as 'not prospectively validated'. The >360 mg/dL (>20 mmol/L) presentation glucose is a usable, test-free discriminator.

findings.assertion: ADA 2026 specifies GAD as the primary autoantibody to measure, with IA-2 and/or ZnT8 as second-line where available, and warns that 5–10% of people with type 1 diabetes are antibody-negative.
findings.value: GAD first; if negative, IA-2 and/or ZnT8 'where these tests are available'; insulin autoantibodies useful only in individuals not treated with insulin. In those diagnosed <35 years with no clinical features of type 2 or monogenic diabetes, a negative antibody result does not change the diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, since 5–10% of people with type 1 diabetes do not have antibodies.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2, Figure 2.1 legend (adapted from Holt et al.)
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Fig. 2.1
findings.quote: Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) should be the primary antibody measured and, if negative, should be followed by islet tyrosine phosphatase 2 (IA-2) and/or zinc transporter 8 (ZnT8) where these tests are available. In individuals who have not been treated with insulin, antibodies against insulin may also be useful. In those diagnosed at <35 years of age who have no clinical features of type 2 diabetes or monogenic diabetes, a negative result does not change the diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, since 5–10% of people with type 1 diabetes do not have antibodies.
findings.notes: CRITICAL EXTERNAL-VALIDITY CAVEAT stated by ADA in the same figure legend: the flowchart is 'based on data from White European populations'. Its transfer to a Ugandan population is NOT established by this source.

findings.assertion: ADA 2026 gives explicit numeric C-peptide interpretation thresholds for classifying diabetes, plus timing rules.
findings.value: C-peptide ≥600 pmol/L (≥1.8 ng/mL): circumstances of testing do not matter (argues against severe insulin deficiency). C-peptide <600 pmol/L (<1.8 ng/mL) with concurrent glucose <4 mmol/L (<70 mg/dL) or possible fasting: consider repeating. Very low levels e.g. <80 pmol/L (<0.24 ng/mL): do not need repeating. C-peptide 200–600 pmol/L (0.6–1.8 ng/mL): usually consistent with type 1 diabetes or MODY, but may occur in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, particularly with normal/low BMI or long duration. Timing: do not test C-peptide within 2 weeks of a hyperglycemic emergency; a random sample with concurrent glucose within 5 h of eating can replace a formal stimulation test.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2, Figure 2.1 legend footnotes 4 and 9 (identical text in the 2025 edition)
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Fig. 2.1
findings.quote: A C-peptide test is only indicated in people receiving insulin treatment. A random sample (with concurrent glucose) within 5 h of eating can replace a formal C-peptide stimulation test in the context of classification. If the result is ≥600 pmol/L (≥1.8 ng/mL), the circumstances of testing do not matter. If the result is <600 pmol/L (<1.8 ng/mL) and the concurrent glucose is <4 mmol/L (<70 mg/dL) or the person may have been fasting, consider repeating the test. Results showing very low levels (e.g., <80 pmol/L [<0.24 ng/mL]) do not need to be repeated. Where a person is insulin treated, C-peptide must be measured prior to insulin discontinuation to exclude severe insulin deficiency. Do not test C-peptide within 2 weeks of a hyperglycemic emergency.
findings.notes: These are the ONLY numeric C-peptide cut-offs found in any fetched primary source — WHO 2019 gives none. Both units are given verbatim in the source. Same external-validity caveat (White European derivation) applies.

findings.assertion: ADA 2026 recommends standardized islet autoantibody testing for CLASSIFICATION in adults whose phenotype overlaps type 1 diabetes.
findings.value: Recommendation 2.10, evidence grade E. Phenotypic triggers: younger age at diagnosis, unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, or short time to insulin treatment.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2, Rec. 2.10
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 2.10 Standardized islet autoantibody tests are recommended for classification of diabetes in adults who have phenotypic risk factors that overlap with those for type 1 diabetes (e.g., younger age at diagnosis, unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, or short time to insulin treatment). E
findings.notes: Grade E = expert consensus/clinical experience, ADA's weakest grade. In the 2025 edition this was numbered 2.9 with identical wording. ADA also warns (2026): 'relying on nonvalidated autoantibody tests for the diagnosis of LADA may lead to misclassification of some individuals with type 2 diabetes' — assay standardisation matters.

findings.assertion: ADA 2026 screening (not classification) autoantibody panel for presymptomatic type 1 diabetes.
findings.value: Recommendation 2.6 (grade B): test autoantibodies against insulin (IA), glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), islet antigen 2 (IA-2), or zinc transporter 8 (ZnT8).
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2, Rec. 2.6
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 2.6 Screen for presymptomatic type 1 diabetes by testing autoantibodies against insulin (IA), glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), islet antigen 2 (IA-2), or zinc transporter 8 (ZnT8). B
findings.notes: Distinguish this (presymptomatic screening in at-risk relatives) from Rec. 2.10 (classification of established diabetes). Conflating the two in decision-support would generate inappropriate test recommendations.

findings.assertion: ADA 2026 uses 'pancreatic diabetes' as the preferred umbrella term for diabetes of the exocrine pancreas (type 3c) and notes it is commonly misdiagnosed as type 2.
findings.value: Aetiologies listed: pancreatitis (acute and chronic), trauma or pancreatectomy, neoplasia, cystic fibrosis, hemochromatosis, fibrocalculous pancreatopathy, rare genetic disorders, idiopathic forms. Screening: Rec. 2.23 — screen within 3–6 months following acute pancreatitis and annually thereafter; annually for chronic pancreatitis.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2, 'Pancreatic Diabetes or Diabetes in the Context of Disease of the Exocrine Pancreas'; Rec. 2.23
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Pancreatic diabetes (also termed pancreatogenic diabetes or type 3c diabetes) includes both structural (e.g., destruction or removal of normal pancreatic tissue) and functional loss of insulin secretion in the context of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and is commonly misdiagnosed as type 2 diabetes. The diverse set of etiologies includes pancreatitis (acute and chronic pancreatic inflammation and associated fibrosis leading to loss of functional exocrine and endocrine pancreatic function), trauma or pancreatectomy, neoplasia, cystic fibrosis (addressed later in this section), hemochromatosis, fibrocalculous pancreatopathy, rare genetic disorders, and idiopathic forms (2); as such, pancreatic diabetes is the preferred umbrella term (136).
findings.notes: ADA and WHO agree that fibrocalculous pancreatopathy belongs here, not in a malnutrition category.

findings.assertion: ADA 2026 monogenic diabetes genetic-testing triggers.
findings.value: Rec. 2.29a (grade A): regardless of current age, all people diagnosed with diabetes in the first 6 months of life should have genetic testing for neonatal diabetes. Rec. 2.29b (grade A): children and young adults without typical type 1 or type 2 characteristics and with a family history of diabetes in successive generations (suggestive of autosomal-dominant inheritance) should have genetic testing for MODY.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2, Recs. 2.29a/2.29b
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 2.29a Regardless of current age, all people diagnosed with diabetes in the first 6 months of life should have genetic testing for neonatal diabetes. A  2.29b Children and young adults who do not have typical characteristics of type 1 or type 2 diabetes and have a family history of diabetes in successive generations (suggestive of an autosomal-dominant pattern of inheritance) should have genetic testing for maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY). A
findings.notes: Both were graded B in the 2025 edition (as Recs. 2.24a/2.24b) and upgraded to A in 2026. ADA 2026 flags in the Fig. 2.1 legend that monogenic diabetes is suggested by A1C <58 mmol/mol (<7.5%) at diagnosis, one parent with diabetes, and a monogenic prediction model probability >5% (diabetesgenes.org ModyCalculator).

findings.assertion: ADA 2026 diagnostic criteria for diabetes, with both units.
findings.value: A1C ≥6.5% (≥48 mmol/mol), NGSP-certified/DCCT-standardized; OR FPG ≥126 mg/dL (≥7.0 mmol/L) after ≥8 h no caloric intake; OR 2-h PG ≥200 mg/dL (≥11.1 mmol/L) during a 75 g OGTT; OR in an individual with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis, a random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL (≥11.1 mmol/L).
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2, Table 2.1
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Table 2.1
findings.quote: A1C ≥6.5% (≥48 mmol/mol). The test should be performed in a laboratory using a method that is NGSP certified and standardized to the DCCT assay.* OR FPG ≥126 mg/dL (≥7.0 mmol/L). Fasting is defined as no caloric intake for at least 8 h.* OR 2-h PG ≥200 mg/dL (≥11.1 mmol/L) during OGTT. […] OR In an individual with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis, a random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL (≥11.1 mmol/L). […] *In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia, diagnosis requires two abnormal results from different tests, which may be obtained at the same time (e.g., A1C and FPG), or the same test at two different time points.
findings.notes: Identical thresholds to WHO 2019. Note the confirmation rule differs subtly: ADA permits two different tests drawn at the same time; WHO 2011 says 'It is advisable to use one test or the other but if both glucose and HbA1c are measured and both are "diagnostic" then the diagnosis is made.'

findings.assertion: IDF recognised malnutrition-related diabetes as 'type 5 diabetes' in 2025, describing a lean, non-autoimmune, insulin-deficient phenotype — a category WHO 2019 does not have.
findings.value: BMI typically below 19 kg/m². Autoantibodies 'usually negative'. Non-autoimmune, non-insulin-resistant; insulin deficiency from underdeveloped pancreatic tissue due to chronic undernutrition. Typically appears in adolescents and young adults. Endorsed at the IDF World Diabetes Congress 2025, Bangkok. No formal diagnostic criteria yet exist.
findings.standardVersion: IDF web position page on type 5 diabetes, accessed 5 September 2026 (endorsement dated 2025)
findings.sourceTitle: Type 5 diabetes (MRDM): Causes, symptoms & treatment — International Diabetes Federation
findings.quote: Previously, the classification of type 5 diabetes was malnutrition-related diabetes mellitus (MRDM). In 2025, the International Diabetes Federation (IDF) endorsed the new classification at the IDF World Diabetes Congress 2025 in Bangkok, Thailand. The condition is now acknowledged as the fifth classification of diabetes, alongside types 1, 2, 3c and gestational diabetes. […] people with type 5 diabetes often have a body mass index (BMI) below 19 kg/m² and do not show signs of autoimmune β-cell destruction, which distinguishes it from type 1 diabetes. […] Until recently, there were no standard diagnostic criteria for type 5 diabetes.
findings.notes: HIGH RELEVANCE to a Ugandan deployment (IDF names sub-Saharan Africa explicitly) but LOW EVIDENCE MATURITY: IDF's own page says diagnostic criteria are still being drafted by a Working Group (chaired by Dr Meredith Hawkins, co-chaired by Dr Nihal Thomas). This is a web page, not a peer-reviewed guideline with a version number. Treat as emerging, not actionable classification.

findings.assertion: ADA 2026 Recommendation 2.4: when the A1C–glycaemia relationship is altered, plasma glucose criteria must be used to diagnose diabetes instead of A1C.
findings.value: Named conditions (2026 wording): some hemoglobin variants, pregnancy, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, HIV, and conditions that may alter red blood cell turnover. Action: use plasma glucose criteria (FPG ≥126 mg/dL / ≥7.0 mmol/L; 2-h PG ≥200 mg/dL / ≥11.1 mmol/L; or random ≥200 mg/dL / ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms). Evidence grade B.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2, Rec. 2.4
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 2.4 In conditions associated with an altered relationship between A1C and glycemia, such as some hemoglobin variants, pregnancy, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, HIV, and conditions that may alter red blood cell turnover, plasma glucose criteria should be used to diagnose diabetes. B
findings.notes: WORDING CHANGED between editions — the 2025 edition enumerated the haematological conditions explicitly. See the paired 2025 finding and the conflicts entry; for a decision-support rule the 2025 enumeration is the more implementable list.

findings.assertion: ADA 2025 Recommendation 2.4 (prior edition) enumerated the specific conditions requiring plasma glucose instead of A1C — a more explicit list than the 2026 wording.
findings.value: Named conditions (2025 wording): some hemoglobin variants; pregnancy (second and third trimesters and the postpartum period); glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; HIV; hemodialysis; recent blood loss or transfusion; hemolysis; erythropoietin therapy. Evidence grade B.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025, Section 2, Rec. 2.4 (Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl. 1):S27–S49)
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025
findings.quote: 2.4 In conditions associated with an altered relationship between A1C and glycemia, such as some hemoglobin variants, pregnancy (second and third trimesters and the postpartum period), glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, HIV, hemodialysis, recent blood loss or transfusion, hemolysis, or erythropoietin therapy, plasma glucose criteria should be used to diagnose diabetes. B
findings.notes: I verified this by grep against the retrieved PMC HTML rather than relying on a summariser. The 2026 compression to 'conditions that may alter red blood cell turnover' appears to be an editorial generalisation, not a withdrawal — Table 2.3 in BOTH editions still names transfusion, hemolysis, blood loss and dialysis. CSO should decide which list to encode.

findings.assertion: ADA (2025 and 2026) narrative: A1C may not be a suitable diagnostic test in anaemia, erythropoietin treatment, haemodialysis, or HIV treatment; thalassaemia and folate deficiency affect A1C; sickle cell trait requires a non-interfering assay.
findings.value: A1C reflects glucose bound to haemoglobin over the erythrocyte lifespan (~120 days). Sickle cell trait (variant with normal RBC turnover): use an A1C assay without interference from haemoglobin variants; assay interference list at ngsp.org/interf.asp. G6PD G202A (X-linked, carried by 11% of Black individuals in the U.S.): decreases A1C by about 0.8% in homozygous men and 0.7% in homozygous women.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2 (near-identical text in the 2025 edition)
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: A1C is an indirect measure of glucose exposure, and factors that affect hemoglobin concentrations or erythrocyte turnover can affect A1C (e.g., thalassemia or folate deficiency) (Table 2.3). A1C may not be a suitable diagnostic test in people with anemia, people treated with erythropoietin, or people undergoing hemodialysis or HIV treatment (1,17). Some A1C assays can be affected by hemoglobin variants. For instance, an A1C assay without interference from hemoglobin variants should be used in individuals with sickle cell trait. An updated list of A1C assays with interferences is available at ngsp.org/interf.asp. Another genetic variant, X-linked glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase G202A, carried by 11% of Black individuals in the U.S., is associated with a decrease in A1C of about 0.8% in homozygous men and 0.7% in homozygous women compared with levels in individuals without the variant (18).
findings.notes: The G6PD −0.8%/−0.7% figures are the only QUANTIFIED A1C bias I could confirm in any fetched guideline. The 2025 edition says '11% of African American individuals in the U.S.'; 2026 changed the wording to 'Black individuals'. Highly relevant to a Ugandan population given G6PD deficiency prevalence, though the 11% figure is a US estimate and does not transfer.

findings.assertion: ADA Table 2.3 lists the individual factors and assay interferences that affect A1C (as distinct from glucose testing).
findings.value: Other individual factors that can affect A1C results: altered erythrocyte turnover (e.g., anemia, iron status, splenectomy, blood loss, transfusion, hemolysis, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, erythropoietin), HIV, cirrhosis, kidney failure, dialysis, pregnancy. A1C test interferences (assay-dependent): hemoglobin variants, severe hypertriglyceridemia, severe hyperbilirubinemia. A1C is unaffected by recent food intake, stress, illness, activity.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2, Table 2.3 (data from Selvin)
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Table 2.3
findings.quote: Altered erythrocyte turnover (e.g., anemia, iron status, splenectomy, blood loss, transfusion, hemolysis, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, erythropoietin), HIV, cirrhosis, kidney failure, dialysis, pregnancy | […] Test interferences | […] Depends on specific assay: hemoglobin variants, severe hypertriglyceridemia, severe hyperbilirubinemia
findings.notes: 2025 edition said 'renal failure'; 2026 says 'kidney failure' — terminology only. Note transfusion, hemolysis and dialysis remain in the 2026 table even though Rec. 2.4's 2026 wording no longer names them individually.

findings.assertion: ADA: people with HIV should be screened for diabetes with FPG — not A1C — around antiretroviral therapy changes.
findings.value: Recommendation 2.17 (2026; numbered 2.16 in 2025), grade E: FPG before starting ART, at the time of switching ART, and 3–6 months after starting or switching ART; if initial screening is normal, FPG annually.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2, Rec. 2.17
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 2.17 People with HIV should be screened for diabetes and prediabetes with an FPG test before starting antiretroviral therapy, at the time of switching antiretroviral therapy, and 3–6 months after starting or switching antiretroviral therapy. If initial screening results are normal, FPG should be checked annually. E
findings.notes: Note the recommendation specifies FPG explicitly, consistent with Rec. 2.4 excluding A1C in HIV. Directly applicable to a Ugandan IM service with high HIV/ART prevalence. WHO 2011 Annex 1 independently lists antiretrovirals as shortening erythrocyte life span and thereby DECREASING HbA1c.

findings.assertion: ADA: A1C is not reliable for screening for gestational diabetes or pre-existing diabetes from 15 weeks of gestation onward.
findings.value: A1C not reliable for GDM screening or for pre-existing diabetes at ≥15 weeks of gestation. Directional effects in pregnancy (2026 wording): increased red blood cell turnover decreases A1C; decreased turnover increases A1C; haemoglobinopathies and iron deficiency anaemia — the latter increases A1C.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025, Section 2 (GDM subsection); directional statement re-worded in the 2026 edition
findings.sourceTitle: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025
findings.quote: A1C is not reliable for screening for GDM or for preexisting diabetes at 15 weeks of gestation or later in part from the higher red blood cell turnover in pregnancy but also from the unknown diabetes status prior to pregnancy, which could help distinguish new-onset diabetes from preexisting diabetes.
findings.notes: The explicit '15 weeks' sentence is verified in the 2025 edition; I could not locate that exact sentence in the 2026 Section 2 text I retrieved (it may have moved to Section 15, which I did not fetch). The 2026 edition does state verbatim: 'Disadvantages include inaccuracies in the presence of conditions such as increased or decreased red blood cell turnover (usually decreases and increases A1C, respectively), hemoglobinopathies, and iron deficiency anemia (increases A1C)'.

findings.assertion: WHO 2011 conditions its recommendation to use HbA1c for diagnosis on the absence of conditions that preclude accurate measurement, and names haemoglobinopathies, certain anaemias and malaria as the most important factors worldwide.
findings.value: HbA1c cut point for diagnosing diabetes: 6.5% (48 mmol/mol). A value <6.5% does not exclude diabetes diagnosed using glucose tests. Most common important factors worldwide: haemoglobinopathies (assay-dependent), certain anaemias, and disorders associated with accelerated red cell turnover such as malaria. GRADE: quality of evidence moderate; strength of recommendation conditional.
findings.standardVersion: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus: Abbreviated Report of a WHO Consultation, 2011 (WHO/NMH/CHP/CPM/11.1)
findings.sourceTitle: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus — Abbreviated Report of a WHO Consultation (2011)
findings.quote: HbA1c can be used as a diagnostic test for diabetes providing that stringent quality assurance tests are in place and assays are standardised to criteria aligned to the international reference values, and there are no conditions present which preclude its accurate measurement. An HbA1c of 6.5% is recommended as the cut point for diagnosing diabetes. A value of less than 6.5% does not exclude diabetes diagnosed using glucose tests. […] However, HbA1c may be affected by a variety of genetic, haematologic and illness-related factors (Annex 1) (24). The most common important factors worldwide affecting HbA1c levels are haemoglobinopathies (depending on the assay employed), certain anaemias, and disorders associated with accelerated red cell turnover such as malaria (16; 25).
findings.notes: MALARIA is named only here, and only qualitatively — no magnitude, no threshold, and no stated alternative test specific to malaria. This is the single best guideline-level citation for malaria affecting HbA1c, and it is 2011. WHO 2019 carries NO HbA1c-unreliability list (I confirmed by grep: only 4 mentions of HbA1c, all diagnostic-threshold context), so WHO's position on this rests entirely on the 2011 document.

findings.assertion: WHO 2011 Annex 1 tabulates factors influencing HbA1c by mechanism WITH DIRECTION of effect — the most complete directional list found in any primary guideline.
findings.value: 1. Erythropoiesis — INCREASED HbA1c: iron deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, decreased erythropoiesis. DECREASED HbA1c: administration of erythropoietin, iron, vitamin B12; reticulocytosis; chronic liver disease. 2. Altered haemoglobin — haemoglobinopathies, HbF, methaemoglobin may INCREASE OR DECREASE HbA1c. 3. Glycation — INCREASED: alcoholism, chronic renal failure, decreased intra-erythrocyte pH. DECREASED: aspirin, vitamin C and E, certain haemoglobinopathies, increased intra-erythrocyte pH. VARIABLE: genetic determinants. 4. Erythrocyte destruction — INCREASED (increased erythrocyte life span): splenectomy. DECREASED (decreased erythrocyte life span): haemoglobinopathies, splenomegaly, rheumatoid arthritis, or drugs such as antiretrovirals, ribavirin and dapsone. 5. Assays — INCREASED: hyperbilirubinaemia, carbamylated haemoglobin, alcoholism, large doses of aspirin, chronic opiate use. VARIABLE: haemoglobinopathies. DECREASED: hypertriglyceridaemia.
findings.standardVersion: WHO 2011 HbA1c consultation report, Annex 1 (adapted from Gallagher et al.)
findings.sourceTitle: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus (WHO 2011), Annex 1
findings.quote: 1. Erythropoiesis Increased HbA1c: iron, vitamin B12 deficiency, decreased erythropoiesis. Decreased HbA1c: administration of erythropoietin, iron, vitamin B12, reticulocytosis, chronic liver disease. 2. Altered Haemoglobin Genetic or chemical alterations in haemoglobin: haemoglobinopathies, HbF, methaemoglobin, may increase or decrease HbA1c. 3. Glycation Increased HbA1c: alcoholism, chronic renal failure, decreased intra-erythrocyte pH. Decreased HbA1c: aspirin, vitamin C and E, certain haemoglobinopathies, increased intra-erythrocyte pH. Variable HbA1c: genetic determinants. 4. Erythrocyte destruction Increased HbA1c: increased erythrocyte life span: Splenectomy. Decreased A1c: decreased erythrocyte life span: haemoglobinopathies, splenomegaly, rheumatoid arthritis or drugs such as antiretrovirals, ribavirin and dapsone. 5. Assays Increased HbA1c: hyperbilirubinaemia, carbamylated haemoglobin, alcoholism, large doses of aspirin, chronic opiate use. Variable HbA1c: haemoglobinopathies. Decreased HbA1c: hypertriglyceridaemia. * Some of the above interfering factors are invisible in certain of the available assays
findings.notes: NOTE THE INTERNAL TENSION: erythropoietin ADMINISTRATION decreases HbA1c here (via stimulated erythropoiesis), which is the mechanism ADA also implies. Splenomegaly (highly relevant in malaria-endemic settings) decreases HbA1c. The asterisk warning that interfering factors are 'invisible in certain of the available assays' is a key safety point: a wrong HbA1c gives no warning flag.

findings.assertion: WHO 2011 Annex 3 contrasts glucose vs HbA1c on interference and affordability — explicitly noting HbA1c is unaffordable in most low- and middle-income settings and that severe illness artefactually reduces HbA1c.
findings.value: Interferences (illness): glucose — 'Severe illness may increase glucose concentration'; HbA1c — 'Severe illness may shorten red-cell life and artifactually reduce HbA1c values.' Haemoglobinopathies: glucose — 'Little problem unless the patient is ill'; HbA1c — 'May interfere with measurement in some assays.' Haemoglobinopathy traits: glucose — 'No problems'; HbA1c — 'Most assays are not affected.' Affordability: glucose — 'Affordable in most low and middle income country settings'; HbA1c — 'Unaffordable in most low and middle-income country settings.' Measurement: HbA1c 'Not readily available world-wide'.
findings.standardVersion: WHO 2011 HbA1c consultation report, Annex 3
findings.sourceTitle: Use of Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) in the Diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus (WHO 2011), Annex 3
findings.quote: Interferences: illness Severe illness may increase glucose concentration. Severe illness may shorten red-cell life and artifactually reduce HbA1c values. Haemoglobinopathies Little problem unless the patient is ill. May interfere with measurement in some assays. Haemoglobinopathy traits No problems. Most assays are not affected. Affordability Affordable in most low and middle income country settings. Unaffordable in most low and middle-income country settings.
findings.notes: WHO's policy instruction in the same document: 'Policy-makers are advised to ensure that accurate blood glucose measurement be generally available at the primary health care level, before introducing HbA1c measurement as a diagnostic test.' Directly relevant to a Ugandan deployment's test-ordering defaults. Useful nuance: WHO says haemoglobinopathy TRAITS (heterozygous) are usually not a problem for most assays — the serious issue is homozygous disease and acute illness.

findings.assertion: NGSP: any condition that shortens erythrocyte survival falsely LOWERS HbA1c regardless of assay method; for HbSS, HbCC and HbSC, glycated serum protein or glycated albumin should be considered instead.
findings.value: Applies regardless of assay method. Named examples: recovery from acute blood loss, haemolytic anaemia. For HbSS/HbCC/HbSC: 'Alternative forms of testing such as glycated serum protein or glycated albumin should be considered for these patients.'
findings.standardVersion: NGSP (National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program), 'Factors that Interfere with HbA1c Test Results', page updated 06/23/2026
findings.sourceTitle: NGSP: Factors that Interfere with HbA1c Test Results
findings.quote: Any condition that shortens erythrocyte survival or decreases mean erythrocyte age (e.g., recovery from acute blood loss, hemolytic anemia) will falsely lower HbA1c test results regardless of the assay method used [2]. HbA1c results from patients with HbSS, HbCC, and HbSC must be interpreted with caution given the pathological processes, including anemia, increased red cell turnover, and transfusion requirements, that adversely impact HbA1c as a marker of long-term glycemic control. Alternative forms of testing such as glycated serum protein or glycated albumin should be considered for these patients.
findings.notes: NGSP is the body ADA's own recommendations defer to for assay interference (ADA links ngsp.org/interf.asp). Note the critical distinction NGSP draws: variant TRAIT with normal RBC turnover = an ASSAY problem (fixable by choosing a non-interfering assay); homozygous DISEASE = an INTERPRETATION problem (not fixable by assay choice). This distinction matters enormously for a sickle-endemic population.

findings.assertion: NGSP: iron deficiency anaemia is associated with HIGHER HbA1c, and alternative glycaemic assessment must be used until the iron deficiency is treated.
findings.value: Iron deficiency anaemia → higher HbA1c and higher fructosamine. Iron replacement therapy lowers both HbA1c and fructosamine in diabetic and non-diabetic individuals. HbA1c (but not glycated albumin) is increased in late pregnancy in non-diabetic individuals owing to iron deficiency. Action: 'Alternative measures of glycemic assessment (e.g., glucose monitoring) must be used in the presence of significant iron deficiency anemia, at least until the iron deficiency has been successfully treated.'
findings.standardVersion: NGSP, 'Factors that Interfere with HbA1c Test Results', updated 06/23/2026
findings.sourceTitle: NGSP: Factors that Interfere with HbA1c Test Results
findings.quote: Iron deficiency anemia, a major public health problem in developing countries, is associated with higher HbA1c and higher fructosamine [3]. Consistent with these observations, iron replacement therapy lowers both HbA1c and fructosamine concentrations in diabetic and non-diabetic individuals [3-5]. HbA1c , but not glycated albumin, is increased in late pregnancy in nondiabetic individuals owing to iron deficiency [6]. […] Alternative measures of glycemic assessment (e.g., glucose monitoring) must be used in the presence of significant iron deficiency anemia, at least until the iron deficiency has been successfully treated.
findings.notes: NGSP itself flags iron deficiency anaemia as 'a major public health problem in developing countries' — highly relevant to the Ugandan context. DIRECTION IS OPPOSITE to haemolytic anaemia: iron deficiency RAISES HbA1c (risking false-positive diagnosis), haemolysis LOWERS it (risking false-negative). No magnitude is quantified.

findings.assertion: NGSP: in chronic renal failure/dialysis, HbA1c underestimates glycaemic control and glycated albumin is reported to be a more robust indicator.
findings.value: 'Recent reports suggest HbA1c underestimates glycemic control in diabetic patients on dialysis and that glycated albumin is a more robust indicator of glycemic control [8-11]. Further studies are needed to clarify the role of HbA1c in diabetic patients with chronic renal failure.' Confounders named: interference from carbamylated Hb, renal anaemia, erythropoietin intake.
findings.standardVersion: NGSP, 'Factors that Interfere with HbA1c Test Results', updated 06/23/2026
findings.sourceTitle: NGSP: Factors that Interfere with HbA1c Test Results
findings.quote: Chronic renal failure develops in many diabetic patients. The role of glycemic control and the value of HbA1c in diabetic subjects with renal disease are controversial. While interference from carbamylated Hb can be evaluated, the role of renal anemia, erythropoietin intake, and other factors in chronic renal failure is more difficult to evaluate. Recent reports suggest HbA1c underestimates glycemic control in diabetic patients on dialysis and that glycated albumin is a more robust indicator of glycemic control [8-11]. Further studies are needed to clarify the role of HbA1c in diabetic patients with chronic renal failure.
findings.notes: NGSP hedges ('controversial', 'further studies are needed'). This DISAGREES with KDIGO 2022 on glycated albumin — see conflicts.

findings.assertion: NGSP: interference from HbS, HbC, HbE, HbD traits, elevated HbF and carbamylated Hb is ASSAY-SPECIFIC, not universal — the answer depends on which analyser the laboratory runs.
findings.value: Most modern assays show no interference from HbC/HbS/HbE/HbD trait, but documented exceptions exist, e.g. Tosoh G8 Standard Mode: interference 'Yes' for HbC, HbS, HbE and HbD traits and elevated HbF >7.6%; Arkray The Lab 001 (POC): 'Yes' for HbS trait; Polymer Tech Systems A1cNow: 'Yes' for HbC and HbS traits; Mindray H120 Standard Mode: 'Yes' for HbE. Elevated HbF causes interference above assay-specific ceilings (e.g. Bio-Rad D-100 'No ≤20%, Yes >29.9%'; Ortho-Clinical Vitros 'Yes >5%'; Roche Cobas c501 'Yes >9.1%'). NGSP guidance: 'In the absence of specific method data, it can generally be assumed that immunoassay, boronate affinity and enzymatic methods show interference from elevated HbF levels.'
findings.standardVersion: NGSP, 'Factors that Interfere with HbA1c Test Results', Table 1, updated 06/23/2026
findings.sourceTitle: NGSP: Factors that Interfere with HbA1c Test Results, Table 1
findings.quote: Genetic variants (e.g. HbS trait, HbC trait), elevated fetal hemoglobin (HbF) and chemically modified derivatives of hemoglobin (e.g. carbamylated Hb in patients with renal failure) can affect the accuracy of HbA1c measurements. The effects vary depending on the specific Hb variant or derivative and the specific HbA1c method. […] When selecting an assay method, laboratories should take into consideration characteristics of the patient population served, (e.g. high prevalence of hemoglobinopathies or renal failure).
findings.notes: OPERATIONAL CONSEQUENCE: 'is HbA1c reliable in this patient?' cannot be answered from the patient record alone — it requires knowing the analyser model in use at that hospital. Any decision-support rule should carry the lab's assay identity as a configuration input. Thalassaemia is NOT in NGSP's Table 1 as such; the relevant proxy is the elevated-HbF column.

findings.assertion: KDIGO 2022: accuracy and precision of HbA1c decline with advanced CKD (G4–G5) and HbA1c has LOW RELIABILITY in dialysis patients; a CGM-derived glucose management indicator can be used instead.
findings.value: Practice Point 2.1.2: accuracy and precision decline with advanced CKD (G4–G5), particularly in patients treated by dialysis, in whom HbA1c measurements have low reliability. Practice Point 2.1.3: a glucose management indicator (GMI) derived from CGM data can be used to index glycemia for individuals in whom HbA1c is not concordant with directly measured blood glucose levels or clinical symptoms. Recommendation 2.1.1 (1C): use HbA1c to monitor glycemic control in patients with diabetes and CKD. Practice Point 2.1.1: HbA1c twice per year is reasonable; up to 4 times per year if target not met or after a change in glucose-lowering therapy.
findings.standardVersion: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease (Kidney Int 2022;102(5S):S1–S127), Chapter 2
findings.sourceTitle: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease, Chapter 2: Glycemic monitoring and targets
findings.quote: Recommendation 2.1.1: We recommend using hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) to monitor glycemic control in patients with diabetes and CKD (1C). Practice Point 2.1.1: Monitoring long-term glycemic control by HbA1c twice per year is reasonable for patients with diabetes. HbA1c may be measured as often as 4 times per year if the glycemic target is not met or after a change in glucose-lowering therapy. Practice Point 2.1.2: Accuracy and precision of HbA1c measurement declines with advanced CKD (G4–G5), particularly among patients treated by dialysis, in whom HbA1c measurements have low reliability. Practice Point 2.1.3: A glucose management indicator (GMI) derived from continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data can be used to index glycemia for individuals in whom HbA1c is not concordant with directly measured blood glucose levels or clinical symptoms.
findings.notes: Note this is MONITORING guidance, not diagnostic. KDIGO stages G4–G5 correspond to eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2 by standard KDIGO staging, but the guideline text I read expresses the threshold as 'G4–G5', not as a numeric eGFR. CGM is largely unavailable in the target setting — see conflicts and unverifiable.

findings.assertion: KDIGO 2022 states HbA1c more commonly UNDERestimates than overestimates glycaemia in advanced CKD, and finds no advantage of glycated albumin or fructosamine over HbA1c for monitoring in CKD.
findings.value: Direction: underestimates (more commonly) or overestimates (less commonly) actual glycaemia versus directly measured blood glucose in advanced CKD. 'No advantages of glycated albumin or fructosamine over HbA1c are known for glycemic monitoring in CKD.' Correlations of directly measured blood glucose with HbA1c, glycated albumin and fructosamine were 'progressively weaker with advanced' CKD.
findings.standardVersion: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes Management in CKD guideline, Chapter 2 narrative (p.S57)
findings.sourceTitle: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
findings.quote: The potential harm of monitoring by HbA1c is that it may underestimate (more commonly) or overestimate (less commonly) the actual degree of glycemia control compared to directly measured blood glucose in advanced CKD. No advantages of glycated albumin or fructosamine over HbA1c are known for glycemic monitoring in CKD.
findings.notes: This directly contradicts NGSP's statement that glycated albumin is 'a more robust indicator' in dialysis. See conflicts. KDIGO also notes glycated albumin 'is biased by' peritoneal dialysis, which may explain part of the divergence.

conflicts.assertion: Where does slowly evolving autoimmune diabetes of adults (LADA) sit in the classification?
positions: WHO 2019: it is a HYBRID FORM — a distinct top-level category ('Slowly evolving immune-mediated diabetes of adults'), separate from both type 1 and type 2. WHO explicitly changed the nomenclature away from 'LADA'. WHO Table 1: 'Similar to slowly evolving type 1 in adults but more often has features of the metabolic syndrome, a single GAD autoantibody and retains greater β-cell function. Nomenclature changed – previously referred to as latent autoimmune diabetes of adults (LADA)'.

ADA 2026: there is NO hybrid category. LADA is subsumed under type 1 diabetes — 'Type 1 diabetes (due to autoimmune β-cell destruction… including latent autoimmune diabetes in adults)' — while acknowledging 'Use of the term LADA is common and acceptable in clinical practice'.
conflicts.recommendation: Do not force a single value. Store WHO 2019 as the primary classification axis (it is the WHO-aligned scheme appropriate to a Ugandan MoH context and it is designed to work without antibody testing), and carry an ADA-mapping field so that a patient recorded as 'slowly evolving immune-mediated diabetes of adults' maps to ADA 'type 1 diabetes' for any ADA-derived logic. Critically, the two schemes agree on MANAGEMENT (earlier progression to insulin than typical type 2), so decision-support should key off the clinical trajectory, not the label. Escalate to the CSO to ratify the mapping table.

conflicts.assertion: Is there a malnutrition-related category of diabetes?
positions: WHO 2019: NO. WHO introduced MRDM in 1985 and 'dropped MRDM because of lack of evidence to support its existence' in 1999; the 2019 classification does not reinstate it. Fibrocalculous pancreatopathy sits under 'Diseases of the exocrine pancreas'.

IDF 2025: YES. IDF 'endorsed the new classification at the IDF World Diabetes Congress 2025 in Bangkok' and states type 5 diabetes 'is now acknowledged as the fifth classification of diabetes, alongside types 1, 2, 3c and gestational diabetes', with a lean phenotype (BMI often <19 kg/m²) and usually negative autoantibodies.
ADA 2026: NO malnutrition category; the closest is 'pancreatic diabetes' (type 3c), which includes fibrocalculous pancreatopathy.
conflicts.recommendation: Do NOT create a 'type 5 / malnutrition-related diabetes' selectable diagnosis yet. IDF's own page concedes there are no standard diagnostic criteria and that a Working Group is still drafting them — an unvalidated category in a decision-support tool would drive treatment decisions off an undefined definition. Interim: use WHO 'unclassified diabetes' for the lean, antibody-negative, non-ketotic young adult, or 'diseases of the exocrine pancreas' where there is imaging/clinical evidence of fibrocalculous pancreatopathy, and add a free-text/flag field to capture suspected malnutrition-related cases so the cohort can be revisited when IDF publishes criteria. This is a CSO decision — the phenotype is common in the target population, so the pressure to add the label will be real.

conflicts.assertion: Should ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes be its own category?
positions: WHO 2019: YES — a named hybrid form, 'Ketosis prone type 2 diabetes', described as 'Presents with ketosis and insulin deficiency but later does not require insulin; common episodes of ketosis, not immune-mediated', with ~90% having further ketotic episodes within 10 years.

ADA 2026: NO separate category — described inside the type 2 narrative: 'Occasionally, people with type 2 diabetes may present with DKA (33) in the context of ketosis-prone diabetes, particularly members of certain racial, ethnic, and ancestral groups (e.g., Black and Hispanic/Latino adults)… The initial requirement for insulin replacement therapy in individuals presenting with ketosis-prone diabetes is generally transient.'
conflicts.recommendation: Follow WHO and make it selectable, because the management implication is specific and safety-relevant in this population: insulin at presentation, then planned reassessment for insulin withdrawal, plus counselling about the ~90%/10-year recurrence risk. Both bodies agree on the clinical course, so this is a labelling conflict rather than a treatment conflict. Encode a hard rule that a DKA presentation must NOT auto-assign type 1 diabetes.

conflicts.assertion: In dialysis/advanced CKD, what should replace or supplement HbA1c?
positions: NGSP (page updated 06/2026): 'Recent reports suggest HbA1c underestimates glycemic control in diabetic patients on dialysis and that glycated albumin is a more robust indicator of glycemic control', while conceding 'Further studies are needed'.

KDIGO 2022 (Chapter 2): 'No advantages of glycated albumin or fructosamine over HbA1c are known for glycemic monitoring in CKD', and instead directs to CGM: Practice Point 2.1.3 recommends a CGM-derived glucose management indicator (GMI) where HbA1c is discordant.
conflicts.recommendation: Both agree HbA1c has low reliability in dialysis — encode that agreement as the actionable fact. For the replacement test, neither option is deployable as stated in the target setting: CGM is generally unavailable, and glycated albumin/fructosamine assays are rarely available in Ugandan district labs. The implementable fallback is structured capnillary/lab glucose profiles (pre-meal and post-meal self- or nurse-monitored blood glucose), which KDIGO also endorses (Practice Point 2.1.4, CGM or SMBG). Flag to the CSO: do not present 'glycated albumin' as a recommended alternative on the strength of NGSP alone, given KDIGO's explicit contrary finding.

conflicts.assertion: Which conditions specifically mandate plasma glucose instead of A1C for DIAGNOSIS?
positions: ADA 2025 Rec. 2.4 (explicit enumeration): 'some hemoglobin variants, pregnancy (second and third trimesters and the postpartum period), glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, HIV, hemodialysis, recent blood loss or transfusion, hemolysis, or erythropoietin therapy'.
ADA 2026 Rec. 2.4 (generalised): 'some hemoglobin variants, pregnancy, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, HIV, and conditions that may alter red blood cell turnover'.

WHO 2011: 'haemoglobinopathies (depending on the assay employed), certain anaemias, and disorders associated with accelerated red cell turnover such as malaria' — WHO names MALARIA, which ADA never does.
conflicts.recommendation: This is version drift plus a genuine coverage gap rather than a contradiction: ADA's 2026 'conditions that may alter red blood cell turnover' is a superset that still subsumes the 2025 list (and ADA Table 2.3 in BOTH editions still names transfusion, haemolysis, blood loss and dialysis explicitly). Encode the UNION: the explicit ADA 2025 enumeration PLUS malaria and other causes of accelerated red-cell turnover from WHO 2011, and cite ADA 2026 as the current framing. Malaria must be in the list for a Ugandan deployment even though ADA omits it — WHO is the appropriate authority there.

conflicts.assertion: Can A1C be used to screen for cystic fibrosis–related diabetes?
positions: ADA 2025 Rec. 2.19: 'A1C is not recommended as a screening test for CFRD due to low sensitivity. However, a value of ≥6.5% (≥48 mmol/mol) is consistent with a diagnosis of CFRD.' (grade B)

ADA 2026 Rec. 2.24b: 'If an OGTT is not feasible, A1C can be used as an alternative method as part of a two-step screening strategy. Individuals with A1C values between 5.5% and 6.4% (37 and 47 mmol/mol, respectively) should undergo an OGTT within 3 months. C An A1C value of ≥6.5% (≥48 mmol/mol) is consistent with a diagnosis of CFRD. B'
conflicts.recommendation: ADA has relaxed its position between editions; use the 2026 two-step strategy as current, noting the A1C-as-first-step arm carries only grade C. Low priority for a Ugandan IM beachhead (CF prevalence is low), but flag it so the rule is not copied from a stale 2025 source.

unverifiable: MALARIA — magnitude and direction. WHO 2011 names malaria qualitatively as a disorder of accelerated red-cell turnover affecting HbA1c, but I found NO primary guideline stating how much HbA1c is shifted, over what parasitaemia or time course, how long after treated malaria HbA1c stays unreliable, or what test is recommended instead specifically in malaria. Given the target setting this is the single most important gap and should not be filled from memory.

RECENT TRANSFUSION — no waiting period. ADA 2025 Rec. 2.4 and ADA Table 2.3 name transfusion as invalidating A1C, but no fetched source states how many weeks or months after transfusion A1C becomes interpretable again. Any '3 months' style rule would be my inference from the ~120-day erythrocyte lifespan, not a sourced value.

IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA — no quantified bias. NGSP states iron deficiency anaemia is 'associated with higher HbA1c' and ADA 2026 says it 'increases A1C', but neither gives a magnitude in % or mmol/mol, and neither gives a haemoglobin or ferritin threshold below which A1C should be rejected.

ANAEMIA GENERALLY — no severity threshold. ADA says 'A1C may not be a suitable diagnostic test in people with anemia' without defining a haemoglobin cut-off. I could not source a numeric Hb threshold from any standards body.

THALASSAEMIA — not directly addressed. ADA mentions thalassaemia once as an example of altered erythrocyte turnover; NGSP's assay table covers HbS/C/E/D traits and elevated HbF but does not have a thalassaemia column. The practical proxy is the elevated-HbF interference ceiling, which is assay-specific — I did not find a guideline that states a thalassaemia-specific rule.

HbE AND HbC — no single answer exists. NGSP's Table 1 shows interference is method-dependent with conflicting published data for several analysers (some rows literally read 'Yes/No' with NGSP adjudicating in bold). Whether HbA1c is usable in a given HbE or HbC patient cannot be determined without knowing the exact analyser and software version in that laboratory. I did not determine which analysers are in use at Mulago or partner sites.

ANTIRETROVIRALS — drug-level detail. WHO 2011 Annex 1 lists 'antiretrovirals' as a class shortening erythrocyte life span and lowering HbA1c, but I did not verify from a primary source which specific agents (e.g. abacavir, zidovudine, dolutegravir) do this or by how much, nor whether the current WHO-recommended first-line regimens in Uganda have this effect.

ERYTHROPOIETIN — direction is asserted, magnitude is not. WHO 2011 places EPO administration under 'Decreased HbA1c'; ADA lists erythropoietin as a factor without direction or magnitude. No quantified effect was sourced.

CKD — no eGFR number tied to the recommendation. KDIGO expresses the threshold as CKD 'G4–G5'. The corresponding eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m² is standard KDIGO staging, but the guideline sentence I read does not itself state an eGFR figure, and I did not verify a non-dialysis eGFR cut-off below which HbA1c should be abandoned for DIAGNOSIS (KDIGO Chapter 2 is monitoring guidance, not diagnostic guidance).

HbA1c FOR DIAGNOSIS IN CKD — unaddressed. All the CKD material I sourced (KDIGO, NGSP) concerns monitoring established diabetes. I did not find a primary source stating whether HbA1c may be used to DIAGNOSE diabetes in non-dialysis CKD.

C-PEPTIDE CUT-OFFS — external validity unestablished. The 600 / 200 / 80 pmol/L thresholds come solely from ADA's Figure 2.1, whose legend states it is 'based on data from White European populations'. No source I retrieved validates these cut-offs in an African population. WHO 2019 gives no numeric C-peptide cut-off at all.

AUTOANTIBODY PERFORMANCE IN AFRICAN POPULATIONS — not sourced. WHO 2019 gives GAD prevalence figures for 'Europe, North America, and Asia' only. I found no primary-source figures for GAD/IA-2/ZnT8 prevalence or predictive value in sub-Saharan African cohorts, which is exactly the population this tool serves.

IDF TYPE 5 DIABETES — no diagnostic criteria exist. IDF's own page states criteria are still being developed by its Working Group. The 'BMI below 19 kg/m²' figure is descriptive prose on a web page, not a validated diagnostic threshold, and the page carries no version number or review date. I did not retrieve any peer-reviewed IDF consensus statement.

ADA 2026 SOURCE ROUTE — diabetesjournals.org returned HTTP 403, so I read ADA Section 2 (2025 and 2026) via their PubMed Central deposits (PMC11635041, PMC12690183). I confirmed PMC12690183 corresponds to doi 10.2337/dc26-S002 / PMID 41358893 via a Europe PMC lookup, but I did not compare it against the publisher's own rendering.

WHO 2019 CARRIES NO HbA1c RELIABILITY GUIDANCE. I confirmed by search that the 2019 classification document mentions HbA1c only four times, all in diagnostic-threshold context. WHO's position on HbA1c unreliability therefore rests entirely on the 2011 consultation report, which is now 15 years old and predates current assay generations.

WHETHER A NEWER WHO CLASSIFICATION EXISTS. I did not affirmatively verify that WHO has published nothing superseding the 2019 classification or the 2011 HbA1c report. The 2019 document was the most recent I located, but absence of a newer document was not proven.
WHO 2019 TABLE 4 (drug- or chemical-induced diabetes) — I extracted Table 3 and Table 5 verbatim but did not recover the contents of Table 4, so the specific drug list is not sourced here.
GDM THRESHOLDS IN mg/dL. WHO states the GDM criteria in mmol/L only. The mg/dL equivalents I give (92–125, ≥180, 153–198) are my own ×18 conversion, not values read in the WHO document.

NO CONTENT SOURCED FROM IWGDF, ICDR, ETDRS, ESC, EASD OR ISH. None of these bodies is a standard-setter for diabetes aetiological classification or HbA1c assay reliability, so I did not fetch them; if the schema expected coverage of them, that expectation is unmet.

POINT-OF-CARE HbA1c DEVICES. ADA Rec. 2.2b restricts POC A1C for diagnosis to FDA-approved devices in CLIA-certified labs — a US regulatory frame with no stated equivalent for Ugandan settings. WHO 2011 advises 'avoiding blood glucose monitoring meters and single-use HbA1c test kits (except where this is the only option available or where there is a stringent quality assurance programme in place)'. How to operationalise this locally is not resolved by any source I retrieved.

audit.assertion: WHO 2019 defines 6 top-level aetiological types of diabetes (type 1; type 2; hybrid forms; other specific types; unclassified; hyperglycaemia first detected during pregnancy), with the stated 'other specific types' sub-list.
audit.reason: Downloaded the bitstream directly (curl GET; content-disposition filename '9789241515702-eng.pdf', matching the cited ISBN 978-92-4-151570-2). Table 1 on printed p.4 (PDF p.6) and Table 2 on printed p.13 (PDF p.15) both list exactly these six top-level headings in this order. Table 2's sub-list under 'Other specific types' reads verbatim: Monogenic diabetes (- Monogenic defects of beta-cell function / - Monogenic defects in insulin action), Diseases of the exocrine pancreas, Endocrine disorders, Drug- or chemical-induced, Infections, Uncommon specific forms of immune-mediated diabetes, Other genetic syndromes sometimes associated with diabetes. Page citations (p.4, p.13) are exact. Note only that Table 1 renders the item as 'Infection-related diabetes' while Table 2 renders it 'Infections' — the finding's wording matches Table 2.

audit.assertion: WHO 2019 §2.4 states the classification prioritises readily available clinical parameters; prerequisites 'internationally applicable and using easy and readily available clinical parameters and resources; being reliable and equitable; and feasible to implement'.
audit.reason: Verbatim match on printed p.11 (PDF p.13), §2.4 'WHO classification of diabetes 2019': 'The group considered that the prerequisites of a clinically based classification system include being internationally applicable and using easy and readily available clinical parameters and resources; being reliable and equitable; and feasible to implement.' The causal framing is also supported in the same section: genotyping/autoantibody/C-peptide approaches 'are not universally available and a classification system which relied on these measures would have limited global applicability.' Page citation exact.

audit.assertion: WHO 2019 §3 (p.24) gives a 5-step clinical subtyping procedure with diagnostic tests as the last, availability-conditional step.
audit.reason: Verbatim on printed p.24 (PDF p.26) under 'Steps in clinical subtyping an individual first diagnosed with diabetes': (1) Confirm diagnosis of diabetes in an asymptomatic individual; (2) Exclude secondary causes of diabetes; (3) Consider the following which may assist in differentiating subtypes: age at diagnosis / family history / physical findings, especially presence of obesity / presence of features of metabolic syndrome; (4) Note presence or absence of ketosis or ketoacidosis; (5) Perform diagnostic tests if available (beta-cell autoantibodies, C-peptide). All five steps and their ordering match. (PDF text extraction renders the list markers as '1.' five times, a list-numbering artefact, not a source error.)

audit.assertion: WHO 2019 §2.4.1 (p.14): the decision to start insulin must be driven by clinical need, not autoantibody results; plus the quoted sentence on the limited clinical value of islet autoantibodies.
audit.reason: Verbatim on printed p.14 (PDF p.16): 'While measuring islet autoantibodies has limited value in clinical practice, in classical T1DM it may have a role when there is uncertainty as to whether a person has T1DM or T2DM. However, the decision to use insulin should not rely on the presence of such markers, but rather on the clinical need.' Quotation and page citation both exact.

audit.assertion: WHO 2019 'unclassified diabetes' (§2.4.5, p.23; Table 1 p.4) is a temporary holding category justified by global unavailability of C-peptide/autoantibody testing.
audit.reason: Table 1 (printed p.4) description matches verbatim: 'Used to describe diabetes that does not clearly fit into other categories. This category should be used temporarily when there is not a clear diagnostic category especially close to the time of diagnosis'. §2.4.5 on printed p.23 (PDF p.25) confirms the availability justification verbatim: 'While further investigation may help – including measurement of C-peptide and T1DM-associated autoantibodies... these investigations are not widely available throughout the world.' Both page citations exact.

audit.assertion: WHO 2019 §3 (p.24) requires that an assigned diabetes type be re-reviewed over time rather than fixed at diagnosis.
audit.reason: Verbatim on printed p.24 (PDF p.26), immediately following the 5 steps: 'It may not be possible to definitively subtype an individual at the time of presentation and classification may only become possible over time... Consequently, the individual should be monitored and the appropriateness of the assigned diabetes classification should be regularly reviewed, especially in individuals without the classical features of diabetes subtypes.'

audit.assertion: WHO 2019 §2.4.1 (p.14): 70–90% of people with T1DM have detectable beta-cell autoantibodies at diagnosis (GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8, insulin); C-peptide low or undetectable at classical presentation, with no numeric cut-off given.
audit.reason: Verbatim on printed p.14 (PDF p.16): 'Between 70% and 90% of people with T1DM at diagnosis have evidence of an immune-mediated process with beta-cell autoantibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65), islet antigen-2 (IA-2), ZnT8 transporter or insulin...'. Same page: 'At the time of classical clinical presentation with T1DM, there is little or no insulin secretion as manifested by low or undetectable levels of C-peptide in blood or urine (32).' I searched the whole document and confirm WHO gives no numeric C-peptide cut-off, as the finding correctly states.

audit.assertion: WHO 2019 §2.4.3 (pp.15–16) renames LADA to 'slowly evolving immune-mediated diabetes of adults' under 'hybrid forms', with three commonly used criteria; GAD prevalence 5–14% among clinically diagnosed T2DM; of antibody-positive, 90% GAD and 18–24% IA-2 or ZnT8.
audit.reason: Verbatim on printed pp.15–16 (PDF pp.17–18): 'There are no universally agreed criteria for this subtype of diabetes, but three criteria are often used: positivity for GAD autoantibodies, age older than 35 years at diagnosis, and no need for insulin therapy in the first 6–12 months after diagnosis.' And: 'with 5–14% in Europe, North America, and Asia having autoantibodies... Of these autoantibody-positive individuals, 90% have GAD autoantibodies and 18–24% have autoantibodies to protein tyrosine phosphatase IA-2 or ZnT8.' Table 1 independently confirms the renaming: 'Nomenclature changed – previously referred to as latent autoimmune diabetes of adults (LADA)'. Every number and the page range are exact.

audit.assertion: WHO 2019 §2.4.3 (pp.16–17) recognises ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes as a hybrid form; ~90% have further ketotic episodes within 10 years; non-immune, no genetic markers.
audit.reason: Verbatim on printed p.16 (PDF p.18): 'Reports suggest that further ketotic episodes occur in 90% of these people within 10 years.' On printed p.17 (PDF p.19): 'No genetic markers or evidence of auto-immunity have been identified.' Table 1 (p.4) description matches verbatim: 'Presents with ketosis and insulin deficiency but later does not require insulin; common episodes of ketosis, not immune-mediated'. Page range exact.

audit.assertion: WHO 2019 Table 3 (p.18) monogenic gene list under 'other specific types', gene-then-syndrome naming, for both beta-cell function and insulin action defects.
audit.reason: Table 3 on printed p.18 (PDF p.20) reproduced exactly, in the same order. Beta-cell function column: GCK MODY, HNF1A MODY, HNF4A MODY, HNF1B RCAD, mtDNA 3243 MIDD, KCNJ11 PNDM, KCNJ11 DEND, 6q24 TNDM, ABCC8 MODY, INS PNDM, WFS1 Wolfram syndrome, FOXP3 IPEX syndrome, EIF2AK3 Wolcott-Rallison syndrome. Insulin action column: INSR Type A insulin resistance, INSR Leprechaunism, INSR Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome, LMNA FPLD, PPARG FPLD, AGPAT2 CGL, BSCL2 CGL. All 20 entries match; the column header itself reads 'mutated gene followed by clinical syndrome', confirming the naming convention claim.

audit.assertion: WHO 2019 places fibrocalculous pancreatopathy under 'Diseases of the exocrine pancreas' (Table 3, p.18) and does not restore a malnutrition-related category; plus exocrine-pancreas epidemiology figures (§2.4.4, pp.20–21).
audit.reason: Table 3 (printed p.18) exocrine list matches verbatim and in order: Fibrocalculous pancreatopathy, Pancreatitis, Trauma/pancreatectomy, Neoplasia, Cystic fibrosis, Haemochromatosis, Others. All epidemiology verbatim on printed p.21 (PDF p.23): 'Diabetes following pancreatic disease (incidence 2.59 per 100 000 person-years) has been reported to be more common than T1DM (incidence 1.64 per 100 000 person-years). The majority of diabetes following pancreatic disease is classified by clinicians as T2DM (87.8%) and uncommonly as diabetes of the exocrine pancreas (2.7%). Proportions of people using insulin within 5 years of diagnosis were 4.1% for T2DM, 20.9% for diabetes following acute pancreatitis, and 45.8% for diabetes following chronic pancreatic disease.' All six numbers exact.

audit.assertion: WHO withdrew 'malnutrition-related diabetes mellitus' (MRDM) in 1999 for lack of evidence; introduced 1985; absent from WHO 2019.
audit.reason: Verbatim in §2.2 across printed pp.9–10 (PDF pp.11–12). p.9: 'The 1985 report omitted the terms "type 1" and "type 2", but retained the classes IDDM and NIDDM, and introduced a class of malnutrition-related diabetes mellitus (MRDM) (22).' p.10: 'In 1999, WHO reintroduced the terms type 1 and type 2 diabetes and dropped MRDM because of lack of evidence to support its existence as a distinct type.' I also grepped the full 2019 document for 'malnutrition': the only other hit is 'fetal malnutrition' in the T2DM aetiology narrative, confirming MRDM is not reinstated. Page range exact.

audit.assertion: WHO 2019 §3.1 (pp.24–26) age-at-diagnosis heuristic, highest-misclassification group 20–40 years, T1DM ~5% of diabetes diagnosed ages 31–60, and the feature lists favouring T2DM and T1DM.
audit.reason: All elements verbatim across printed pp.24–26 (PDF pp.26–28). Age bands, the monogenic peak ('The peak age at diagnosis of people with monogenic diabetes is around 15–20 years of age'), and 'The group with highest heterogeneity and risk of misclassification is that of young adults aged 20 to 40 years' all match. Both feature lists match verbatim and in order, including the parenthetical qualifiers '(if measured)' and '(if assessed)'. IMPORTANT CAVEAT surfaced by my check: the 5% figure is correctly quoted from §3.1.4 on printed p.26 ('T1DM accounts for an estimated 5% of diabetes diagnosed between the ages of 31 and 60 years (29)'), but the SAME document states 4% on printed p.13 in §2.4.1 ('accounted for 4% of all cases of diabetes diagnosed between the ages of 31 and 60 years'), citing the same reference 29. The finding is accurately attributed to §3.1, but WHO 2019 is internally inconsistent between 4% and 5% for this statistic — this belongs in 'conflicts' and should not be presented as a single settled number.

audit.assertion: WHO 2019 §1 (p.6) diagnostic thresholds: FPG ≥7.0 mmol/L (≥126 mg/dL); 2-h ≥11.1 mmol/L (≥200 mg/dL); HbA1c ≥6.5% (≥48 mmol/mol); random ≥11.1 mmol/L (≥200 mg/dL) with signs and symptoms.
audit.reason: Verbatim on printed p.6 (PDF p.8), §1 'Diabetes: Definition and diagnosis': 'People with fasting plasma glucose values of >= 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dl), 2-h post-load plasma glucose >= 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dl) (5), HbA1c >= 6.5% (48 mmol/mol); or a random blood glucose >= 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dl) in the presence of signs and symptoms are considered to have diabetes (6).' All four criteria, both unit systems, and the random-glucose symptom qualifier are in the source; the dual units are the source's own, not an added conversion. Page citation exact. (Note the Table 1 footnote on p.4 gives an abbreviated three-criterion SI-only version; the finding correctly cites §1, the fuller statement.)

audit.assertion: WHO 2019 GDM criteria (2013 WHO criteria): FPG 5.1–6.9 mmol/L; 1-h ≥10.0 mmol/L; 2-h 8.5–11.0 mmol/L; diabetes in pregnancy diagnosed by non-pregnant criteria. Source is SI-only.
audit.reason: Table 1 footnote (printed p.4) verbatim: 'Diagnostic criteria for gestational diabetes: fasting plasma glucose 5.1–6.9 mmol/L or 1-hour post-load plasma glucose >= 10.0 mmol/L or 2-hour post-load plasma glucose 8.5–11.0 mmol/L'. §2.4.6 (printed p.23) confirms the pregnancy-diabetes point verbatim: 'One is diabetes mellitus, defined by the same criteria as in non-pregnant persons', and 'In 2013 WHO updated its 1999 definition and diagnostic criteria', supporting the '2013 WHO criteria' attribution (Table 1 likewise: 'Defined by 2013 diagnostic criteria'). Credit to the finding for explicitly flagging that the mg/dL values are its own conversions and not in the source — I confirm the source is SI-only here. The conversions themselves check out (5.1→92, 10.0→180, 8.5→153, 11.0→198 mg/dL); the 6.9→125 mg/dL upper bound is a rounding-up convention (6.9 mmol/L is strictly ~124 mg/dL, expressed as 125 so the range abuts the 126 mg/dL diabetes threshold).

audit.assertion: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Section 2 classifies diabetes into four conventional clinical categories, with no 'hybrid forms' or 'unclassified' category.
audit.reason: Fetched PMC12690183 and confirmed the citation exactly: '2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026', Diabetes Care, vol 49, Suppl 1, S27–S49, doi 10.2337/dc26-S002. The four categories appear verbatim: '1. Type 1 diabetes (due to autoimmune beta-cell destruction, usually leading to absolute insulin deficiency, including latent autoimmune diabetes in adults) 2. Type 2 diabetes (due to a nonautoimmune progressive loss of adequate beta-cell insulin secretion, frequently on the background of insulin resistance) 3. Specific types of diabetes due to other causes, e.g., monogenic diabetes syndromes, diseases of the exocrine pancreas, and drug- or chemical-induced diabetes 4. Gestational diabetes mellitus'. I searched the article for 'hybrid' and 'unclassified' as category headings and found none, confirming the negative claim. The ADA/WHO structural divergence is real and correctly characterised.

audit.assertion: ADA 2026 Section 2: misdiagnosis in up to 40% of adults with new type 1 diabetes; features most useful for type 1 (<35 y, BMI <25, weight loss, DKA, glucose >360 mg/dL / >20 mmol/L); AABBCC = Age, Autoimmunity, Body habitus, Background, Control, Comorbidities.
audit.reason: All three elements verbatim. Misdiagnosis: 'misdiagnosis can occur in up to 40% of adults with new type 1 diabetes (e.g., adults with type 1 diabetes misdiagnosed as having type 2 diabetes)'. Features: 'The features most useful in determination of type 1 diabetes include younger age at diagnosis (<35 years), lower BMI (<25 kg/m2), unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, and plasma glucose >360 mg/dL (>20 mmol/L) at presentation' — both units present in the source. AABBCC: 'the AABBCC approach is a useful tool to help distinguish type 1 from type 2 diabetes: Age...; Autoimmunity...; Body habitus...; Background...; Control...; and Comorbidities', with the source adding that it is 'not prospectively validated' — a caveat worth carrying forward into any clinical use.

audit.assertion: ADA 2026 Figure 2.1 legend: GAD is the primary autoantibody, IA-2 and/or ZnT8 second-line where available; 5–10% of people with type 1 diabetes are antibody-negative.
audit.reason: Verbatim in the Figure 2.1 legend (footnote 2): 'Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) should be the primary antibody measured and, if negative, should be followed by islet tyrosine phosphatase 2 (IA-2) and/or zinc transporter 8 (ZnT8) where these tests are available. In individuals who have not been treated with insulin, antibodies against insulin may also be useful. In those diagnosed at <35 years of age who have no clinical features of type 2 diabetes or monogenic diabetes, a negative result does not change the diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, since 5–10% of people with type 1 diabetes do not have antibodies.' The 'adapted from Holt et al.' attribution is also confirmed: the legend ends 'Reprinted and adapted from Holt et al. (32)'.

audit.assertion: ADA 2026 Figure 2.1 legend footnotes 4 and 9 give numeric C-peptide interpretation thresholds (≥600, <600 with glucose <4 mmol/L, <80, 200–600 pmol/L) plus timing rules; identical text in the 2025 edition.
audit.reason: All thresholds verbatim, both units, and the footnote numbering is correct. Footnote 4: 'A C-peptide test is only indicated in people receiving insulin treatment. A random sample (with concurrent glucose) within 5 h of eating can replace a formal C-peptide stimulation test in the context of classification. If the result is >=600 pmol/L (>=1.8 ng/mL), the circumstances of testing do not matter. If the result is <600 pmol/L (<1.8 ng/mL) and the concurrent glucose is <4 mmol/L (<70 mg/dL) or the person may have been fasting, consider repeating the test. Results showing very low levels (e.g., <80 pmol/L [<0.24 ng/mL]) do not need to be repeated... Do not test C-peptide within 2 weeks of a hyperglycemic emergency.' Footnote 9: 'C-peptide values 200–600 pmol/L (0.6–1.8 ng/mL) are usually consistent with type 1 diabetes or maturity-onset diabetes of the young but may occur in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, particularly in people with normal or low BMI or after long duration.' I separately downloaded the 2025 edition (PMC11635041) and string-matched all four passages: present and identical, so the '2025 identical text' claim also holds.

audit.assertion: ADA 2026 Recommendation 2.10 (grade E) recommends standardized islet autoantibody testing for classification in adults with phenotype overlapping type 1 diabetes.
audit.reason: Verbatim: '2.10 Standardized islet autoantibody tests are recommended for classification of diabetes in adults who have phenotypic risk factors that overlap with those for type 1 diabetes (e.g., younger age at diagnosis, unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, or short time to insulin treatment). E'. Recommendation number, all four phenotypic triggers, and evidence grade E all match. The classification-versus-screening distinction the finding draws is correct and is borne out by contrast with Rec 2.6.

audit.assertion: ADA 2026 Recommendation 2.6 (grade B) is the screening panel for presymptomatic type 1 diabetes: IA, GAD, IA-2, or ZnT8.
audit.reason: Verbatim: '2.6 Screen for presymptomatic type 1 diabetes by testing autoantibodies against insulin (IA), glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), islet antigen 2 (IA-2), or zinc transporter 8 (ZnT8). B'. Number, all four antibodies, and grade B match. The finding's framing that this is screening rather than classification is correct on the face of the recommendation text.

audit.assertion: ADA 2026 uses 'pancreatic diabetes' as the preferred umbrella term for exocrine-pancreas diabetes (type 3c), commonly misdiagnosed as type 2; Rec 2.23 screening intervals 3–6 months post-acute-pancreatitis then annually, annually for chronic pancreatitis.
audit.reason: Verbatim: 'Pancreatic diabetes (also termed pancreatogenic diabetes or type 3c diabetes) includes both structural... and functional loss of insulin secretion in the context of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and is commonly misdiagnosed as type 2 diabetes. The diverse set of etiologies includes pancreatitis (acute and chronic...), trauma or pancreatectomy, neoplasia, cystic fibrosis..., hemochromatosis, fibrocalculous pancreatopathy, rare genetic disorders, and idiopathic forms (2); as such, pancreatic diabetes is the preferred umbrella term (136).' Rec 2.23 verbatim: 'Screen people for diabetes within 3–6 months following an episode of acute pancreatitis and annually thereafter. Screening for diabetes is recommended annually for people with chronic pancreatitis. E'. Aetiology list, preferred-term claim, recommendation number and grade all match.

audit.assertion: ADA 2026 Recs 2.29a and 2.29b (both grade A): genetic testing for neonatal diabetes if diagnosed in the first 6 months of life; MODY testing for children/young adults with autosomal-dominant family history.
audit.reason: Verbatim: '2.29a Regardless of current age, all people diagnosed with diabetes in the first 6 months of life should have genetic testing for neonatal diabetes. A' and '2.29b Children and young adults who do not have typical characteristics of type 1 or type 2 diabetes and have a family history of diabetes in successive generations (suggestive of an autosomal-dominant pattern of inheritance) should have genetic testing for maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY). A'. Both numbers, both grade A designations, and the substantive triggers match exactly.

audit.assertion: ADA 2026 Table 2.1 diagnostic criteria for diabetes, with both unit systems.
audit.reason: Table 2.1 reproduced verbatim: 'A1C >=6.5% (>=48 mmol/mol). The test should be performed in a laboratory using a method that is NGSP certified and standardized to the DCCT assay. OR FPG >=126 mg/dL (>=7.0 mmol/L). Fasting is defined as no caloric intake for at least 8 h. OR 2-h PG >=200 mg/dL (>=11.1 mmol/L) during OGTT... OR In an individual with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis, a random plasma glucose >=200 mg/dL (>=11.1 mmol/L).' All four criteria, both unit systems, the NGSP/DCCT standardisation clause and the >=8 h fasting definition match exactly. Dual units are the source's own.

audit.assertion: IDF recognised malnutrition-related diabetes as 'type 5 diabetes' in 2025: BMI typically below 19 kg/m2, autoantibodies usually negative, non-autoimmune and non-insulin-resistant, adolescents/young adults, endorsed at IDF World Diabetes Congress 2025 Bangkok, no formal diagnostic criteria yet.
audit.reason: The URL initially appeared broken — WebFetch failed with 'too many redirects' and curl showed an infinite /__sentry/transparent/ redirect loop — so I flagged it as a possible hallucinated source. It is not: the loop is bot protection, and the page retrieves fine (HTTP 200, 337 KB) with a browser user-agent plus a cookie jar. Title 'Type 5 diabetes (MRDM): Causes, symptoms & treatment'; Published 19 Aug 2025, Last Modified 21 Aug 2026, consistent with the stated access date. All claims verbatim: 'people with type 5 diabetes often have a body mass index (BMI) below 19 kg/m2 and do not show signs of autoimmune beta-cell destruction'; autoantibodies 'Usually negative (helps distinguish from Type 1 when tests are available)'; 'Damage to the pancreas is not the result of autoimmune reactions, as in type 1 diabetes, or insulin resistance, as in type 2 diabetes. Instead, it is a non-autoimmune diabetes type, caused by an inability of the pancreas to produce enough insulin due to underdeveloped pancreatic tissue'; 'chronic undernutrition during adolescence and young adulthood'; 'In 2025, the International Diabetes Federation (IDF) endorsed the new classification at the IDF World Diabetes Congress 2025 in Bangkok, Thailand'. On diagnostic criteria the page says 'Until recently, there were no standard diagnostic criteria' and that a Working Group (chaired by Dr Meredith Hawkins, co-chaired by Dr Nihal Thomas) has been established 'to develop formal diagnostic criteria' — so no published criteria exist and the finding is substantively right, though 'Until recently' is looser than the finding's flat 'No formal diagnostic criteria yet exist'. Two caveats for downstream use: this is an IDF patient-education page, not a standards document, and the page frames type 5 as sitting 'alongside types 1, 2, 3c and gestational diabetes', which is IDF's own framing, not a WHO or ADA category.

audit.assertion: ADA 2026 Rec 2.4 (grade B): when the A1C–glycaemia relationship is altered, use plasma glucose criteria instead of A1C; named conditions in 2026 wording.
audit.reason: Verbatim: '2.4 In conditions associated with an altered relationship between A1C and glycemia, such as some hemoglobin variants, pregnancy, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, HIV, and conditions that may alter red blood cell turnover, plasma glucose criteria should be used to diagnose diabetes. B'. The named-condition list matches exactly, including the generalised trailing clause. Grade B confirmed. The plasma glucose thresholds the finding appends are correctly taken from Table 2.1 rather than from Rec 2.4 itself, which is a fair reading of 'plasma glucose criteria'.

audit.assertion: ADA 2025 Rec 2.4 (grade B) enumerated a more explicit condition list than the 2026 wording.
audit.reason: Fetched PMC11635041 independently and confirmed it is '2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025'.
