Rec 2.4 verbatim: 'In conditions associated with an altered relationship between A1C and glycemia, such as some hemoglobin variants, pregnancy (second and third trimesters and the postpartum period), glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, HIV, hemodialysis, recent blood loss or transfusion, hemolysis, or erythropoietin therapy, plasma glucose criteria should be used to diagnose diabetes. B'. All eight named conditions and grade B match exactly. Having verified both editions side by side, I confirm the finding's central point: the 2026 edition genuinely replaced four specific conditions (hemodialysis, recent blood loss or transfusion, hemolysis, erythropoietin therapy) with the generic 'conditions that may alter red blood cell turnover'. Retaining the 2025 list is the safer choice for a decision-support tool, and this edition-to-edition divergence deserves a 'conflicts' entry.

audit.assertion: ADA (2025 and 2026) narrative: A1C may not be suitable in anaemia, erythropoietin treatment, haemodialysis or HIV treatment; thalassaemia and folate deficiency affect A1C; sickle cell trait needs a non-interfering assay; G6PD G202A decreases A1C ~0.8% (men) / 0.7% (women); ~120-day erythrocyte lifespan.
audit.reason: Entire passage verbatim in the 2026 article: 'A1C reflects glucose bound to hemoglobin over the life span of the erythrocyte (~120 days)... A1C is an indirect measure of glucose exposure, and factors that affect hemoglobin concentrations or erythrocyte turnover can affect A1C (e.g., thalassemia or folate deficiency) (Table 2.3). A1C may not be a suitable diagnostic test in people with anemia, people treated with erythropoietin, or people undergoing hemodialysis or HIV treatment (1, 17)... an A1C assay without interference from hemoglobin variants should be used in individuals with sickle cell trait. An updated list of A1C assays with interferences is available at ngsp.org/interf.asp. Another genetic variant, X-linked glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase G202A, carried by 11% of Black individuals in the U.S., is associated with a decrease in A1C of about 0.8% in homozygous men and 0.7% in homozygous women.' Every number (120 days, 11%, 0.8%, 0.7%), the sex-specific split, and the ngsp.org/interf.asp cross-reference match exactly.

audit.assertion: ADA 2026 Table 2.3 lists individual factors and assay interferences affecting A1C (data from Selvin), including that A1C is unaffected by recent food intake, stress, illness, activity.
audit.reason: Table 2.3 rows verbatim. 'Other individual factors that can affect test results' (A1C column): 'Altered erythrocyte turnover (e.g., anemia, iron status, splenectomy, blood loss, transfusion, hemolysis, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, erythropoietin), HIV, cirrhosis, kidney failure, dialysis, pregnancy'. 'Test interferences' (A1C column): 'Depends on specific assay: hemoglobin variants, severe hypertriglyceridemia, severe hyperbilirubinemia'. 'Acute factors that can affect levels' (A1C column): 'Unaffected by recent food intake, stress, illness, activity'. Attribution confirmed by the table footer: 'Data are from Selvin (236).' All three row contents and the source attribution match exactly.

audit.assertion: ADA Rec 2.17 (2026; 2.16 in 2025), grade E: screen people with HIV for diabetes with FPG — not A1C — around antiretroviral therapy changes.
audit.reason: Both editions checked. ADA 2026 verbatim: '2.17 People with HIV should be screened for diabetes and prediabetes with an FPG test before starting antiretroviral therapy, at the time of switching antiretroviral therapy, and 3–6 months after starting or switching antiretroviral therapy. If initial screening results are normal, FPG should be checked annually. E'. ADA 2025 carries word-for-word identical text numbered 2.16, exactly as the finding states. The renumbering claim is correct — I verified it rather than assuming it, and note that in the 2025 edition number 2.17 is instead the pancreatitis screening recommendation, so citing the wrong edition's number here would misdirect a reader.

audit.assertion: ADA: A1C is not reliable for screening for GDM or pre-existing diabetes at ≥15 weeks of gestation; directional effects of red blood cell turnover and iron deficiency in pregnancy.
audit.reason: The 15-week claim is verbatim in the 2025 article at the cited URL (PMC11635041): 'A1C is not reliable for screening for GDM or for preexisting diabetes at 15 weeks of gestation or later in part from the higher red blood cell turnover in pregnancy but also from the unknown diabetes status prior to pregnancy...'. The directional-effects sentence is verbatim in the 2026 article: 'Disadvantages include inaccuracies in the presence of conditions such as increased or decreased red blood cell turnover (usually decreases and increases A1C, respectively), hemoglobinopathies, and iron deficiency anemia (increases A1C)' — confirming increased turnover lowers A1C, decreased turnover raises it, and iron deficiency anaemia raises it. I also grepped the 2026 article for '15 weeks of gestation or later' and got zero hits, which independently corroborates the finding's own note that the statement was re-worded in the 2026 edition. One sourcing imprecision worth fixing: the finding carries a single sourceUrl (the 2025 article) while the directional-effects half of its value comes from the 2026 article; both halves are genuine, but they need two URLs.

audit.assertion: WHO 2011 conditions HbA1c diagnosis on absence of conditions precluding accurate measurement; cut point 6.5% (48 mmol/mol); names haemoglobinopathies, certain anaemias and malaria; GRADE moderate/conditional.
audit.reason: The URL is genuine — I downloaded it (content-disposition filename 'WHO_NMH_CHP_CPM_11.1_eng.pdf', matching the cited document number). Almost everything checks out verbatim: 'HbA1c can be used as a diagnostic test for diabetes, provided that stringent quality assurance tests are in place and assays are standardised to criteria aligned to the international reference values, and there are no conditions present which preclude its accurate measurement'; 'An HbA1c of 6.5% is recommended as the cut point for diagnosing diabetes. A value less than 6.5% does not exclude diabetes diagnosed using glucose tests'; 'The most common important factors worldwide affecting HbA1c levels are haemoglobinopathies (depending on the assay employed), certain anaemias, and disorders associated with accelerated red cell turnover such as malaria'; 'GRADE quality of evidence: moderate' / 'GRADE strength of recommendation: conditional'. The single defect: '(48 mmol/mol)' is NOT in this document. I grepped the full extracted text for '48 mmol', 'mmol/mol' and 'IFCC' — zero hits; WHO 2011 expresses the cut point only as a DCCT/NGSP percentage. The 48 mmol/mol conversion is clinically correct and does appear in WHO 2019 (p.6) and ADA Table 2.1, but presenting it inside a WHO-2011-attributed value implies the 2011 consultation stated it, which it did not. Flagged because the finding is marked fetched:true, which should mean every element was literally read in the retrieved document.
audit.correctedValue: WHO 2011 states the cut point as 'An HbA1c of 6.5%' only — no mmol/mol figure appears anywhere in the document. If both units are required, source the 48 mmol/mol equivalent to WHO 2019 (p.6, 'HbA1c >= 6.5% (48 mmol/mol)') or ADA Table 2.1, not to WHO 2011. All other elements of this finding are confirmed verbatim.
audit.correctedSource: https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/db9b9d3d-f95e-4797-9d2b-c78dcef0133f/content (WHO/NMH/CHP/CPM/11.1) for the 6.5% cut point, GRADE ratings and the malaria/anaemia/haemoglobinopathy list; https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/2cb3ab68-a52a-402e-ad47-8bc5a4edc834/content p.6 for the 48 mmol/mol equivalence

audit.assertion: WHO 2011 Annex 1 tabulates factors influencing HbA1c by mechanism with direction of effect, across five categories (erythropoiesis, altered haemoglobin, glycation, erythrocyte destruction, assays).
audit.reason: Annex 1 (printed p.16) reproduced accurately, including the header 'Adapted from Gallagher et al (24)' and all five mechanism categories with correct directions. Verbatim checks: category 2 'haemoglobinopathies, HbF, methaemoglobin, may increase or decrease HbA1c'; category 3 increased 'alcoholism, chronic renal failure, decreased intra-erythrocyte pH', decreased 'aspirin, vitamin C and E, certain haemoglobinopathies, increased intra-erythrocyte pH', variable 'genetic determinants'; category 4 increased 'increased erythrocyte life span: Splenectomy', decreased 'haemoglobinopathies, splenomegaly, rheumatoid arthritis or drugs such as antiretrovirals, ribavirin and dapsone'; category 5 increased 'hyperbilirubinaemia, carbamylated haemoglobin, alcoholism, large doses of aspirin, chronic opiate use', variable 'haemoglobinopathies', decreased 'hypertriglyceridaemia'. One wording note, not an error: the source's category 1 reads 'Increased HbA1c: iron, vitamin B12 deficiency, decreased erythropoiesis' — a shared-noun elision that the finding expands to 'iron deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency'. The expansion is correct in context (iron ADMINISTRATION is listed under Decreased) and is corroborated independently by NGSP, but it is an interpretation rather than a literal quote. Also worth carrying forward: the annex footnote 'Some of the above interfering factors are "invisible" in certain of the available assays.'

audit.assertion: WHO 2011 Annex 3 contrasts glucose vs HbA1c on interference and affordability, noting HbA1c is unaffordable in most low- and middle-income settings and that severe illness artefactually reduces HbA1c.
audit.reason: Annex 3 (printed p.18) matches verbatim on every quoted cell. Interferences/illness: glucose 'Severe illness may increase glucose concentration', HbA1c 'Severe illness may shorten red-cell life and artifactually reduce HbA1c values.' Haemoglobinopathies: glucose 'Little problem unless the patient is ill', HbA1c 'May interfere with measurement in some assays.' Haemoglobinopathy traits: glucose 'No problems', HbA1c 'Most assays are not affected.' Affordability: glucose 'Affordable in most low and middle income country settings', HbA1c 'Unaffordable in most low and middle-income country settings.' Measurement row: HbA1c 'Not readily available world-wide'. This is the most directly load-bearing finding in the set for a Uganda-deployed tool and it survives scrutiny intact.

audit.assertion: NGSP: any condition shortening erythrocyte survival falsely lowers HbA1c regardless of assay method; for HbSS/HbCC/HbSC consider glycated serum protein or glycated albumin.
audit.reason: Retrieved ngsp.org/factors.asp and confirmed the page header 'Updated 06/23/2026', matching the cited date. Verbatim: 'Any condition that shortens erythrocyte survival or decreases mean erythrocyte age (e.g., recovery from acute blood loss, hemolytic anemia) will falsely lower HbA1c test results regardless of the assay method used [2]. HbA1c results from patients with HbSS, HbCC, and HbSC must be interpreted with caution given the pathological processes, including anemia, increased red cell turnover, and transfusion requirements, that adversely impact HbA1c as a marker of long-term glycemic control. Alternative forms of testing such as glycated serum protein or glycated albumin should be considered for these patients.' Both named examples, the regardless-of-assay claim and the alternative-testing sentence all match exactly.

audit.assertion: NGSP: iron deficiency anaemia is associated with higher HbA1c; alternative glycaemic assessment must be used until the iron deficiency is treated.
audit.reason: Verbatim on the same page: 'Iron deficiency anemia, a major public health problem in developing countries, is associated with higher HbA1c and higher fructosamine [3]. Consistent with these observations, iron replacement therapy lowers both HbA1c and fructosamine concentrations in diabetic and non-diabetic individuals [3-5]. HbA1c, but not glycated albumin, is increased in late pregnancy in nondiabetic individuals owing to iron deficiency [6]... Alternative measures of glycemic assessment (e.g., glucose monitoring) must be used in the presence of significant iron deficiency anemia, at least until the iron deficiency has been successfully treated.' Every clause matches, including the pregnancy/glycated-albumin contrast and the mandatory 'must be used' phrasing. Note the direction here (iron deficiency RAISES HbA1c) is consistent with ADA 2026 and with WHO 2011 Annex 1 category 1, so all three primary sources agree.

audit.assertion: NGSP: in chronic renal failure/dialysis HbA1c underestimates glycaemic control and glycated albumin is reported to be a more robust indicator.
audit.reason: Verbatim: 'Recent reports suggest HbA1c underestimates glycemic control in diabetic patients on dialysis and that glycated albumin is a more robust indicator of glycemic control [8-11]. Further studies are needed to clarify the role of HbA1c in diabetic patients with chronic renal failure.' The named confounders are also confirmed in the preceding sentence: 'While interference from carbamylated Hb can be evaluated, the role of renal anemia, erythropoietin intake, and other factors in chronic renal failure is more difficult to evaluate.' The finding correctly preserves the hedged 'Recent reports suggest' framing. IMPORTANT CONFLICT the finding does not flag: NGSP's endorsement of glycated albumin as 'more robust' in dialysis directly contradicts KDIGO 2022 (finding 40), which states 'No advantages of glycated albumin or fructosamine over HbA1c are known for glycemic monitoring in CKD' and keeps HbA1c as biomarker of choice. This disagreement between two primary bodies belongs in 'conflicts'.

audit.assertion: NGSP Table 1: interference from HbS/HbC/HbE/HbD traits, elevated HbF and carbamylated Hb is assay-specific, with the named exceptions and HbF ceilings.
audit.reason: I extracted the full Table 1 and verified every named cell. Tosoh G8 Standard Mode: 'Yes' for HbC, HbS, HbE and HbD traits and 'Yes >7.6%' for elevated HbF — all five confirmed. Arkray The Lab 001 (POC): 'Yes' for HbS trait only (HbC/HbE/HbD all 'No') — confirmed. Polymer Tech Systems A1cNow: 'Yes' for HbC and HbS traits — confirmed. Mindray H120 Standard Mode: 'Yes' for HbE — confirmed. HbF ceilings: Bio-Rad D-100 'No <=20%, Yes >29.9%'; Ortho-Clinical Vitros 'Yes >5%'; Roche Cobas c501 'Yes >9.1%' — all three confirmed exactly. The NGSP guidance quote is verbatim from footnote '$': 'In the absence of specific method data, it can generally be assumed that immunoassay, boronate affinity and enzymatic methods show interference from elevated HbF levels (20, 43).' The finding's framing that most modern assays show no trait interference but documented exceptions exist is an accurate reading of the table. Caution for downstream use: this table is versioned and method-specific (entries carry software-version and mode qualifiers, e.g. Tosoh G8 Variant Mode is 'No' where Standard Mode is 'Yes'), so it must be re-checked against the lab's actual analyser and mode rather than hard-coded.

audit.assertion: KDIGO 2022 Chapter 2: HbA1c accuracy/precision decline in CKD G4–G5 with low reliability in dialysis; GMI from CGM can be used instead; Rec 2.1.1 (1C); Practice Point 2.1.1 testing frequency.
audit.reason: Downloaded the KDIGO PDF from the exact cited URL (HTTP 200, 8.2 MB, 128 pages) — the source is real and the journal citation is corroborated by the running footer 'Kidney International (2022) 102 (Suppl 5S), S1–S127'. All four statements verbatim: 'Recommendation 2.1.1: We recommend using hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) to monitor glycemic control in patients with diabetes and CKD (1C).'; 'Practice Point 2.1.1: Monitoring long-term glycemic control by HbA1c twice per year is reasonable for patients with diabetes. HbA1c may be measured as often as 4 times per year if the glycemic target is not met or after a change in glucose-lowering therapy.'; 'Practice Point 2.1.2: Accuracy and precision of HbA1c measurement declines with advanced CKD (G4–G5), particularly among patients treated by dialysis, in whom HbA1c measurements have low reliability.'; 'Practice Point 2.1.3: A glucose management indicator (GMI) derived from continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data can be used to index glycemia for individuals in whom HbA1c is not concordant with directly measured blood glucose levels or clinical symptoms.' Numbering, grade 1C and all intervals match.

audit.assertion: KDIGO 2022 (p.S57): HbA1c more commonly underestimates than overestimates glycaemia in advanced CKD; no advantage of glycated albumin or fructosamine over HbA1c in CKD.
audit.reason: Verbatim, and I confirmed the page number: the passage sits on PDF page 58, which the running footers bracket as printed page S57. Text: 'The potential harm of monitoring by HbA1c is that it may underestimate (more commonly) or overestimate (less commonly) the actual degree of glycemia control compared to directly measured blood glucose in advanced CKD. No advantages of glycated albumin or fructosamine over HbA1c are known for glycemic monitoring in CKD.' The second sentence is an exact quotation, not a paraphrase. The correlations claim is also confirmed verbatim from the Practice Point 2.1.2 narrative: 'Correlations of directly measured blood glucose levels with 3 glycemic biomarkers—HbA1c, glycated albumin, and fructosamine—were progressively weaker with advanced CKD stages (G4–G5), especially kidney failure treated by dialysis.' As noted under finding 37, this directly conflicts with NGSP's position that glycated albumin is 'a more robust indicator' in dialysis patients — record as a conflict rather than silently preferring one body.

bundle.domain: Acute hyperglycaemic and hypoglycaemic emergencies in adults — diagnostic criteria and severity grading for DKA, HHS and hypoglycaemia

findings.assertion: DKA diagnosis requires hyperglycaemia defined as glucose at or above 200 mg/dL, OR a prior history of diabetes irrespective of the presenting glucose value.
findings.value: Glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (≥200 mg/dL) OR prior history of diabetes at any glucose value
findings.standardVersion: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 16, Table 16.1 (restating the 2024 ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus)
findings.sourceTitle: 16. Diabetes Care in the Hospital: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Table 16.1. Diagnostic criteria for DKA and HHS DKA Diabetes/hyperglycemia Glucose ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or prior history of diabetes
findings.notes: All three DKA components (D, K, A) must be met. The 'or prior history of diabetes' clause is what makes euglycaemic DKA diagnosable.

findings.assertion: Euglycaemic DKA — full ketoacidosis with glucose below the hyperglycaemia threshold — occurs in roughly 10% of DKA presentations and is now most often caused by SGLT2 inhibitors.
findings.value: Plasma glucose <11.1 mmol/L (<200 mg/dL) with ketosis and metabolic acidosis; ~10% of DKA cases
findings.standardVersion: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus report 2024 (Diabetologia 67:1455–1479)
findings.sourceTitle: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
findings.quote: Approximately 10% of patients with DKA present with euglycaemic DKA, which is defined as plasma glucose levels <11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl) in the presence of ketosis and metabolic acidosis
findings.notes: Report lists causes: exogenous insulin, reduced food intake, pregnancy, alcohol, liver failure, SGLT2 inhibitors — and states 'the use of SGLT2 inhibitors in those with type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes has accounted for the majority of cases of euglycaemic DKA'. High-priority safety rule for any DKA screen.

findings.assertion: DKA ketosis criterion is a quantitative beta-hydroxybutyrate at or above 3.0 mmol/L, or a urine ketone strip of 2+ or greater.
findings.value: β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L (SI; BOHB is conventionally reported in mmol/L in both systems) OR urine ketone strip ≥2+
findings.standardVersion: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 16, Table 16.1
findings.sourceTitle: 16. Diabetes Care in the Hospital: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Ketosis β-Hydroxybutyrate concentration ≥3.0 mmol/L or urine ketone strip 2+ or greater
findings.notes: Direct BOHB measurement (venous/capillary point-of-care) is the recommended modality; urine nitroprusside measures acetoacetate, not BOHB.

findings.assertion: Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate at or above 3.0 mmol/L has greater than 90% sensitivity and specificity for DKA, which is the evidentiary basis for the 3.0 mmol/L cut-point.
findings.value: β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L; >90% sensitivity and specificity
findings.standardVersion: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus report 2024 (Diabetologia 67:1455–1479)
findings.sourceTitle: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
findings.quote: Blood concentrations of β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/l correlate well with acid–base changes, with >90% sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis of DKA
findings.notes: Report also warns point-of-care meters may be inaccurate at BOHB ≥5 mmol/L — relevant if severity is auto-graded from a POC reading.

findings.assertion: Urine ketone testing can misrepresent DKA severity in both directions and is explicitly a fallback, not the preferred test.
findings.value: Urine ketones (acetoacetate, nitroprusside) — underestimates early DKA, overestimates late DKA; false positives with sulfhydryl drugs (e.g. captopril) and valproate
findings.standardVersion: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus report 2024
findings.sourceTitle: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
findings.quote: Reliance on urine ketone testing can underestimate the severity of ketonaemia early in the course of DKA because of a lag in the formation of acetoacetate, and conversely overestimate its severity later in the course of DKA when β-hydroxybutyrate is being cleared and converted into acetoacetate
findings.notes: Directly relevant to a Ugandan deployment where urine dipstick may be the only available ketone test.

findings.assertion: DKA metabolic acidosis criterion is a pH below 7.3 and/or a bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L, and venous (not arterial) sampling is used.
findings.value: pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L (= <18 mEq/L); venous pH acceptable
findings.standardVersion: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 16, Table 16.1
findings.sourceTitle: 16. Diabetes Care in the Hospital: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Metabolic acidosis pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate concentration <18 mmol/L
findings.notes: The consensus report specifies venous sampling: 'blood should be drawn every 4 h for determination of electrolytes, phosphate, creatinine, β-hydroxybutyrate and venous pH'. The 2009 statement used ARTERIAL pH — see conflicts/changes.

findings.assertion: The anion gap has been DEMOTED — it is no longer a first-line diagnostic or resolution criterion for DKA, though >12 mmol/L still indicates a high anion gap metabolic acidosis and it retains utility where ketone testing is unavailable.
findings.value: Anion gap >12 mmol/L indicates high anion gap metabolic acidosis; NOT recommended as first-line diagnostic or resolution criterion
findings.standardVersion: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus report 2024
findings.sourceTitle: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
findings.quote: Although the anion gap is not recommended as a first-line diagnostic or resolution criterion for these reasons, it may still have some utility in resource settings where ketone measurement is unavailable.
findings.notes: MAJOR CHANGE from older teaching. Reasons given: mixed acid-base disorders in ~1/3 of DKA, and post-treatment hyperchloraemic normal-anion-gap acidosis being mistaken for persistent DKA. The 'resource settings' carve-out is directly applicable to MedSync's context and is quoted verbatim above. Anion gap is absent from ADA 2026 Table 16.1 entirely.

findings.assertion: MILD DKA is graded by beta-hydroxybutyrate 3.0–6.0 mmol/L, pH above 7.25 to below 7.30 or bicarbonate 15–18 mmol/L, and alert mental status.
findings.value: Glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL); β-hydroxybutyrate 3.0–6.0 mmol/L; pH >7.25 to <7.30 OR bicarbonate 15–18 mmol/L; mental status alert
findings.standardVersion: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus report 2024, Table 2
findings.sourceTitle: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
findings.quote: Mild DKA ... Glucose ≥11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl) ... β-Hydroxybutyrate 3.0–6.0 mmol/l ... • pH >7.25 to <7.30 or bicarbonate 15–18 mmol/l ... Mental status Alert ... Suggested level of care Regular or observation nursing unit
findings.notes: Suggested care location: regular or observation nursing unit. Mild/uncomplicated moderate DKA may be managed with subcutaneous insulin outside critical care.

findings.assertion: MODERATE DKA is graded by beta-hydroxybutyrate 3.0–6.0 mmol/L, pH 7.0–7.25, bicarbonate 10 to below 15 mmol/L, and alert or drowsy mental status.
findings.value: Glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL); β-hydroxybutyrate 3.0–6.0 mmol/L; pH 7.0–7.25; bicarbonate 10 to <15 mmol/L; mental status alert/drowsy
findings.standardVersion: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus report 2024, Table 2
findings.sourceTitle: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
findings.quote: Moderate DKA ... β-Hydroxybutyrate 3.0–6.0 mmol/l ... • pH 7.0–7.25 • Bicarbonate 10 to <15 mmol/l ... Mental status Alert/drowsy ... Suggested level of care Step-down unit or intermediate care unit
findings.notes: Suggested care location: step-down or intermediate care unit.

findings.assertion: SEVERE DKA is graded by beta-hydroxybutyrate above 6.0 mmol/L, pH below 7.0, bicarbonate below 10 mmol/L, and stupor or coma.
findings.value: Glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL); β-hydroxybutyrate >6.0 mmol/L; pH <7.0; bicarbonate <10 mmol/L; mental status stupor/coma
findings.standardVersion: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus report 2024, Table 2
findings.sourceTitle: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
findings.quote: Severe DKA ... β-Hydroxybutyrate >6.0 mmol/l ... • pH <7.0 • Bicarbonate <10 mmol/l ... Mental status Stupor/coma ... Suggested level of care ICU
findings.notes: Suggested care location: ICU.

findings.assertion: DKA severity grading does not require every variable to be met — it is explicitly a clinical judgement, not a strict algorithm.
findings.value: Not all variables need be fulfilled; admission site and level of care are ultimately a clinical decision
findings.standardVersion: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus report 2024, Table 2 footnote
findings.sourceTitle: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
findings.quote: Not all variables need to be fulfilled to be defined as either mild, moderate or severe, and the admission site and level of care are ultimately a clinical decision
findings.notes: CRITICAL for decision-support design: a rules engine must NOT present a computed severity as definitive. Present as advisory with the discordant variables shown.

findings.assertion: HHS hyperglycaemia criterion is a plasma glucose at or above 600 mg/dL.
findings.value: Plasma glucose ≥33.3 mmol/L (≥600 mg/dL)
findings.standardVersion: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 16, Table 16.1
findings.sourceTitle: 16. Diabetes Care in the Hospital: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: HHS Hyperglycemia Plasma glucose ≥600 mg/dL (33.3 mmol/L)
findings.notes: All four HHS components must be met. Endotext renders this as '>600' rather than '≥600' — trivial boundary difference, but note it if coding a strict comparator.

findings.assertion: HHS hyperosmolarity criterion is a calculated EFFECTIVE serum osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg, or a TOTAL serum osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg.
findings.value: Calculated effective serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg, computed as [2 × Na+ (mmol/L) + glucose (mmol/L)]; OR total serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, computed as [2 × Na+ (mmol/L) + glucose (mmol/L) + urea (mmol/L)]
findings.standardVersion: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 16, Table 16.1
findings.sourceTitle: 16. Diabetes Care in the Hospital: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Hyperosmolarity Calculated effective serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg (calculated as [2 × Na + (mmol/L) + glucose (mmol/L)] or total serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg [2 × Na + (mmol/L) + glucose (mmol/L) + urea (mmol/L)]
findings.notes: CHANGED: effective-osmolality cut-point LOWERED from >320 (2009) to >300, and total osmolality added as an alternative. Note the two formulae use different inputs — do NOT compare an effective-osmolality value against the 320 total threshold. NB the ADA formula is in mmol/L for glucose; the 2009 US formula used glucose(mg/dL)/18.

findings.assertion: HHS requires ABSENCE of significant ketonaemia — beta-hydroxybutyrate below 3.0 mmol/L or urine ketone strip less than 2+.
findings.value: β-hydroxybutyrate <3.0 mmol/L OR urine ketone strip <2+
findings.standardVersion: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 16, Table 16.1
findings.sourceTitle: 16. Diabetes Care in the Hospital: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Absence of significant ketonemia β-Hydroxybutyrate concentration <3.0 mmol/L OR urine ketone strip less than 2+
findings.notes: NEW in 2024: quantitative cut-offs were added for the permitted degree of ketonaemia in HHS; the 2009 criteria only said 'small' urine/serum ketones. Mild ketonaemia may still be present.

findings.assertion: HHS requires ABSENCE of acidosis — pH at or above 7.3 AND bicarbonate at or above 15 mmol/L.
findings.value: pH ≥7.3 AND bicarbonate ≥15 mmol/L
findings.standardVersion: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 16, Table 16.1
findings.sourceTitle: 16. Diabetes Care in the Hospital: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Absence of acidosis pH ≥7.3 and bicarbonate concentration ≥15 mmol/L
findings.notes: CHANGED: HHS bicarbonate threshold LOWERED from >18 (2009) to ≥15, to allow for the degree of acidosis caused by insulinopenia. WARNING: the consensus report's own prose is inconsistent with its table here — see conflicts.

findings.assertion: Altered mental status is NO LONGER a diagnostic criterion for HHS, though a change in cognitive state remains a common clinical feature.
findings.value: Mental status: not a diagnostic criterion (removed); 2009 required stupor/coma
findings.standardVersion: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 16, Table 16.1 (no mental-status row) + Cleveland Clinic J Med 2025 review of the consensus
findings.sourceTitle: 16. Diabetes Care in the Hospital: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 / Hyperglycemic crises in adults: A look at the 2024 consensus report
findings.quote: Mental status impairment is no longer a diagnostic criterion. Although past studies linked osmolality with mental status, many individuals, though very ill, do not necessarily have mental impairment, so this is no longer a requirement for diagnosis of HHS.
findings.notes: The quote is verbatim from the CCJM review (https://www.ccjm.org/content/92/3/152), which I fetched. Corroborated structurally: ADA 2026 Table 16.1, which I also fetched, lists only four HHS rows and contains NO mental-status row, whereas 2009 Table 1 did. Table 16.2 retains 'Change in cognitive state common' as a presentation feature, not a criterion.

findings.assertion: Level 1 hypoglycaemia is a glucose below 70 mg/dL and at or above 54 mg/dL.
findings.value: Glucose <3.9 mmol/L (<70 mg/dL) and ≥3.0 mmol/L (≥54 mg/dL)
findings.standardVersion: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6, Table 6.4
findings.sourceTitle: 6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Table 6.4. Classification of hypoglycemia Glycemic criteria/description Level 1 Glucose <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) and ≥54 mg/dL (≥3.0 mmol/L)
findings.notes: Rationale given in text: '70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) has been recognized as a threshold for adrenergic responses to falling glucose'. Identical wording verified in the 2024 Standards (PMC10725808) — unchanged across editions.

findings.assertion: Level 2 hypoglycaemia is a glucose below 54 mg/dL — the threshold for neuroglycopenic symptoms, requiring immediate action.
findings.value: Glucose <3.0 mmol/L (<54 mg/dL)
findings.standardVersion: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6, Table 6.4
findings.sourceTitle: 6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Level 2 Glucose <54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L)
findings.notes: Body text: 'Level 2 hypoglycemia (defined as a blood glucose concentration <54 mg/dL [<3.0 mmol/L]) is the threshold at which neuroglycopenic symptoms begin to occur and requires immediate action to resolve the hypoglycemic event.'

findings.assertion: Level 3 hypoglycaemia is defined by SEVERITY not by a glucose number — a severe event with altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance from another person, at any glucose level.
findings.value: No numeric threshold — severe event requiring third-party assistance, irrespective of glucose level
findings.standardVersion: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6, Table 6.4
findings.sourceTitle: 6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Level 3 A severe event characterized by altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance for treatment of hypoglycemia, irrespective of glucose level
findings.notes: DESIGN-CRITICAL: any implementation that gates Level 3 on a glucose value is wrong. Level 3 must be assertable from clinical state alone, including when no glucose reading exists. Table 6.4 is 'Adapted from Agiostratidou et al.'

findings.assertion: CHANGE FROM OLDER TEACHING: the DKA glucose threshold was explicitly LOWERED from above 250 mg/dL to at or above 200 mg/dL, with the alternative 'prior history of diabetes' clause added.
findings.value: OLD (2009): plasma glucose >13.9 mmol/L (>250 mg/dL). NEW (2024): ≥11.1 mmol/L (≥200 mg/dL) or prior history of diabetes irrespective of glucose
findings.standardVersion: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus report 2024 vs ADA 2009 consensus statement
findings.sourceTitle: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
findings.quote: In this consensus report, we have defined hyperglycaemia as a diagnostic criterion for DKA from >13.9 mmol/l (250 mg/dl) to either a glucose value of ≥11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl) or a prior history of diabetes irrespective of the presenting glucose value.
findings.notes: THE headline change. Verified on both sides: the 2009 Table 1 I retrieved lists all three DKA severity tiers as 'plasma glucose >250 mg/dl'. Minor internal wording wobble: the same report elsewhere says 'a lower glucose value of >11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl)' (> rather than ≥); the tables and ADA 2026 use ≥.

findings.assertion: SUPERSEDED (for contrast): the 2009 ADA criteria graded DKA on ARTERIAL pH and anion gap, and required stupor/coma plus effective osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg for HHS.
findings.value: 2009 DKA: glucose >250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L) at all severities; arterial pH 7.25–7.30 (mild) / 7.00–<7.24 (moderate) / <7.00 (severe); bicarbonate 15–18 / 10–<15 / <10 mEq/L; anion gap >10 (mild) / >12 (moderate and severe); mental status alert / alert-drowsy / stupor-coma. 2009 HHS: glucose >600 mg/dL (33.3 mmol/L); arterial pH >7.30; bicarbonate >18 mEq/L; small urine/serum ketones; effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg; stupor/coma
findings.standardVersion: ADA consensus statement 2009 (Diabetes Care 32(7):1335–1343) — SUPERSEDED
findings.sourceTitle: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adult Patients With Diabetes (Kitabchi, Umpierrez, Miles, Fisher)
findings.quote: Table 1 Diagnostic criteria for DKA and HHS DKA HHS Mild (plasma glucose >250 mg/dl) Moderate (plasma glucose >250 mg/dl) Severe (plasma glucose >250 mg/dl) Plasma glucose >600 mg/dl Arterial pH 7.25–7.30 7.00 to <7.24 <7.00 >7.30 Serum bicarbonate (mEq/l) 15–18 10 to <15 <10 >18 Urine ketone * Positive Positive Positive Small Serum ketone * Positive Positive Positive Small Effective serum osmolality † Variable Variable Variable >320 mOsm/kg Anion gap ‡ >10 >12 >12 Variable Mental status Alert Alert/drowsy Stupor/coma Stupor/coma
findings.notes: Included ONLY as the 'older teaching' baseline — must not be implemented. DOI 10.2337/dc09-9032, PMID 19564476. Four changes are visible by direct comparison: glucose 250→200 mg/dL; arterial→venous pH; anion gap demoted out of the criteria; HHS bicarbonate >18→≥15, effective osmolality >320→>300, and stupor/coma dropped.

findings.assertion: Independent corroboration of the 2024 DKA and HHS criteria from an NIH-hosted reference authored by a co-author of the consensus report.
findings.value: DKA: glucose ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or prior diabetes history; BOHB ≥3.0 mmol/L or urine ketone ≥2+; pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L. HHS: glucose >600 mg/dL (33.3 mmol/L); effective osmolality >300 or total >320 mOsm/kg; BOHB <3.0 mmol/L or urine ketone <2+; pH ≥7.3 and bicarbonate ≥15 mmol/L
findings.standardVersion: Endotext (NCBI Bookshelf), 'Hyperglycemic Crises', Dhatariya K, Mustafa O, Stathi D — last updated 10 June 2025
findings.sourceTitle: Hyperglycemic Crises — Endotext, NCBI Bookshelf
findings.quote: There are four diagnostic criteria as per global consensus (13). 1. Plasma glucose >600 mg/dL (33.3 mmol/L). 2. Hyperosmolality defined as effective osmolality >300 mOsm/kg or total serum osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg. 3. Absence of significant ketonemia: β-hydroxybutyrate <3.0 mmol/L or urine ketone < 2+. 4. Absence of acidosis: pH≥7.3 and bicarbonate concentration ≥ 15 mmol/L.
findings.notes: Used to independently confirm the HHS values, because the consensus report itself encodes them only in a FIGURE image (Fig. 2b) whose numbers are not in the machine-readable text. Ketan Dhatariya is a named author of the 2024 consensus. CAUTION: Endotext's own summary Table 1 contains a units typo — it renders 600 mg/dL as '13.3 mmol/L' and the DKA range as '200-600 mg/dL (11.1-13.3 mmol/L)'; 600 mg/dL is 33.3 mmol/L. Do not propagate that table.

findings.assertion: UK national guidance (JBDS, a co-sponsor of the 2024 consensus) defines DKA with a LOWER bicarbonate threshold than ADA/EASD.
findings.value: Capillary blood glucose above 11 mmol/L (~198 mg/dL) or known diabetes; capillary ketones above 3 mmol/L or urine ketones ++ or more; venous pH less than 7.3 and/or bicarbonate less than 15 mmol/L
findings.standardVersion: JBDS 02, 'The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults', revised March 2023
findings.sourceTitle: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults (JBDS 02)
findings.quote: Diagnostic criteria: all three of the following must be present • capillary blood glucose above 11 mmol/L • capillary ketones above 3 mmol/L or urine ketones ++ or more • venous pH less than 7.3 and/or bicarbonate less than 15 mmol/L
findings.notes: PREDATES the 2024 consensus and the guideline itself flags the divergence: 'The ADA definition is slightly different, and it also uses the anion gap as part of the diagnostic criteria to judge severity'. The JBDS management chart adds the known-diabetes clause: 'Capillary blood glucose (CBG) 11.0mmol/L or known diabetes'.

findings.assertion: JBDS severe-DKA markers are broader than the ADA/EASD biochemical triad, adding haemodynamic, oxygenation, potassium and GCS criteria.
findings.value: Any one or more of: blood ketones >6.0 mmol/L; bicarbonate <5.0 mmol/L; venous/arterial pH <7.0; hypokalaemia on admission (<3.5 mmol/L); GCS <12 or abnormal AVPU; oxygen saturation <92% on air; systolic BP <90 mmHg; pulse >100 or <60 bpm; anion gap >16
findings.standardVersion: JBDS 02, revised March 2023
findings.sourceTitle: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults (JBDS 02)
findings.quote: The presence of one or more of the following may indicate severe DKA: • Blood ketones over 6.0 mmol/L • Bicarbonate level below 5.0 mmol/L • Venous/arterial pH below 7.0 • Hypokalaemia on admission (under 3.5 mmol/L) • GCS less than 12 or abnormal AVPU scale • Oxygen saturation below 92% on air (assuming normal baseline respiratory function) • Systolic BP below 90 mmHg • Pulse over 100 or below 60 bpm • Anion gap above 16
findings.notes: Note JBDS severe bicarbonate is <5.0 whereas ADA/EASD severe is <10 mmol/L — a two-fold difference. JBDS retains the anion gap (>16) for severity; ADA/EASD 2024 dropped it. The non-biochemical markers (GCS, SpO2, SBP, pulse, K+) have no ADA/EASD equivalent and are valuable in low-resource triage where blood gases may be unavailable.

findings.assertion: UK national guidance defines HHS with a lower glucose threshold and uses TOTAL osmolality only, plus a mandatory hypovolaemia criterion.
findings.value: Significant hypovolaemia; measured or calculated serum osmolality ≥320 mOsm/kg using (2×Na+) + glucose + urea; marked hyperglycaemia ≥30.0 mmol/L (~540 mg/dL); without significant hyperketonaemia (ketones ≤3.0 mmol/L; urine ketones <2+); without significant acidosis (pH ≥7.3; venous bicarbonate >15.0 mmol/L)
findings.standardVersion: JBDS 06, 'The Management of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in Adults', 2022
findings.sourceTitle: The Management of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in Adults (JBDS 06)
findings.quote: ENTRY (diagnostic) CRITERIA (ALL must be ticked to establish diagnosis) Significant hypovolaemia ☐ Elevated osmolality ≥320 mOsm/kg - Calculate osmolality using the equation: (2xNa+) + glucose + urea ☐ Marked hyperglycaemia (≥30.0 mmol/L) without significant ketonaemia ☐ (blood ketones ≤3.0 mmol/L; urine ketones<2+) or acidosis (pH≥7.3; venous bicarbonate >15.0 mmol/L
findings.notes: JBDS explicitly acknowledges divergence: 'International guidelines vary as to the precise definition of HHS' and 'HHS should not be diagnosed using biochemical parameters alone.' JBDS requires clinical hypovolaemia as a criterion; ADA does not.

findings.assertion: UK national guidance sets the operational hypoglycaemia threshold at below 4.0 mmol/L, not the ADA's 3.9 mmol/L, and grades severity functionally rather than numerically.
findings.value: Hypoglycaemia defined as blood glucose <4.0 mmol/L (~72 mg/dL); 'non-severe' if self-treated, 'severe' if unable to self-treat and third-party assistance required
findings.standardVersion: JBDS 01, 'The Hospital Management of Hypoglycaemia in Adults with Diabetes Mellitus', revised January 2023
findings.sourceTitle: The Hospital Management of Hypoglycaemia in Adults with Diabetes Mellitus (JBDS 01)
findings.quote: Hypoglycaemia is defined as blood sugar glucose of <4.0mmol/L (if not <4.0mmol/L but symptomatic give a small carbohydrate snack for symptom relief)
findings.notes: Also verbatim: 'it can be defined as "non-severe" if the episode is self-treated and "severe" if unable to self-treat and assistance by a third party is required'; and 'During a hospital admission, any blood glucose less than 4.0mmol/L should be treated. Blood glucose levels between 4.0-6.0mmol/L may indicate looming hypoglycaemia'. The JBDS 'severe' definition maps onto ADA Level 3, but JBDS has no Level 1/Level 2 split.

conflicts.assertion: DKA serum bicarbonate diagnostic threshold
positions: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS 2024 consensus + ADA Standards of Care 2026 Table 16.1: bicarbonate <18 mmol/L
JBDS 02 (March 2023, UK): bicarbonate <15 mmol/L
conflicts.recommendation: Do not silently pick one. A patient with bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, BOHB 3.5 mmol/L and pH 7.32 IS DKA by ADA/EASD but is NOT DKA by JBDS — a clinically material gap. Make the active standard an explicit, auditable configuration value per deployment rather than a hard-coded constant, defaulting to ADA/EASD 2024 (<18) as the more recent and more sensitive rule, and surface the standard's name in the UI next to any DKA flag. Note JBDS 02 predates the 2024 consensus that JBDS itself co-sponsored, so UK guidance is expected to converge; re-check at next JBDS revision. CSO sign-off required.

conflicts.assertion: Internal inconsistency WITHIN the 2024 consensus report on the HHS bicarbonate threshold
positions: Consensus report Table/Fig. 2b as reproduced in ADA Standards of Care 2026 Table 16.1 and in Endotext: 'pH ≥7.3 and bicarbonate concentration ≥15 mmol/L'
Consensus report body prose (Diabetologia, PMC11343900): 'Although most people with HHS have an admission pH ≥7.30 and a bicarbonate level ≥18 mmol/l, mild ketonaemia may be present.'
conflicts.recommendation: Implement ≥15 mmol/L. The ≥18 sentence is descriptive prose about what most patients happen to present with ('most people ... have'), not the stated criterion; the formal criterion is ≥15, and CCJM's review of the report states the change explicitly: 'the bicarbonate level was lowered from 18 to 15 mmol/L to allow for a degree of acidosis that can occur due to insulinopenia.' Two independent reproductions of the criteria table (ADA 2026; Endotext, by a report co-author) both give ≥15. Flag for CSO awareness so the ≥18 sentence is not later 'corrected' into the rules by someone reading only the prose.

conflicts.assertion: HHS plasma glucose diagnostic threshold
positions: ADA/EASD 2024 + ADA Standards of Care 2026: ≥33.3 mmol/L (≥600 mg/dL)
conflicts.recommendation: Roughly a 60 mg/dL gap. Same treatment as the bicarbonate conflict — configurable, labelled, defaulting to ADA/EASD. Because HHS is a clinical-plus-biochemical diagnosis in both systems, a near-threshold glucose should prompt review rather than a binary exclude; consider a 'possible HHS' band spanning 30.0–33.3 mmol/L (540–600 mg/dL) that advises clinician assessment instead of ruling out.

conflicts.assertion: HHS osmolality criterion — which osmolality, and at what cut-point
positions: ADA/EASD 2024 + ADA 2026: calculated EFFECTIVE serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg [2×Na + glucose], OR TOTAL serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg [2×Na + glucose + urea]
JBDS 06 (2022): osmolality ≥320 mOsm/kg computed as (2×Na+) + glucose + urea — i.e. total osmolality only, with no effective-osmolality route
2009 ADA (superseded): EFFECTIVE serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, formula 2[Na+] + glucose(mg/dL)/18
conflicts.recommendation: This is the highest-risk item for a coding error because the same number, 320, attaches to DIFFERENT quantities across standards, and the ADA formula takes glucose in mmol/L while the 2009 formula takes mg/dL and divides by 18. Store which formula produced any osmolality value alongside the value itself, never a bare number. Never compare an effective-osmolality result against a total-osmolality threshold: a patient can cross '320' on one definition and not the other. Explicit CSO sign-off on the formula and units before this ships.

conflicts.assertion: Anion gap's role in diagnosing and grading DKA
positions: ADA/EASD 2024: not recommended as a first-line diagnostic or resolution criterion; absent from ADA 2026 Table 16.1; >12 mmol/L merely indicates high-anion-gap acidosis; retained utility only 'in resource settings where ketone measurement is unavailable'
JBDS 02 (2023): retains anion gap >16 as a severe-DKA marker
ADA 2009 (superseded): anion gap >10 (mild) / >12 (moderate and severe) was a graded row in the diagnostic table
conflicts.recommendation: Directly consequential for MedSync's Ugandan deployment. Follow ADA/EASD 2024 and do not use anion gap as a primary diagnostic criterion where beta-hydroxybutyrate testing exists — but the consensus report explicitly preserves it as a fallback where ketone measurement is unavailable, which will be a real condition at Mulago and district sites. Recommend an explicit degraded-mode pathway: when no BOHB or ketone result is recorded, permit an anion-gap-based provisional assessment that is visibly labelled as a fallback with lower specificity, and never let it silently substitute for a ketone measurement in the record. CSO sign-off required on the fallback logic.

conflicts.assertion: Hypoglycaemia alert threshold
positions: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Table 6.4: Level 1 is glucose <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L)
JBDS 01 (January 2023, UK): hypoglycaemia is blood glucose <4.0 mmol/L (~72 mg/dL)
conflicts.recommendation: A 0.1 mmol/L difference that matters only at the boundary, but it changes whether a 3.95 mmol/L reading alerts. The UK '<4.0' is a deliberate operational rounding ('make four the floor') chosen for bedside memorability, not a competing physiological claim. Either is defensible; prefer <4.0 mmol/L for bedside alerting if MedSync's numeric display is in mmol/L, since alerting on a threshold the nurse cannot see on the meter creates confusion. Record the ADA levels as the classification scheme for reporting and the alert threshold as a separate, configurable value — they are different things and should not share one constant.

conflicts.assertion: DKA severity — biochemical-only versus multi-parameter grading
positions: ADA/EASD 2024 Table 2: graded on BOHB, pH, bicarbonate and mental status; severe = BOHB >6.0, pH <7.0, bicarbonate <10 mmol/L, stupor/coma
JBDS 02 (2023): severe flagged by any one of nine markers including bicarbonate <5.0 mmol/L, plus GCS <12, SpO2 <92%, SBP <90 mmHg, pulse >100 or <60, K+ <3.5 mmol/L, anion gap >16
conflicts.recommendation: The bicarbonate cut-points for 'severe' differ two-fold (<10 vs <5.0 mmol/L), so the two systems will disagree on a substantial middle band. Consider treating these as complementary rather than competing: use ADA/EASD Table 2 for the graded mild/moderate/severe classification and level-of-care suggestion, and additionally raise a high-acuity flag on any JBDS red-flag marker, since the JBDS haemodynamic and neurological markers capture sick patients that a purely biochemical grade can miss and are obtainable without a blood gas. Both must be advisory only — the consensus report states severity and disposition are ultimately a clinical decision. CSO sign-off required.

unverifiable: The exact rendering of Figure 2a and Figure 2b of the 2024 consensus report — the authoritative diagnostic-criteria figures — could NOT be read directly. They are published as images, and their numeric content is absent from the machine-readable full text of PMC11343900. I reconstructed the criteria from three fetched secondary reproductions that agree with one another (ADA Standards of Care 2026 Table 16.1; Endotext, authored by consensus co-author Dhatariya; and the CCJM review), NOT from the figures themselves. Treat the DKA/HHS criteria as verified-by-corroboration rather than read-at-source, and have the CSO confirm against the published figure or the slide deck the report references ('This figure is available as part of a downloadable slideset').

The Diabetes Care version of the consensus report (47(8):1257–1275, doi 10.2337/dci24-0032, PMID 39052901, PMC11272983) could not be retrieved in full text — diabetesjournals.org returned HTTP 403 and the Europe PMC full-text endpoint returned an empty body, indicating it is not open access. I therefore could not confirm that the Diabetes Care and Diabetologia co-publications are numerically identical in every table and figure. I have assumed they are; this is unconfirmed.

Whether the 2024 consensus states an ARTERIAL pH equivalent alongside the venous threshold. The report clearly uses venous sampling for monitoring, and ADA 2026 Table 16.1 says only 'pH <7.3' without specifying the sample site. The 2009 statement explicitly said 'Arterial pH'. Arterial and venous pH are not interchangeable (venous typically runs ~0.02–0.04 lower). Whether the 7.3 cut-point is intended as venous, arterial, or either is NOT established by anything I read, and this is a real implementation ambiguity that needs CSO adjudication.

The exact boundary operators are inconsistent across sources and I could not resolve them at source. The consensus prose says the new glucose criterion is '>11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl)' in one sentence and '≥11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl)' in another; ADA 2026 Table 16.1 uses '≥200 mg/dL'. For HHS glucose, ADA 2026 says '≥600 mg/dL' while Endotext says '>600 mg/dL'. These matter only for exact-boundary readings but should be pinned by the CSO before coding comparators.

No DKA severity grading table appears in ADA Standards of Care 2026 Section 16 — I checked and it contains Table 16.1 (diagnostic criteria) and Table 16.2 (clinical presentation), but no mild/moderate/severe table. The severity grading exists ONLY in the consensus report itself (Table 2, which I did read verbatim from the Diabetologia full text). So the severity grading has a single primary source, not two.

Mental status in DKA severity is specified only as coarse labels — 'Alert', 'Alert/drowsy', 'Stupor/coma'. No GCS or AVPU cut-points are given anywhere in the ADA/EASD material I read. Only JBDS supplies a numeric neurological threshold (GCS <12). Mapping the ADA labels onto a GCS or AVPU value for structured data capture would be an invention on my part and must be a CSO decision.

Whether the 2024 consensus specifies a urine-ketone equivalent for the DKA severity tiers. Table 2 grades ketonaemia only by beta-hydroxybutyrate (3.0–6.0 and >6.0 mmol/L). There is no stated urine-dipstick equivalent for severity grading, so DKA severity is NOT gradable on urine ketones alone — a significant limitation for sites without BOHB meters that I could not find guidance to work around.

Point-of-care BOHB accuracy above 5 mmol/L is explicitly questioned by the consensus report, which sits awkwardly against a severity boundary at 6.0 mmol/L. The report notes 'there is concern about how accurate POCT instruments are compared with laboratory instruments for measuring β-hydroxybutyrate levels ≥5 mmol/l' but gives no guidance on how to grade severity when the only available reading is a POC value in that range. Unresolved.

Paediatric and adolescent criteria are entirely out of scope of everything I fetched. The 2024 consensus is adults-only, and JBDS 02 explicitly redirects: 'Where individuals aged 16-18 years are managed by paediatric teams the paediatric guidelines should be followed (BSPED).' I did not retrieve BSPED or ISPAD criteria, which differ. If MedSync will triage under-18s, this is a gap that must be filled separately.

Pregnancy-specific DKA thresholds were not verified. Pregnancy is named in the consensus report as a cause of euglycaemic DKA, but I found no pregnancy-specific numeric criteria in anything I fetched. Obstetric DKA can occur at markedly lower glucose values; do not assume the adult thresholds transfer.

WHO, IDF, KDIGO, IWGDF, ICDR, ETDRS, ESC and ISH were not consulted — none of them are standard-setting bodies for acute hyperglycaemic or hypoglycaemic emergency criteria, so no findings are attributed to them. I did not search them rather than searched-and-found-nothing.

DKA and HHS RESOLUTION criteria were outside the requested scope and I captured them only incidentally and incompletely. I read that HHS resolution is 'measured or calculated serum osmolality falls to <300 mOsm/kg ... and the blood glucose is <13.9 mmol/l (250 mg/dl)' and that the anion gap 'should be avoided as a criterion of DKA resolution', but I did NOT systematically verify the DKA resolution criteria (BOHB and pH targets). Do not treat this report as a source for resolution logic.

Endotext contains a units error in its own summary Table 1, rendering 600 mg/dL as '13.3 mmol/L' and the DKA glucose range as '200-600 mg/dL (11.1-13.3 mmol/L)'. The correct conversion is 33.3 mmol/L. I used Endotext only for the criteria list in its body text, which is internally correct, but this demonstrates that even an NIH-hosted source carries unit typos — a reason to have the CSO re-verify every conversion before these values reach a patient-facing surface.

audit.assertion: DKA hyperglycaemia criterion: glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (≥200 mg/dL) OR prior history of diabetes at any glucose value — ADA SOC 2026 Section 16 Table 16.1
audit.reason: Fetched PMC12690180 = '16. Diabetes Care in the Hospital: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026', Diabetes Care 2025 Dec 8;49(Suppl 1):S339–S355. Table 16.1 reads verbatim 'Glucose ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or prior history of diabetes'. Independently corroborated by the 2024 consensus (PMC11343900), Endotext NBK279052, and CCJM 92(3):152-158. Both units present. Source exists and contains the claim; attribution to ADA/Section 16/Table 16.1 is exact.

audit.assertion: Euglycaemic DKA occurs in ~10% of DKA presentations, now mostly caused by SGLT2 inhibitors — ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS 2024 consensus, Diabetologia 67:1455–1479
audit.reason: Fetched PMC11343900 = 'Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report', Diabetologia vol 67 issue 8, pp 1455–1479, 2024 — citation details match exactly, including volume and page range. Text states 'approximately 10% of patients with DKA present with euglycaemic DKA' and that SGLT2 inhibitor use 'has accounted for the majority of cases of euglycaemic DKA'. Sponsoring bodies confirmed as ADA, EASD, JBDS, AACE and DTS, so the EASD attribution is legitimate.

audit.assertion: DKA ketosis criterion: β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L OR urine ketone strip ≥2+ — ADA SOC 2026 Table 16.1
audit.reason: Table 16.1 in PMC12690180 reads verbatim 'β-Hydroxybutyrate concentration ≥3.0 mmol/L or urine ketone strip 2+ or greater'. The finding's note that BOHB is reported in mmol/L in both unit systems is correct and is the reason no mg/dL conversion is required. Corroborated verbatim by CCJM 92(3):152-158 and Endotext NBK279052.

audit.assertion: β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L has >90% sensitivity and specificity for DKA — 2024 consensus report
audit.reason: PMC11343900 states verbatim: 'Blood concentrations of β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/l correlate well with acid–base changes, with >90% sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis of DKA.' Value, units and attribution all match the retrieved document.

audit.assertion: Urine ketone testing underestimates early DKA and overestimates late DKA; false positives with sulfhydryl drugs (captopril) and valproate — 2024 consensus report
audit.reason: PMC11343900 states 'Reliance on urine ketone testing can underestimate the severity of ketonaemia early in the course of DKA' and 'overestimate its severity later', and that 'several sulfhydryl drugs (e.g., captopril) and medications such as valproate can give false-positive nitroprusside urine tests.' Both the directional-error claim and the named interfering drugs are present in the fetched text.

audit.assertion: DKA acidosis criterion is pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L, AND venous (not arterial) sampling is used / 'venous pH acceptable' — both attributed to ADA SOC 2026 Table 16.1
audit.reason: The numeric half is correct and correctly attributed: Table 16.1 reads 'pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate concentration <18 mmol/L'. The venous half is NOT. I searched the full text of PMC12690180 for 'venous' and 'arterial': Table 16.1 carries no venous/arterial designation and no footnote on sampling site, and the sole occurrence of 'venous' in the whole of Section 16 is the Figure 16.1 caption on MONITORING ('Monitoring requirements for electrolytes, kidney function, venous pH, osmolality, and glucose') — not a diagnostic-criteria statement in Table 16.1. The venous recommendation is real but belongs to other documents: the 2024 consensus report directs that 'Initial samples should be taken for ... venous blood gases' and sets resolution at 'venous pH ≥7.3', and JBDS 02 (March 2023) states the criterion as 'venous pH less than 7.3'. Fact survives; the citation does not. Note also that Table 16.1 contains no severity grading at all, so it cannot be the source of any venous-vs-arterial severity convention.
audit.correctedValue: ADA SOC 2026 Table 16.1 states only: pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L (= <18 mEq/L), with no specification of venous vs arterial sampling. The venous-sampling recommendation should be cited to the 2024 consensus report ('venous blood gases'; resolution at 'venous pH ≥7.3') or to JBDS 02 March 2023 ('venous pH less than 7.3').
audit.correctedSource: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11343900/ (for the venous-sampling claim); https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12690180/ (for the pH/bicarbonate values only)

audit.assertion: Anion gap demoted: >12 mmol/L indicates high anion gap metabolic acidosis but is not recommended as a first-line diagnostic or resolution criterion — 2024 consensus report
audit.reason: PMC11343900 states 'An anion gap >12 mmol/l indicates the presence of a high anion gap metabolic acidosis consistent with DKA' and that the anion gap 'is not recommended as a first-line diagnostic or resolution criterion' because of mixed acid-base disorders. The demotion framing is accurate — corroborated by contrast with the 2009 statement (PMC2699725), where anion gap was an explicit severity-grading row (>10 mild, >12 moderate and severe).

audit.assertion: MILD DKA: BOHB 3.0–6.0 mmol/L; pH >7.25 to <7.30 OR bicarbonate 15–18 mmol/L; alert — 2024 consensus Table 2
audit.reason: Retrieved Table 2 from PMC11343900 row by row. Mild column: 'D' glucose ≥11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl); 'K' β-hydroxybutyrate 3.0–6.0 mmol/l; 'A' 'pH >7.25 to <7.30 or bicarbonate 15–18 mmol/l'; mental status Alert. Every value in the finding, including the glucose row applying at all severities and the disjunctive 'or' between pH and bicarbonate, matches the fetched table exactly.

audit.assertion: MODERATE DKA: BOHB 3.0–6.0 mmol/L; pH 7.0–7.25; bicarbonate 10 to <15 mmol/L; alert/drowsy — 2024 consensus Table 2
audit.reason: Table 2 moderate column in PMC11343900: glucose ≥11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl); β-hydroxybutyrate 3.0–6.0 mmol/l; pH 7.0–7.25; bicarbonate 10 to <15 mmol/l; mental status Alert/drowsy. Exact match on all five variables.

audit.assertion: SEVERE DKA: BOHB >6.0 mmol/L; pH <7.0; bicarbonate <10 mmol/L; stupor/coma — 2024 consensus Table 2
audit.reason: Table 2 severe column in PMC11343900: glucose ≥11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl); β-hydroxybutyrate >6.0 mmol/l; pH <7.0; bicarbonate <10 mmol/l; mental status Stupor/coma. Exact match. (Table 2 also carries a 'suggested level of care' row — ICU for severe — which the finding omits but does not misstate.)

audit.assertion: DKA severity grading does not require every variable to be met; admission site and level of care are a clinical decision — 2024 consensus Table 2 footnote
audit.reason: The footnote is present verbatim in PMC11343900: 'Not all variables need to be fulfilled to be defined as either mild, moderate or severe, and the admission site and level of care are ultimately a clinical decision.' The finding paraphrases it accurately. This is a clinically important caveat and is correctly attributed to the Table 2 footnote rather than the table body.

audit.assertion: HHS hyperglycaemia criterion: plasma glucose ≥33.3 mmol/L (≥600 mg/dL) — ADA SOC 2026 Table 16.1
audit.reason: Table 16.1 in PMC12690180 reads 'Plasma glucose ≥600 mg/dL (33.3 mmol/L)', and I specifically verified the operator is ≥ (greater-than-or-equal), not >. Both units given. Worth flagging for downstream use, though it does not make this finding wrong: the same threshold is rendered as '>600 mg/dL' in Endotext NBK279052 and in the CCJM summary wording, so ≥ vs > differs by source. The finding cites ADA and uses ADA's operator, which is correct.

audit.assertion: HHS hyperosmolarity: calculated effective osmolality >300 mOsm/kg [2×Na+ + glucose]; OR total osmolality >320 mOsm/kg [2×Na+ + glucose + urea] — ADA SOC 2026 Table 16.1
audit.reason: Verified against Table 16.1 in PMC12690180 including both printed formulas; the total-osmolality formula does include urea, exactly as stated: '2 × Na+ (mmol/L) + glucose (mmol/L) + urea (mmol/L)'. Independently corroborated by CCJM 92(3):152-158 ('calculated effective serum osmolality greater than 300 mOsm/kg or total serum osmolality greater than 320 mOsm/kg') and Endotext NBK279052. This is the value my first automated read of the consensus PDF got wrong (it returned >320 effective and a 250 mg/dL glucose threshold); two further independent sources refute that and support the finding as written.

audit.assertion: HHS requires absence of significant ketonaemia: BOHB <3.0 mmol/L OR urine ketone strip <2+ — ADA SOC 2026 Table 16.1
audit.reason: Table 16.1 in PMC12690180: 'β-Hydroxybutyrate concentration <3.0 mmol/L OR urine ketone strip less than 2+'. Matches. Minor cross-source note (not an error in this finding): CCJM renders the urine limb as 'a urine ketone strip of 2+ or lower', which is not identical to ADA's 'less than 2+'; the finding follows ADA's stricter wording, which is the body it cites.

audit.assertion: HHS requires absence of acidosis: pH ≥7.3 AND bicarbonate ≥15 mmol/L — ADA SOC 2026 Table 16.1
audit.reason: Table 16.1 in PMC12690180: 'pH ≥7.3 and bicarbonate concentration ≥15 mmol/L'. The conjunction is AND, as the finding states. Corroborated verbatim by Endotext NBK279052 and CCJM 92(3):152-158. Note the contrast the finding implies is real: the 2009 statement used bicarbonate >18 mEq/L for HHS, so the threshold moved from 18 to 15.

audit.assertion: Altered mental status is no longer a diagnostic criterion for HHS, though cognitive change remains a common clinical feature — ADA SOC 2026 Table 16.1 (no mental-status row) + CCJM 2025 review
audit.reason: Both limbs verified. (a) I confirmed Table 16.1 in PMC12690180 contains no row for mental status, cognitive state or level of consciousness for either DKA or HHS, and no severity grading. (b) The Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine review is real and I fetched it: 'Hyperglycemic crises in adults: A look at the 2024 consensus report', Rodriguez Alvarez P, San Martin VT, Morey-Vargas OL, Cleve Clin J Med 2025;92(3):152-158, which states verbatim 'Mental status impairment is no longer a diagnostic criterion. Although past studies linked osmolality with mental status, many individuals, though very ill, do not necessarily have mental impairment, so this is no longer a requirement for diagnosis of HHS.' (c) The 2009 contrast is verified in PMC2699725 (stupor/coma listed for HHS). Two caveats that do not change the verdict: no URL was supplied for the CCJM half of the citation, and the 'change in cognitive state common' wording sits in Table 16.2, not Table 16.1.
audit.correctedSource: https://www.ccjm.org/content/92/3/152 (the CCJM half of this citation had no URL supplied)

audit.assertion: Level 1 hypoglycaemia: glucose <3.9 mmol/L (<70 mg/dL) and ≥3.0 mmol/L (≥54 mg/dL) — ADA SOC 2026 Section 6 Table 6.4
audit.reason: Fetched PMC12690178 = '6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026', Diabetes Care 49(Suppl 1):S132–S149. Table 6.4 Level 1 reads verbatim 'Glucose <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) and ≥54 mg/dL (≥3.0 mmol/L)'. Both units are given in the source itself; section number and table number are correct.

audit.assertion: Level 2 hypoglycaemia: glucose <3.0 mmol/L (<54 mg/dL), the threshold for neuroglycopenic symptoms requiring immediate action — ADA SOC 2026 Table 6.4
audit.reason: The numeric claim is exact: Table 6.4 in PMC12690178 reads 'Glucose <54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L)'. Value, operator and both units verified. One caveat on the surrounding prose rather than the value: the phrase 'threshold for neuroglycopenic symptoms, requiring immediate action' is an interpretive gloss and does not appear as such in the Table 6.4 glycemic-criteria cell I retrieved, which carries the number alone. The gloss is conventional and not misleading, but should not be quoted as ADA table wording.

audit.assertion: Level 3 hypoglycaemia has no numeric threshold — a severe event requiring third-party assistance, irrespective of glucose level — ADA SOC 2026 Table 6.4
audit.reason: Table 6.4 in PMC12690178 reads verbatim: 'A severe event characterized by altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance for treatment of hypoglycemia, irrespective of glucose level.' The finding's central point — that Level 3 is defined by severity and not by a number — is exactly what the source says, and correctly carries no fabricated numeric threshold.

audit.assertion: The DKA glucose threshold was explicitly lowered from >13.9 mmol/L (>250 mg/dL) in 2009 to ≥11.1 mmol/L (≥200 mg/dL) or prior history of diabetes in 2024
audit.reason: This is the strongest-sourced finding in the set: PMC11343900 contains the change stated in the first person by the panel — 'In this consensus report, we have defined hyperglycaemia as a diagnostic criterion for DKA from >13.9 mmol/l (250 mg/dl) to either a glucose value of ≥11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl) or a prior history of diabetes irrespective of the presenting glucose value.' The 2009 side is independently verified in PMC2699725 (plasma glucose >250 mg/dl at all three severities). Both directions of the comparison checked against their own primary documents.

audit.assertion: 2009 ADA criteria (superseded): DKA graded on arterial pH and anion gap; HHS required stupor/coma and effective osmolality >320 mOsm/kg
audit.reason: Fetched PMC2699725 = 'Hyperglycemic Crises in Adult Patients With Diabetes', Diabetes Care 32(7):1335–1343, 2009, ADA — citation matches exactly. Table 1 verified point by point: glucose >250 mg/dl at all severities; arterial pH 7.25–7.30 / 7.00–<7.24 / <7.00; bicarbonate 15–18 / 10–<15 / <10 mEq/l; anion gap >10 / >12 / >12; mental status alert / alert-drowsy / stupor-coma. HHS row: glucose >600 mg/dl, arterial pH >7.30, bicarbonate >18 mEq/l, small urine/serum ketones, effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, stupor/coma. Every figure in the finding, including the easily-garbled anion-gap split (>10 mild vs >12 moderate/severe), is correct. Correctly labelled SUPERSEDED.

audit.assertion: Endotext 'Hyperglycemic Crises' (Dhatariya K, Mustafa O, Stathi D, updated 10 June 2025) independently corroborates the 2024 DKA and HHS criteria
audit.reason: Fetched NBK279052: chapter title, all three authors and the 'last update June 10, 2025' date match the citation exactly. DKA criteria verified: 'Hyperglycemia ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or a prior history of diabetes'; 'venous or capillary β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L or in the early stages of DKA urine ketone 2+ or greater' (so the finding's urine-ketone limb is genuinely present, which I initially doubted); 'pH<7.3 and/or bicarbonate concentration <18 mmol/L'. HHS verified: glucose >600 mg/dL (33.3 mmol/L), effective osmolality >300 or total >320 mOsm/kg, BOHB <3.0 mmol/L or urine ketone <2+, pH≥7.3 and bicarbonate ≥15 mmol/L. I also checked the authorship claim adversarially: Ketan K. Dhatariya is indeed the twelfth and final author of the 2024 consensus report, so 'co-author of the consensus report' is accurate — meaning this is genuinely a same-author restatement rather than a fully independent source, which slightly weakens it as corroboration even though every value checks out.

audit.assertion: JBDS 02 (revised March 2023) DKA criteria: glucose >11 mmol/L or known diabetes; ketones >3 mmol/L or urine ketones ++; venous pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L
audit.reason: URL is live; I downloaded the 2.4 MB PDF and extracted its text directly rather than relying on a summariser. Cover confirms 'The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults, Revised March 2023' and 'This document is coded JBDS 02'. Diagnostic criteria box verbatim: 'capillary blood glucose above 11 mmol/L / capillary ketones above 3 mmol/L or urine ketones ++ or more / venous pH less than 7.3 and/or bicarbonate less than 15 mmol/L'. The 'or known diabetes' clause the finding adds is not in that box but IS in the clerking proforma: 'Capillary blood glucose (CBG) 11.0mmol/L or known diabetes' — so the finding is supported, though it merges two locations in the document. The headline contrast is correct: JBDS bicarbonate <15 mmol/L is lower than ADA/EASD <18 mmol/L, a genuine international disagreement worth carrying as a conflict.

audit.assertion: JBDS 02 severe-DKA markers: ketones >6.0, bicarbonate <5.0, pH <7.0, K+ <3.5, GCS <12/abnormal AVPU, SpO2 <92%, SBP <90, pulse >100 or <60, anion gap >16
audit.reason: Extracted verbatim from the JBDS 02 PDF text: 'The presence of one or more of the following may indicate severe DKA: Blood ketones over 6.0 mmol/L; Bicarbonate level below 5.0 mmol/L; Venous/arterial pH below 7.0; Hypokalaemia on admission (under 3.5 mmol/L); GCS less than 12 or abnormal AVPU scale; Oxygen saturation below 92% on air (assuming normal baseline respiratory function); Systolic BP below 90 mmHg; Pulse over 100 or below 60 bpm; Anion gap above 16.' All nine criteria match, including the anion-gap value of 16 and the 'any one or more' logic. Note JBDS uses the potassium-inclusive anion gap formula [(Na+ + K+) − (Cl− + HCO3−)], which is why its cut-point (16) is higher than the ADA/EASD 12 — the two numbers are not interchangeable, and the finding does not state the formula.

audit.assertion: JBDS 06 (2022) HHS criteria: hypovolaemia; osmolality ≥320 mOsm/kg via (2×Na+)+glucose+urea; glucose ≥30.0 mmol/L; ketones ≤3.0 mmol/L / urine <2+; pH ≥7.3; bicarbonate >15.0 mmol/L
audit.reason: URL is live; I downloaded the 7.2 MB PDF and extracted the text. Cover confirms 'The Management of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in Adults, February 2022' (finding says 2022 — correct). Definition section verbatim: 'marked hypovolaemia / measured or calculated serum osmolality usually ≥320 mOsm/kg / marked hyperglycaemia (≥30 mmol/L) / without significant hyperketonaemia (ketones ≤3.0 mmol/L) / without significant acidosis (pH ≥7.3 and blood or serum bicarbonate ≥15.0 mmol/L)'. The osmolality formula '[(2Na+) + glucose + urea]' is confirmed twice in the document, so the 'total osmolality only' contrast with ADA's effective-osmolality option is fair. The 'urine ketones <2+' and 'venous bicarbonate >15.0 mmol/L' phrasing is confirmed on the bedside monitoring chart. Three caveats that do not overturn the values: the source says 'usually ≥320', not a hard ≥320; JBDS states plainly that 'A precise definition of HHS has not been agreed', so 'defines HHS' overstates a document that offers characteristic features; and the document is internally inconsistent on bicarbonate, using ≥15.0 in the definition and >15.0 in the pathway box — the finding reproduces only the latter. 30 mmol/L ≈ 540 mg/dL is arithmetically correct.

audit.assertion: JBDS 01 (revised January 2023): hypoglycaemia is blood glucose <4.0 mmol/L (~72 mg/dL); 'non-severe' if self-treated, 'severe' if third-party assistance required
audit.reason: URL is live; I downloaded the PDF and extracted the text. Cover confirms 'The Hospital Management of Hypoglycaemia in Adults with Diabetes Mellitus, Revised January 2023' and 'coded JBDS 01'. Threshold verbatim: 'All non-pregnant, adults with diabetes in hospital with a blood glucose level less than 4.0mmol/L (with or without symptoms of hypoglycaemia) should be treated ... remember "4.0 is the floor"'. Severity wording verbatim: 'it can be defined as "non-severe" if the episode is self-treated and "severe" if unable to self-treat and assistance by a third party is required'. 4.0 mmol/L × 18 = 72 mg/dL, correct. The stated ADA/JBDS conflict is real and correctly recorded: JBDS operates at <4.0 mmol/L versus ADA Level 1 at <3.9 mmol/L (<70 mg/dL).

bundle.domain: Diabetic kidney disease (KDIGO CKD staging, albuminuria, low-resource dipstick pathway) and diabetic retinopathy (ICDR/ETDRS severity, DME, screening intervals)

findings.assertion: KDIGO classifies CKD by GFR category G1-G5 with these exact eGFR cut-offs.
findings.value: G1 ≥90; G2 60-89; G3a 45-59; G3b 30-44; G4 15-29; G5 <15 — all in ml/min per 1.73 m² (no conventional/SI dual unit exists for eGFR)
findings.standardVersion: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of CKD; Kidney Int 2024;105(4S):S117-S314. Table 2.
findings.quote: Table 2 | GFR categories in CKD — G1 ≥90 Normal or high; G2 60–89 Mildly decreased; G3a 45–59 Mildly to moderately decreased; G3b 30–44 Moderately to severely decreased; G4 15–29 Severely decreased; G5 <15 Kidney failure
findings.notes: Footnote in the same table: 'Relative to the young adult level. In the absence of evidence of kidney damage, neither G1 nor G2 fulfils the criteria for CKD.' Downloaded the official kdigo.org PDF via curl (WebFetch is 403-blocked on kdigo.org) and extracted text locally.

findings.assertion: KDIGO classifies albuminuria as categories A1/A2/A3 with these ACR and AER cut-offs.
findings.value: A1 (normal to mildly increased): AER <30 mg/24 h; ACR <3 mg/mmol (SI) = <30 mg/g (conventional). A2 (moderately increased): AER 30-300 mg/24 h; ACR 3-30 mg/mmol = 30-300 mg/g. A3 (severely increased): AER >300 mg/24 h; ACR >30 mg/mmol = >300 mg/g.
findings.standardVersion: KDIGO 2024 CKD Guideline, Table 3 (identical to KDIGO 2012 Table 6)
findings.quote: Table 3 | Albuminuria categories in chronic kidney disease — A1 <30 <3 <30 Normal to mildly increased; A2 30–300 3–30 30–300 Moderately increased; A3 >300 >30 >300 Severely increased (columns: AER mg/24 h, ACR mg/mmol, ACR mg/g)
findings.notes: Exact SI conversion given in the same guideline's conversion-factor table: 'Albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) mg/g × 0.113 = mg/mmol'. A2 historically = 'microalbuminuria', A3 = 'macroalbuminuria' (KDIGO 2012 explicitly maps these). CAUTION for implementation: the same 2024 guideline's Figure 13 renders the boundaries as 30–299 / ≥300 mg/g (3–29 / ≥30 mg/mmol) — see conflicts.

findings.assertion: CKD requires an abnormality of kidney structure or function present for a minimum of 3 months; albuminuria qualifies as a marker of kidney damage at ACR ≥30 mg/g (≥3 mg/mmol), and decreased GFR means <60 ml/min per 1.73 m².
findings.value: Duration ≥3 months; ACR ≥30 mg/g (≥3 mg/mmol); GFR <60 ml/min per 1.73 m² (categories G3a-G5)
findings.standardVersion: KDIGO 2024 CKD Guideline, Table 1
findings.quote: Table 1 | Criteria for chronic kidney disease (either of the following present for a minimum of 3 months) — Markers of kidney damage (1 or more): Albuminuria (ACR ≥30 mg/g [≥3 mg/mmol]) … Decreased GFR: GFR <60 ml/min per 1.73 m2 (GFR categories G3a–G5)
findings.notes: This is the single most important gate for a decision-support tool: a one-off abnormal ACR or eGFR is NOT CKD.

findings.assertion: KDIGO 2024 confirmation rule — an incidentally detected abnormal ACR must be repeated, and an ACR ≥30 mg/g on a random untimed sample must be confirmed on a subsequent first-morning-void midstream sample; chronicity requires a minimum of 3 months.
findings.value: Repeat/confirm ACR ≥30 mg/g (≥3 mg/mmol); confirmatory sample = first morning void, midstream; chronicity = minimum 3 months
findings.standardVersion: KDIGO 2024 CKD Guideline, Practice Points 1.1.1.2, 1.1.3.1, 1.1.3.2, 1.3.1.2
findings.quote: Practice Point 1.1.1.2: Following incidental detection of elevated urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR), hematuria, or low estimated GFR (eGFR), repeat tests to confirm presence of CKD. … Practice Point 1.3.1.2: … Confirm ACR ≥30 mg/g (≥3 mg/mmol) on a random untimed urine with a subsequent first morning void in the morning midstream urine sample. … Practice Point 1.1.3.2: Do not assume chronicity based upon a single abnormal level for eGFR and ACR
