findings.sourceTitle: IWGDF Practical Guidelines (2023 update), Appendix 2: Toe pressure and TBI measurement using photoplethysmography
findings.quote: A TBI below 0.7 is considered to be abnormal, i.e. indicative for PAD
findings.notes: TBI = toe pressure / highest of left and right brachial pressures. Toe cuff placed at base of hallux (or second digit), cuff size approx. 1.5x digit diameter, PPG probe at distal toe pulp. TBI is more reliable than ABI when medial calcification is present.

findings.assertion: Toe pressure thresholds predict healing and major amputation in people with diabetes and a foot ulcer or gangrene.
findings.value: Toe pressure >=30 mmHg (approx. 4.0 kPa) increases pre-test probability of healing by up to 30%; toe pressure <30 mmHg increases pre-test probability of major amputation by approximately 20%
findings.standardVersion: 2023 intersocietal IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline, Recommendation 7 (Conditional, Low)
findings.sourceTitle: Intersocietal IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline (2023 update)
findings.quote: A toe pressure ≥ 30 mmHg increases the pre-test probability of healing by up to 30% and a value < 30mmHg increases the pretest probability of major amputation by approximately 20%.
findings.notes: UNITS: the guideline states mmHg only. The kPa figure is my arithmetic conversion (1 mmHg = 0.1333 kPa), NOT a value printed in the source — flag it as derived if displayed. mmol/L and mg/dL do not apply to any value in this domain.

findings.assertion: TcPO2 is the IWGDF fallback perfusion test when toe pressure cannot be measured.
findings.value: TcPO2 >=25 mmHg (approx. 3.3 kPa) increases pre-test probability of healing by up to 45%
findings.standardVersion: 2023 intersocietal IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline, Recommendation 8 (Conditional)
findings.sourceTitle: Intersocietal IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline (2023 update)
findings.quote: A TcPO2 ≥ 25 mmHg increases the pre-test probability of healing by up to 45% and value < 25 mmHg
findings.notes: kPa value is my derived conversion, not printed in source. Note the guideline separately uses a <30 mmHg TcPO2 figure for defining severe ischaemia — see conflicts. TcPO2/SPP require expensive equipment, hence the conditional recommendation.

findings.assertion: IWGDF defines a set of clinical findings of ischaemia that should prompt considering revascularisation in a person with diabetes, PAD and a foot ulcer.
findings.value: Findings of ischaemia: absent pulses; monophasic or absent pedal Doppler waveforms; ankle pressure <100 mmHg (approx. 13.3 kPa); or toe pressure <60 mmHg (approx. 8.0 kPa)
findings.standardVersion: 2023 intersocietal IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline, Best Practice Statement 12
findings.sourceTitle: Intersocietal IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline (2023 update)
findings.quote: Findings of ischaemia include absent pulses, monophasic or absent pedal Doppler waveforms, ankle pressure <100 mmHg or toe pressure <60 mmHg. Consult a vascular specialist unless major amputation is considered medically urgent.
findings.notes: This is a Best Practice Statement, not a GRADE-rated recommendation. Note these thresholds are considerably less severe than the urgent-referral thresholds in BPS 13 — two different action tiers. kPa values derived by me.

findings.assertion: IWGDF defines severe ischaemia requiring urgent vascular specialist consultation by a specific threshold set.
findings.value: Severe ischaemia: ABI <0.4, OR ankle pressure <50 mmHg (approx. 6.7 kPa), OR toe pressure <30 mmHg (approx. 4.0 kPa), OR TcPO2 <30 mmHg (approx. 4.0 kPa), OR monophasic/absent pedal Doppler waveforms
findings.standardVersion: 2023 intersocietal IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline, Best Practice Statement 13
findings.sourceTitle: Intersocietal IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline (2023 update)
findings.quote: severe ischaemia i.e., an ankle-brachial index <0.4, ankle pressure <50mmHg, toe pressure <30mmHg or transcutaneous oxygen pressure <30mmHg or monophasic or absent pedal Doppler waveforms, urgently consult a vascular specialist regarding possible revascularisation
findings.notes: Best Practice Statement. The Practical Guidelines restate this with TcPO2 <25 mmHg rather than <30 mmHg — see conflicts. kPa values derived by me, not in source.

findings.assertion: An ulcer failing to heal despite optimal management mandates vascular reassessment regardless of non-invasive test results.
findings.value: Practical Guidelines: no signs of healing within 4-6 weeks. PAD Guideline BPS 15: less than 50% reduction in wound area within 4 weeks
findings.standardVersion: 2023 update (Practical Guidelines s4.2.2; PAD Guideline BPS 15)
findings.sourceTitle: IWGDF Practical Guidelines (2023 update), section 4.2.2 Restoration of tissue perfusion
findings.quote: When an ulcer fails to show signs of healing within 4-6 weeks, despite optimal management, consider angiography and revascularisation, irrespective of the results of the vascular diagnostic tests described above.
findings.notes: The 'irrespective of the results' clause is a deliberate safety override — normal ABI/TBI must not suppress this escalation. The two IWGDF documents phrase the trigger differently (4-6 weeks/no signs of healing vs 4 weeks/<50% area reduction).

findings.assertion: An absent or monophasic pedal Doppler signal is abnormal and indicates PAD; triphasic and biphasic waveforms are normal.
findings.value: Triphasic or biphasic = normal; monophasic or absent = abnormal, indicative of PAD
findings.standardVersion: 2023 update (Practical Guidelines, Appendix 2, Figure 7)
findings.sourceTitle: IWGDF Practical Guidelines (2023 update), Appendix 2
findings.quote: An absent signal or a monophasic signal is abnormal (see Figure 7) and is indicative of the presence of peripheral artery disease
findings.notes: Method: hand-held 5-10 MHz Doppler, probe at 40-60 degrees pointing upstream. If the machine cannot display a waveform, assess the Doppler sound audibly.

findings.assertion: IWGDF specifies standardised measurement conditions for ankle and toe pressures that materially affect the result.
findings.value: Room 22-24 degrees C; no alcohol, exercise or caffeine for 2 hours before; supine 10 minutes before measurement; calf cuff approx. 2 cm above the malleolus; deflate at 2-3 mmHg per second; inflate to approx. 30 mmHg above signal loss
findings.standardVersion: 2023 update (Practical Guidelines, Appendix 2)
findings.sourceTitle: IWGDF Practical Guidelines (2023 update), Appendix 2
findings.quote: Quiet surroundings in room with comfortable temperature for the patient, such as 22–24 °C. Alcohol, exercise and caffeine should be avoided for 2 hours prior to testing. Patient in supine horizontal position, for 10 minutes prior to the measurement.
findings.notes: Cuff must be large enough to have approx. 40% extra to wrap around. If a toe measurement is suboptimal, repeat after a 3-minute wait. These preconditions are often ignored in practice and are a common source of spurious ABI values.

findings.assertion: IWGDF recommends SINBAD as the first-choice ulcer classification for communication between health professionals, scoring six items 0 or 1 for a total of 0-6.
findings.value: SINBAD components and scoring — Site: forefoot=0, midfoot/hindfoot=1; Ischaemia: pedal flow intact (>=1 palpable pulse)=0, clinical evidence of reduced flow=1; Neuropathy: protective sensation intact=0, lost=1; Bacterial infection: none=0, present=1; Area: <1 cm2=0, >=1 cm2=1; Depth: confined to skin/subcutaneous tissue=0, reaching muscle/tendon or deeper=1. Total 0-6
findings.standardVersion: 2023 update (Classification Guideline, Table 2, Recommendation 1a)
findings.sourceTitle: IWGDF Guidelines on the classification of foot ulcers in people with diabetes (2023 update), Table 2
findings.quote: Site Forefoot 0 / Midfoot and hindfoot 1; Ischemia Pedal blood flow intact: at least one palpable pulse 0 / Clinical evidence of reduced pedal flow 1; Neuropathy Protective sensation intact 0 / Protective sensation lost 1; Bacterial infection None 0 / Present 1; Area Ulcer <1cm2 0 / Ulcer ≥1 cm2 1; Depth Ulcer confined to skin and subcutaneous tissue 0 / Ulcer reaching muscle, tendon or deeper 1; Total possible score 0 – 6
findings.notes: Chosen for low-resource settings: 'requires no specialist equipment beyond clinical examination alone'. Directly relevant to a Ugandan deployment. Validated in 12 studies. Note the SINBAD acronym letter order (S-I-N-B-A-D) — the guideline's own prose in one place lists it as 'Site, Ischaemia, Bacterial infection, Area and Depth', omitting Neuropathy, which appears to be a typographical slip in the source; Table 2 authoritatively includes Neuropathy.

findings.assertion: IWGDF directs that SINBAD be reported as individual clinical descriptors for communication, and only used as a summed score for audit.
findings.value: Communication (Rec 1a): describe individual variables, not merely the total score. Audit (Rec 5): use the SINBAD total score
findings.standardVersion: 2023 update (Classification Guideline, Recommendations 1a and 5)
findings.sourceTitle: IWGDF Classification Guideline (2023 update)
findings.quote: If used for the purpose of communication among healthcare professionals, it is important to use the individual clinical descriptors and not merely the total score.
findings.notes: Data-model implication: store the six SINBAD components separately and derive the total, rather than storing only a 0-6 integer.

findings.assertion: IWGDF explicitly forbids using any current ulcer classification system to give an individual patient a prognosis.
findings.value: Recommendation 2: Do not use any currently available classification/scoring system to offer an individual outcome prognosis (Strong; Low)
findings.standardVersion: 2023 update (Classification Guideline, Recommendation 2)
findings.sourceTitle: IWGDF Classification Guideline (2023 update)
findings.quote: Do not use any of the currently available classification/scoring systems to offer an individual outcome prognosis for a person with diabetes and a foot ulcer. (Strong; Low)
findings.notes: HIGHEST-PRIORITY SAFETY CONSTRAINT for this domain. A decision-support tool must NOT render a SINBAD or WIfI score as an individualised healing or amputation probability. This is a Strong recommendation. It aligns with the project's 'decision-support, never autonomous' rule.

findings.assertion: The WIfI system is the IWGDF alternative/adjunct classification, grading Wound, Ischaemia and foot Infection each 0-3.
findings.value: WIfI Ischaemia grades — Grade 0: ABI >=0.80, ankle systolic pressure >100 mmHg, TP/TcPO2 >=60 mmHg. Grade 1: ABI 0.6-0.79, ankle SP 70-100 mmHg, TP/TcPO2 40-59 mmHg. Grade 2: ABI 0.4-0.59, ankle SP 50-70 mmHg, TP/TcPO2 30-39 mmHg. Grade 3: ABI <=0.39, ankle SP <50 mmHg, TP/TcPO2 <30 mmHg
findings.standardVersion: 2023 update (Classification Guideline, Table 3), reproducing the SVS WIfI system
findings.sourceTitle: IWGDF Classification Guideline (2023 update), Table 3: WIfI system
findings.quote: Ischaemia Grade ABI Ankle systolic pressure (mmHg) TP, TcPO2 (mmHg) / 0 ≥ 0.80 > 100 ≥ 60 / 1 0.6 – 0.79 70 – 100 40 – 59 / 2 0.4 – 0.59 50 – 70 30 – 39 / 3 ≤ 0.39 < 50 < 30
findings.notes: Recommended when 'the required equipment is available in addition to an appropriate level of expertise and it is considered feasible' — i.e. explicitly NOT the default in resource-limited settings. Note the ankle-SP band boundaries overlap at 70 mmHg and there is a gap between grade 1 (ABI 0.6-0.79) and grade 0 (ABI >=0.80) — see conflicts. I read this from the IWGDF reproduction, not the original Mills et al. 2014 paper.

findings.assertion: WIfI Wound grades 0-3 describe ulcer depth and gangrene extent with an associated salvage description.
findings.value: Grade 0: no ulcer, no gangrene. Grade 1: small shallow ulcer on distal leg or foot, no exposed bone unless limited to distal phalanx; no gangrene. Grade 2: deeper ulcer with exposed bone, joint or tendon, generally not involving the heel, or shallow heel ulcer without calcaneal involvement; gangrenous changes limited to digits. Grade 3: extensive deep ulcer involving forefoot and/or midfoot, or deep full-thickness heel ulcer +/- calcaneal involvement; extensive gangrene of forefoot/midfoot or full-thickness heel necrosis
findings.standardVersion: 2023 update (Classification Guideline, Table 3)
findings.sourceTitle: IWGDF Classification Guideline (2023 update), Table 3: WIfI system
findings.quote: 2 Deeper ulcer with exposed bone, joint or tendon; generally not involving the heel; shallow heel ulcer, without calcaneal involvement | Gangrenous changes limited to digits
findings.notes: In the source table, the 'minor tissue loss. Salvageable with simple digital amputation' clinical description text appears against both grade 0 and grade 1 rows, which looks like a layout artefact of the PDF table. Verify against the original SVS WIfI publication before encoding the clinical-description strings.

findings.assertion: The WIfI foot Infection component is the IDSA/IWGDF infection grading, 0-3, with an explicit two-sign threshold for diagnosing infection.
findings.value: Infection present = >=2 of: local swelling or induration; erythema >0.5 to <=2 cm around the ulcer; local tenderness or pain; local warmth; purulent discharge. Grade 0 = no signs. Grade 1 = local infection of skin/subcutaneous tissue only. Grade 2 = erythema >2 cm or involving deeper structures (abscess, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, fasciitis) without systemic signs. Grade 3 = local infection with >=2 SIRS criteria
findings.standardVersion: 2023 update (Classification Guideline, Table 3; IWGDF/IDSA infection grading)
findings.sourceTitle: IWGDF Classification Guideline (2023 update), Table 3: WIfI system, Foot Infection
findings.quote: 3 Local infection (as described above) with the signs of SIRS, as manifested by two or more of the following: ● Temperature > 38ºC or < 36ºC ● Heart rate > 90 beats/min ● Respiratory rate > 20 breaths/min or PaCO2 < 32 mm Hg ● White blood cell count > 12,000 or < 4000 cu/mm or 10% immature (band) forms
findings.notes: Grade 2 and 3 definitions require excluding mimics: trauma, gout, acute Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy, fracture, thrombosis, venous stasis. The Practical Guidelines warn these signs 'may be blunted by neuropathy or ischaemia' and systemic findings are often absent in mild/moderate infection.

findings.assertion: IWGDF provides a simple ulcer typology derived from the LOPS/PAD combination.
findings.value: Neuropathic = LOPS but no PAD; neuro-ischaemic = LOPS and PAD; ischaemic = PAD but no LOPS
findings.standardVersion: 2023 update (Practical Guidelines, section 4.1.1)
findings.sourceTitle: IWGDF Practical Guidelines (2023 update), section 4.1.1
findings.quote: the ulcer type can be described as neuropathic (LOPS, but no PAD), neuro-ischaemic (LOPS and PAD), or ischaemic (PAD, but no LOPS)
findings.notes: Maps cleanly onto the same two boolean inputs (LOPS, PAD) that drive the risk stratification, so a single assessment can populate both.

findings.assertion: IWGDF requires establishing LOPS and PAD status before any foot surgery in a person with diabetes.
findings.value: Pre-operative requirement: establish presence of LOPS and PAD status prior to any surgical procedure on the foot
findings.standardVersion: 2023 update (Practical Guidelines, section 3.1)
findings.sourceTitle: IWGDF Practical Guidelines (2023 update), section 3.1
findings.quote: Prior to any surgical procedure on the foot in a person with diabetes, the presence of LOPS and PAD status should be established in order to assess the suitability for and risks of the procedure.
findings.notes: Useful as a hard gate in a pre-operative checklist surface.

findings.assertion: Absence of symptoms does not exclude diabetic foot disease, which is the stated rationale for systematic rather than symptom-triggered screening.
findings.value: Asymptomatic patients may still have neuropathy, PAD, pre-ulcerative signs, or an ulcer
findings.standardVersion: 2023 update (Practical Guidelines, section 3.1)
findings.sourceTitle: IWGDF Practical Guidelines (2023 update), section 3.1
findings.quote: The absence of symptoms in a person with diabetes does not exclude foot disease; they may have asymptomatic neuropathy, PAD, pre-ulcerative signs, or even an ulcer.
findings.notes: Argues against building any screening flow that is gated on a patient-reported symptom question.

conflicts.assertion: How many abnormal tests are required to establish loss of protective sensation
positions: IWGDF 2023 (Practical Guidelines s3.1): a SINGLE test suffices — 'Loss of protective sensation (LOPS): assess with one of the following techniques' listing monofilament OR 128 Hz tuning fork OR light touch of the toe tips. Prevention Guideline positions vibration testing as an add-on only 'if outcomes from monofilament testing do not show LOPS'.

ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2024 (Section 12): requires TWO — 'The monofilament test should be performed with at least one other neurologic assessment tool (e.g., pinprick, temperature perception, ankle reflexes, or vibratory perception with a 128-Hz tuning fork or similar device)' and 'Absent monofilament sensation and one other abnormal test confirms the presence of LOPS.'
conflicts.recommendation: This is a genuine substantive disagreement, not a wording difference, and it changes who gets classified as at-risk. For a Ugandan/Mulago deployment I would follow IWGDF (single test), because it is the body that owns this domain, it is the source ADA itself adapts its risk table from, and it is deliberately calibrated for resource-limited settings where a second instrument may not exist. Encode the number and identity of tests performed as data rather than collapsing to a boolean, so the same record can be evaluated under either rule. Surface both rules to the CSO for sign-off.

conflicts.assertion: Which pedal artery pressure to use as the ABI numerator
positions: IWGDF 2023 (Practical Guidelines, Appendix 2), diabetes-specific: use the LOWER of the dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pressure, because below-knee disease may affect only one tibial artery.

Traditional method, acknowledged in the same IWGDF appendix and used by the AHA scientific statement the guideline cites: use the HIGHER pedal pressure, which the guideline describes as giving 'a best-case scenario of blood flow to the foot'.
conflicts.recommendation: IWGDF does not forbid the traditional method, it contrasts them — so this is a documented divergence rather than an error. Use the IWGDF lower-pressure convention for diabetic patients (it is the more conservative, ischaemia-sensitive choice), but store dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pressures as separate fields and record which convention produced the displayed ABI. Never display a bare ABI number without its convention, since the two methods yield different values for the same patient and could cross a 0.9 or 0.4 action threshold.

conflicts.assertion: ABI value below which ischaemia is considered present
positions: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline 2023 (Rec 2 and 4): PAD is less likely with ABI 0.9-1.3, i.e. below 0.9 is abnormal. Practical Guidelines Appendix 2 states the same: 'An ABI above 1.3 or below 0.9 is abnormal'.
WIfI system as reproduced in IWGDF Classification Guideline 2023 (Table 3): Ischaemia grade 0 (no significant ischaemia) is ABI >=0.80, with grade 1 starting at 0.6-0.79.
conflicts.recommendation: Both sit inside the same 2023 IWGDF guideline set, so this cannot be resolved by preferring one body. They answer different questions: 0.9 is a PAD DIAGNOSIS threshold, 0.80 is a WIfI LIMB-STAGING threshold tied to revascularisation benefit. Keep them as two distinct rules with distinct labels and never let one overwrite the other. Also note the WIfI ABI bands leave 0.79-0.80 and 0.59-0.60 as gaps and the ankle-pressure bands overlap at exactly 70 mmHg (grade 1 = 70-100, grade 2 = 50-70) — any implementation must define boundary handling explicitly and have the CSO sign off on it.

conflicts.assertion: TcPO2 threshold defining severe ischaemia warranting urgent revascularisation assessment
positions: IWGDF Practical Guidelines 2023, s4.2.2: 'Also consider urgent assessment for revascularisation if the toe pressure is <30mmHg or TcpO2 is <25 mmHg.'
IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline 2023, Best Practice Statement 13: severe ischaemia is defined as '... toe pressure <30mmHg or transcutaneous oxygen pressure <30mmHg ...'
conflicts.recommendation: A direct 5 mmHg numeric discrepancy between two documents in the same 2023 release, on a threshold that triggers urgent vascular referral. The toe-pressure figure (<30 mmHg) agrees across both; only TcPO2 differs. The Practical Guidelines explicitly state they are derived from the intersocietal PAD guideline, which argues for the PAD guideline's <30 mmHg as the source of truth; but <25 mmHg is the value tied to the published healing-probability evidence in PAD Recommendation 8. Escalate to the CSO. Until resolved, the safer implementation is to trigger at the HIGHER value (<30 mmHg), which refers more patients rather than fewer.

conflicts.assertion: Toe pressure threshold that should prompt vascular referral
positions: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline 2023, BPS 12 (consider revascularisation): toe pressure <60 mmHg counts as a finding of ischaemia.
IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline 2023, BPS 13 (urgent consult): toe pressure <30 mmHg indicates severe ischaemia.
IWGDF Practical Guidelines 2023, s4.2.2 surfaces only the <30 mmHg figure and does not mention <60 mmHg.
conflicts.recommendation: Not a true contradiction — these are two escalation tiers (consider vs urgent) — but the Practical Guidelines omit the intermediate tier, so a tool built only from the Practical Guidelines would under-refer patients with toe pressures of 30-60 mmHg. Implement both tiers with distinct urgency labels, citing the PAD guideline for each. Have the CSO confirm the two-tier design.

unverifiable: Vibration perception threshold (VPT) / biothesiometer / neurothesiometer numeric cut-off. This was explicitly requested and I could NOT confirm it. I grepped all five IWGDF 2023 PDFs I retrieved (Practical, Prevention, Classification, intersocietal PAD, Definitions and Criteria) for 'biothesiomet', 'neurothesiomet', 'volt', 'VPT' and 'vibration perception threshold'. The only hit is one sentence in the Prevention Guideline endorsing the device with NO threshold attached. The widely quoted >25 V cut-off derives from older primary literature (Young/Boulton-era cohorts), not from IWGDF 2023. Do not attribute any volt threshold to IWGDF. I did not fetch the primary VPT papers.

The exact anatomical labels of the 10 g monofilament test sites. IWGDF Figure 4 is a picture with no text labels; the guideline text says only 'Test three different sites on both feet, selecting from those shown in Figure 4.' I rendered page 25 and read three marked plantar points per foot which appear to be the hallux and the first and fifth metatarsal head regions, but that naming is my visual interpretation, not IWGDF wording. Needs CSO confirmation before being encoded.

Whether 'three sites' is a minimum, a maximum, or an exact requirement, and whether the same three sites must be used bilaterally. The phrase 'selecting from those shown in Figure 4' implies a choice from a larger candidate set, but the candidate set size is not stated in text.

A numeric or operational definition of 'foot deformity' for IWGDF risk category 2. The guideline gives examples (claw or hammer toes, abnormally large bony prominences, limited joint mobility) but no threshold, angle, or scoring instrument. This is a real gap for anything trying to compute the risk category automatically.

Dual SI/conventional units (mmol/L and mg/dL) do not apply anywhere in this domain. Every threshold captured is a pressure (mmHg), a dimensionless index (ABI/TBI), a force (10 g), a frequency (128 Hz), an area (cm2) or a count. Where I supplied kPa figures alongside mmHg they are MY arithmetic conversions (1 mmHg = 0.1333 kPa) and are not printed in the IWGDF sources; they should be labelled as derived or dropped. No glycaemic thresholds appear in the IWGDF foot guidelines (the Practical Guidelines say only 'Optimise glycaemic control, if necessary, with insulin', with no target value).

The original WIfI publication (Mills et al., J Vasc Surg 2014) was not fetched. I read the WIfI tables only as reproduced in the IWGDF 2023 Classification Guideline. The apparent duplication of the 'minor tissue loss / salvageable with simple digital amputation' clinical description across WIfI Wound grades 0 and 1 looks like a PDF table layout artefact and should be checked against the original before the clinical-description strings are encoded.

The original SINBAD derivation and validation paper (Ince et al.) was not fetched; SINBAD content comes from the IWGDF Classification Guideline Table 2 only. Note also that the Classification Guideline's own prose expands the acronym in one place as 'Site, Ischaemia, Bacterial infection, Area and Depth' — omitting Neuropathy — while Table 2 includes Neuropathy. I treated Table 2 as authoritative but did not confirm which is the erratum.

The Ipswich Touch Test primary validation papers (Rayman et al.; Sharma et al., cited as refs 23 and 24 in the Prevention Guideline) were not fetched. IWGDF itself states its ulcer-prediction accuracy 'has not been established', so its performance characteristics remain unverified here.

The full WIfI composite staging (how W, I and fI grades combine into clinical stages 1-4 for amputation risk and revascularisation benefit) was not captured — the IWGDF Classification Guideline reproduces the component grade tables but I did not retrieve the combination matrices.

ESC, ESVS-standalone, NICE and WHO positions on diabetic foot screening and ABI were not fetched. The only non-IWGDF standard I verified is the ADA (2024 edition). Conflicts with other bodies may therefore be undercounted.

ADA Standards of Care editions after 2024 were not checked; the ADA publishes annually, so the 2026 edition may differ from what I quote. My ADA citation is specifically Diabetes Care 47(Suppl 1):S231–S243.

Content of the forthcoming IWGDF 2027 update. I confirmed on iwgdfguidelines.org that the 2023 update remains the current version and that the next update is scheduled for presentation at the International Symposium on the Diabetic Foot, May 2027, in The Hague. Nothing about its content is knowable now.

Wiley Online Library full-text versions (dmrr.3657, dmrr.3651, dmrr.3654) returned HTTP 403 and could not be fetched. All IWGDF content above comes from the PDFs hosted on iwgdfguidelines.org, which is the standard-setting body's own site and is the preferred primary source anyway, but I could not cross-check the journal typesetting against the IWGDF PDFs.

Whether the IWGDF risk stratification has been validated in a sub-Saharan African or Ugandan population specifically. The Classification Guideline notes that 'the dominant factors for poor outcomes in foot ulcers in people with diabetes vary worldwide', which implies caution, but I found no region-specific validation data.

audit.assertion: IWGDF risk category 0 = no LOPS AND no signs of PAD; screened once a year (IWGDF 2023 Practical Guidelines, Table 1)
audit.reason: Independently fetched the PDF (HTTP 200, 30pp) and extracted text. Table 1, p8, reads verbatim: '0 | Very low | No LOPS and no signs of PAD | Once a year'. Table is titled 'The IWGDF 2023 Risk Stratification System and corresponding foot screening frequency'. Also verified the currency claim in the bracket: iwgdfguidelines.org confirms 2023 is still the current version and states the next update is 2027, to be presented at the International Symposium on the Diabetic Foot, May 2027, The Hague. Source URL exists and contains the value.

audit.assertion: IWGDF risk category 1 = LOPS OR PAD; screened once every 6-12 months
audit.reason: Table 1, p8, verbatim: '1 | Low | LOPS or PAD | Once every 6-12 months'. Exact match including the disjunction and the interval.

audit.assertion: IWGDF risk category 2 = two of LOPS/PAD/foot deformity; screened once every 3-6 months
audit.reason: Table 1, p8, verbatim: '2 | Moderate | LOPS + PAD, or LOPS + foot deformity or PAD + foot deformity | Once every 3-6 months'. The finding's expansion into the three pairwise combinations is an exact restatement, not an inference.

audit.assertion: IWGDF risk category 3 = (LOPS OR PAD) AND >=1 of foot ulcer history / lower-extremity amputation (minor or major) / end-stage renal disease; screened once every 1-3 months
audit.reason: Table 1, p8, verbatim: '3 | High | LOPS or PAD, and one or more of the following: - history of a foot ulcer - a lower-extremity amputation (minor or major) - end-stage renal disease | Once every 1-3 months'. I specifically probed the ESRD element because a web summary I retrieved first (RNAO/secondary) omitted it and listed only ulcer/amputation; the primary IWGDF document does include end-stage renal disease. The finding is right and the secondary summary is the incomplete one.

audit.assertion: All four IWGDF screening intervals carry an explicit expert-opinion caveat (Table 1 footnote)
audit.reason: Footnote to Table 1, p8, verbatim: '* Screening frequency is based on expert opinion, since there is no published evidence to support these intervals'. The asterisk is attached to the 'Frequency*' column header, so it does govern all four intervals as claimed. Independently corroborated in the Prevention Guideline: 'Although evidence for a screening interval is non-existent, we recommend an annual screening...'. This caveat is correctly characterised and is material for a decision-support tool.

audit.assertion: ADA Standards of Care 2024 Section 12 'independently adopts' the IWGDF risk stratification unchanged, which 'corroborates' the four categories and screening frequencies
audit.reason: The numbers and the bibliographic citation are real and correct, but the epistemic claim is false and this is the one genuinely misleading item in the set. I bypassed the PMC captcha by curling the article HTML directly. Table 12.1 is titled 'International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot risk stratification system and corresponding foot screening frequency' and carries the attribution line 'Adapted with permission from Schaper et al. (81)'. Schaper et al. IS the IWGDF 2023 Practical Guidelines - the very same document cited in findings 1-5. So ADA is not independently adopting or corroborating anything; it is reprinting the identical source under licence. Citing it as corroboration is circular and would create a false impression of two-source agreement in a clinical tool. Two further inaccuracies in 'identical': ADA's column is 'Examination frequency', not 'screening frequency'; and ADA's footnote reads 'Examination frequency suggestions are based on expert opinion and person-centered requirements', dropping IWGDF's explicit 'since there is no published evidence to support these intervals' clause. Verified correct: title '12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2024', Diabetes Care 47(Suppl 1):S231-S243, and the category/frequency cells do match.
audit.correctedValue: ADA Table 12.1 does reproduce categories 0-3 with the same criteria and frequencies, but it is an adapted reprint of the IWGDF Practical Guidelines (Schaper et al.) published with permission. It provides NO independent corroboration. ADA's footnote also omits IWGDF's 'no published evidence' clause.
audit.correctedSource: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10725803/ - Table 12.1, attribution line 'Adapted with permission from Schaper et al. (81)'

audit.assertion: IWGDF defines LOPS as a sign of peripheral neuropathy, an inability to sense light pressure such as from a 10 g Semmes-Weinstein monofilament
audit.reason: Fetched DMRR3654.pdf; confirmed it is genuinely 'Definitions and criteria for diabetes-related foot disease (IWGDF 2023 update)', van Netten et al., DOI 10.1002/dmrr.3654. Verbatim: 'Loss of protective sensation: A sign of peripheral neuropathy, characterised by an inability to sense light pressure, for example, as applied with a 10 g Semmes-Weinstein monofilament.' One minor conflation: the '(5.07)' filament designation in the stated VALUE does NOT appear in this definitions document - it comes from Practical Guidelines Appendix 1. The two documents are being merged in a single citation. Substantively harmless but the citation should be split.

audit.assertion: IWGDF monofilament technique: 3 sites per foot, 10 g filament, perpendicular to buckling, total approx. 2 seconds
audit.reason: Practical Guidelines Appendix 1 ('DOING A SENSORY FOOT EXAMINATION'), p24, verbatim: 'Test three different sites on both feet, selecting from those shown in Figure 4'; 'Apply the monofilament perpendicular to the skin surface (Figure 5a) with sufficient force to cause the filament to bend or buckle (Figure 5b)'; 'The total duration of the approach -> skin contact -> and removal of the filament should be approximately 2 seconds.' Appendix 1 is the correct location. All four elements confirmed.

audit.assertion: IWGDF monofilament scoring: three questions per site (two real applications alternating with at least one mock), 2-out-of-3 rule
audit.reason: Appendix 1 verbatim: 'Repeat this application twice at the same site, but alternate this with at least one mock application in which no filament is applied (a total of three questions per site)' and 'Protective sensation is: present at each site if the patient correctly answers on two out of three applications; absent with two out of three incorrect answers.' Exact match on both the mock-application structure and the 2/3 threshold in both directions.

audit.assertion: Figure 4 (p25) shows 3 marked plantar sites per foot - hallux, first and fifth metatarsal head regions - with no text labels
audit.reason: This was the hardest claim to falsify because the site names are not in the extracted text, so I extracted the embedded JPEG XObject (/Im4, 1026x838, DCTDecode) from PDF page 25 and viewed the image directly. It shows two plantar foot outlines, each with exactly three orange filled circles: one on the plantar hallux, one large circle at the first metatarsal head region, one smaller circle at the fifth metatarsal head region. No text labels anywhere in the figure. The finding's description is accurate, and its explicit acknowledgement that the sites are diagram-only is honest. Caveat worth carrying into any implementation: the body text says 'selecting from those shown in Figure 4', so the figure marks candidate regions rather than three mandatory fixed points.

audit.assertion: Monofilament maintenance: rest 24 hours after 10-15 patients; replace after 70-90 patients
audit.reason: Appendix 1 verbatim: 'Depending on the type of monofilament, we suggest not using the monofilament for the next 24 hours after assessing 10-15 patients and replacing it after using it on 70-90 patients.' Both numeric ranges exact. Minor framing note: IWGDF hedges this as 'we suggest' and 'depending on the type of monofilament'; the finding's word 'specifies' is slightly firmer than the source.

audit.assertion: 128 Hz tuning fork applied to bony dorsal distal phalanx of hallux, 2-out-of-3 rule with mock application
audit.reason: Appendix 1, p26, verbatim: 'Apply the tuning fork to a bony part on the dorsal side of the distal phalanx of the first toe (or another toe if the hallux is absent)'; 'Repeat this application twice, but alternate this with at least one mock application in which the tuning fork is not vibrating'; 'The test is positive if the patient correctly answers at least two out of three applications, and negative if two out of three answers are incorrect.' Every element including the hallux-absent fallback is exact.

audit.assertion: Ipswich Touch Test: tips of 1st, 3rd, 5th toes bilaterally, 1-2 seconds, LOPS likely if not sensed at >=2 sites
audit.reason: Appendix 1, p26, verbatim: 'This simple test (also called the Ipswich Touch test) can be used to screen for loss of protective sensation (LOPS), when the 10 gram monofilament or 128 HZ tuning fork is not available'; 'lightly sequentially touches with the tip of hers/his index finger the tips of the first, third, and fifth toes of both feet for 1-2 s'; 'LOPS is likely when light touch is not sensed in >= 2 sites'. All exact. One safety-relevant omission: the source immediately adds that the test 'has reasonable agreement with these tests to determine LOPS, but its accuracy in predicting foot ulcers has not been established' - that caveat should travel with the test in any decision-support tool and is absent from the finding.

audit.assertion: IWGDF 2023 endorses biothesiometer/neurothesiometer as second-line vibration screen but publishes NO numeric vibration perception threshold
audit.reason: I tried hard to refute this negative claim and could not. Ran a comprehensive regex sweep for volt values, 'biothesiometer', 'neurothesiometer' and 'vibration perception threshold' across all five extracted documents (Practical, Prevention, Classification, PAD, Definitions - 157 pages total). Exactly one hit, in the Prevention Guideline: 'Because limited vibratory sensation may also predict risk of foot ulceration (5), we suggest to screen for this with a tuning fork or biothesiometer/neurothesiometer, if outcomes from monofilament testing do not show LOPS.' This sits in the rationale to Recommendation 1 (annual screening of IWGDF risk 0), as the finding states. No volt threshold of any kind appears - the commonly cited >25 V cut-off is genuinely absent. Correctly reported and correctly flagged as a gap rather than filled from memory.

audit.assertion: IWGDF PAD Guideline Rec 1: history, inspection for ischaemia and pedal pulse palpation at least annually or with any change in foot status (Strong, Low)
audit.reason: Intersocietal IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline, Recommendation 1, verbatim: 'In a person with diabetes without a foot ulcer, take a relevant history for peripheral artery disease, examine the foot for signs of ischaemia and palpate the foot pulses at least annually, or with any change in clinical status of the feet. (Strong, Low)'. Recommendation number, wording, scope restriction (without a foot ulcer) and GRADE rating all exact.

audit.assertion: PAD less likely if ABI 0.9-1.3 AND TBI >=0.70 AND triphasic/biphasic pedal Doppler waveforms; no value excludes PAD (Recs 2 and 4)
audit.reason: Both cited recommendations verified and both genuinely contain the sentence, which is why the dual citation is correct rather than padded. Rec 2 (no foot ulcer): 'No single modality has been shown to be optimal for the diagnosis of PAD, and there is no value above which PAD can be excluded. However, PAD is less likely in the presence of ABI 0.9-1.3; TBI >= 0.70; and triphasic or biphasic pedal Doppler waveforms. (Conditional, Low)'. Rec 4 (with foot ulcer or gangrene) repeats it verbatim but is graded (Strong, Low). Worth noting the grading differs between the two contexts, which the finding does not mention.

audit.assertion: ABI >1.3 or <0.9 is abnormal, indicative of PAD; 0.9-1.3 normal
audit.reason: Practical Guidelines Appendix 2, p28, verbatim: 'An ABI above 1.3 or below 0.9 is abnormal, i.e. indicative of PAD (4, 12).' The 0.9-1.3 normal band is stated explicitly in PAD Guideline Recs 2 and 4. Appendix 2 is the correct location.

audit.assertion: IWGDF diabetes-specific ABI uses the LOWER of dorsalis pedis / posterior tibial pressures, unlike the traditional higher-pressure method
audit.reason: This is an unusual claim that inverts the standard vascular convention, so I checked it closely. Appendix 2, p28, verbatim: 'calculate the ankle-brachial index (ABI) for each limb by dividing the lower value of the dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pressures of that foot by the highest of the left or right brachial pressures.' And immediately after: 'The ABI has traditionally been calculated using the higher of the dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pressures. This gives a best-case scenario of blood flow to the foot.' Both halves of the finding - the IWGDF method and the contrast with tradition - are exact. The rationale given is below-knee disease that may affect only one tibial artery. Correctly reported.

audit.assertion: TBI <0.70 is abnormal, indicative of PAD
audit.reason: Practical Guidelines Appendix 2, p29, verbatim: 'A TBI below 0.7 is considered to be abnormal, i.e. indicative for PAD (4, 12).' The >=0.70 'PAD less likely' half is separately confirmed in PAD Guideline Recs 2 and 4. Consistent across both documents.

audit.assertion: Toe pressure >=30 mmHg increases pre-test probability of healing by up to 30%; <30 mmHg increases probability of major amputation by approx. 20% (Rec 7, Conditional Low)
audit.reason: PAD Guideline Recommendation 7 verbatim: 'A toe pressure >= 30 mmHg increases the pre-test probability of healing by up to 30% and a value <30mmHg increases the pretest probability of major amputation by approximately 20%. (Conditional, Low)'. Recommendation number, both percentages, direction of each effect, and GRADE rating all exact. The '(approx. 4.0 kPa)' conversion is arithmetically correct (30 mmHg = 4.00 kPa) but is the reporting agent's own conversion - kPa values appear nowhere in the IWGDF text.

audit.assertion: TcPO2 >=25 mmHg increases pre-test probability of healing by up to 45% (Rec 8, Conditional)
audit.reason: PAD Guideline Recommendation 8 verbatim: 'A TcPO2 >= 25 mmHg increases the pre-test probability of healing by up to 45% and value <25 mmHg has been shown to increase the pre-test probability of major amputation by approximately 20%. An SPP >= 40mmHg increases the pre-test probability of healing by up to 30%. (Conditional, Low)'. The quoted value and grading are exact. Two omissions worth correcting before clinical use: TcPO2 is NOT the sole fallback - Rec 8 gives skin perfusion pressure (SPP) as a co-equal alternative with its own threshold (SPP >=40 mmHg, up to 30% healing) - and the finding drops the TcPO2 <25 mmHg / ~20% major-amputation half. 25 mmHg = 3.33 kPa, so the stated conversion is correct but again is the agent's own, not IWGDF's.

audit.assertion: Findings of ischaemia prompting revascularisation: absent pulses; monophasic or absent pedal Doppler waveforms; ankle pressure <100 mmHg; or toe pressure <60 mmHg
audit.reason: Values exact. PAD Guideline verbatim: 'Findings of ischaemia include absent pulses, monophasic or absent pedal Doppler waveforms, ankle pressure < 100 mm Hg or toe pressure < 60 mm Hg. Consult a vascular specialist unless major amputation is considered medically urgent. Best Practice Statement'. Citation-label correction: this is Recommendation 12, not 'Best Practice Statement 12'. I checked the guideline's LIST OF RECOMMENDATIONS and it uses a single continuous 1-22+ numbering, with 'Best Practice Statement' being a GRADE label applied to some items rather than a parallel numbering series. There is no item findable as 'BPS 12'. Rec 12 is indeed graded Best Practice Statement, so the label is loose rather than wrong, but it should be cited as Recommendation 12 for traceability. kPa figures (13.3, 8.0) are correct conversions but are the agent's own.
audit.correctedSource: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline 2023, Recommendation 12 (graded Best Practice Statement) - not a separately numbered 'Best Practice Statement 12'

audit.assertion: Severe ischaemia = ABI <0.4, OR ankle pressure <50 mmHg, OR toe pressure <30 mmHg, OR TcPO2 <30 mmHg, OR monophasic/absent pedal Doppler waveforms
audit.reason: Values exact. PAD Guideline verbatim: 'In a person with diabetes, peripheral artery disease, a foot ulcer, and severe ischaemia i.e. an ankle-brachial index <0.4, ankle pressure <50mmHg, toe pressure <30mmHg or transcutaneous oxygen pressure <30mmHg or monophasic or absent pedal Doppler waveforms, urgently consult a vascular specialist regarding possible revascularisation. Best Practice Statement'. Two corrections. (1) Same labelling issue as the previous item: this is Recommendation 13, not 'Best Practice Statement 13'. (2) Provenance: the rationale immediately states 'Severe ischaemia is defined in The Global Vascular Guidelines (GVG) as an ABI <0.4, AP pressure <50mmHg, TP <30mmHg or TcPO2 <30mmHg or monophasic or absent pedal Doppler waveforms (17, 78).' So IWGDF is adopting the GVG definition, not originating it. Attributing the threshold set to IWGDF is defensible since IWGDF states it as its own recommendation, but the underlying standard-setting body is GVG and a tool citing this should say so.
audit.correctedSource: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS PAD Guideline 2023, Recommendation 13 (graded Best Practice Statement); threshold set adopted from the Global Vascular Guidelines (GVG) per the stated rationale

audit.assertion: Non-healing ulcer mandates vascular reassessment: Practical Guidelines no signs of healing within 4-6 weeks; PAD Guideline <50% reduction in wound area within 4 weeks
audit.reason: Both halves independently verified in their respective documents, and the section attribution checks out. Practical Guidelines, under heading '4.2.2 Restoration of tissue perfusion' (I listed all section headings to confirm the line falls inside 4.2.2): 'When an ulcer fails to show signs of healing within 4-6 weeks, despite optimal management, consider angiography and revascularisation, irrespective of the results of the vascular diagnostic tests described above.' PAD Guideline Recommendation 15 (graded Best Practice Statement): 'when the wound deteriorates or fails to significantly improve (e.g. a less than 50% reduction in wound area within 4 weeks) despite appropriate infection and glucose control, wound care, and offloading, reassess the vascular status'. Good practice by the reporting agent: it presented the two different timeframes side by side rather than silently reconciling them into one number.

audit.assertion: Triphasic/biphasic pedal Doppler waveforms normal; monophasic or absent abnormal and indicative of PAD
audit.reason: Practical Guidelines Appendix 2, p27-28, verbatim: 'An absent signal or a monophasic signal is abnormal (see Figure 7) and is indicative of the presence of peripheral artery disease (Figure 7).' Figure 7 caption confirms: 'triphasic (A), biphasic (B) and monophasic Doppler (C) signals.' Precision note: Appendix 2 explicitly states only the abnormal half; the 'triphasic or biphasic = normal' half is stated explicitly in PAD Guideline Recs 2 and 4 ('PAD is less likely in the presence of... triphasic or biphasic pedal Doppler waveforms') rather than in Appendix 2/Figure 7. The claim is substantively correct but draws on two documents while citing one.

audit.assertion: Standardised ankle/toe pressure measurement conditions: 22-24 C; no alcohol/exercise/caffeine 2h; supine 10 min; calf cuff approx. 2 cm above malleolus; deflate 2-3 mmHg/s; inflate approx. 30 mmHg above signal loss
audit.reason: All six parameters verified verbatim in Practical Guidelines Appendix 2, p27-28: 'room with comfortable temperature for the patient, such as 22-24 C'; 'Alcohol, exercise and caffeine should be avoided for 2 hours prior to testing'; 'Patient in supine horizontal position, for 10 minutes prior to the measurement'; 'Place the calf cuff approximately 2 cm above the malleolus'; 'Slowly deflate the cuff at a rate of 2-3mmHg per second'; 'Inflate the cuff to supra-systolic values, i.e. about 30 mmHg above the pressure when the signal disappears completely'. This was the densest numeric cluster in the set and every value held up. Small nuance: 22-24 C is given as an example of a comfortable room temperature ('such as'), not a hard requirement.

audit.assertion: SINBAD is first-choice classification for communication; six items scored 0 or 1, total 0-6, with the stated component definitions
audit.reason: Table 2 is genuinely titled 'SINBAD system' (I listed all four tables in the document to confirm the table number). Every one of the twelve cell definitions matches verbatim: Site forefoot=0 / midfoot and hindfoot=1; Ischemia pedal blood flow intact: at least one palpable pulse=0 / clinical evidence of reduced pedal flow=1; Neuropathy protective sensation intact=0 / lost=1; Bacterial infection none=0 / present=1; Area ulcer <1cm2=0 / >=1 cm2=1; Depth ulcer confined to skin and subcutaneous tissue=0 / reaching muscle, tendon or deeper=1; 'Total possible score 0 - 6'. Recommendation 1a confirms SINBAD as first option for communication (Strong; Low). No discrepancies.

audit.assertion: SINBAD reported as individual descriptors for communication (Rec 1a); summed score used for audit (Rec 5)
audit.reason: Recommendation 1a verbatim: 'use the SINBAD system for communication about the characteristics of an ulcer between healthcare professionals, and clearly stating the presence or absence of each of the composing variables. (Strong; Low)'. Supporting text: 'If used for the purpose of communication among healthcare professionals, it is important to use the individual clinical descriptors and not merely the total score... we consider that the use of the final score is insufficient.' Recommendation 5 verbatim: 'Use the SINBAD system for any regional/national/international audits' - and the numbered LIST OF RECOMMENDATIONS and executive summary both render it as 'the SINBAD system score' / 'the use of the SINBAD score', confirming the score-for-audit reading. The communication/audit split is correctly captured.

audit.assertion: IWGDF Recommendation 2 forbids using any current classification/scoring system to offer an individual prognosis (Strong; Low)
audit.reason: Classification Guideline Recommendation 2 verbatim: 'Do not use any of the currently available classification/scoring systems to offer an individual outcome prognosis for a person with diabetes and a foot ulcer. (Strong; Low)'. Recommendation number and GRADE rating exact, and the executive summary independently states 'for predicting the outcome of an ulcer in a specific individual: no existing system could be recommended'. This is the single most important constraint in the set for a decision-support tool and it is accurately reported.

audit.assertion: WIfI Ischaemia grades 0-3 with the stated ABI, ankle systolic pressure and TP/TcPO2 bands (Table 3)
audit.reason: Table 3 is genuinely titled 'WIfI system'. Ischaemia sub-table verified cell by cell against the claim: Grade 0 ABI >=0.80 / ankle SP >100 / TP,TcPO2 >=60; Grade 1 ABI 0.6-0.79 / 70-100 / 40-59; Grade 2 ABI 0.4-0.59 / 50-70 / 30-39; Grade 3 ABI <=0.39 / <50 / <30. All twelve values match exactly, including the asymmetric operators (>100 for grade 0 vs >=60). Note the source table has genuinely overlapping ankle-pressure boundaries (grade 1 '70-100', grade 2 '50-70') - that ambiguity is in IWGDF's own table, faithfully carried over rather than silently tidied.

audit.assertion: WIfI Wound grades 0-3 describing ulcer depth and gangrene extent with salvage descriptions (Table 3)
audit.reason: Table 3 Wound sub-table verified: Grade 0 'No ulcer / No gangrene'; Grade 1 'Small, shallow ulcer(s) on distal leg or foot; no exposed bone, unless limited to distal phalanx / No gangrene'; Grade 2 'Deeper ulcer with exposed bone, joint or tendon; generally not involving the heel; shallow heel ulcer, without calcaneal involvement / Gangrenous changes limited to digits'; Grade 3 'Extensive, deep ulcer involving forefoot and/or midfoot; deep, full thickness heel ulcer +/- calcaneal involvement / Extensive gangrene involving forefoot and/or midfoot; full thickness heel necrosis +/- calcaneal involvement'. Salvage/clinical descriptions are present as claimed. Accurate paraphrase with no invented detail.

audit.assertion: WIfI foot Infection component (IDSA/IWGDF grading 0-3) with two-sign threshold for diagnosing infection
audit.reason: Table 3 Foot Infection sub-table verified verbatim: 'Infection present, as defined by the presence of at least 2 of the following items: Local swelling or induration; Erythema > 0.5 to <= 2 cm around the ulcer; Local tenderness or pain; Local warmth; Purulent discharge'. Grades 0-3 match the claim including 'erythema >2 cm or involving structures deeper than skin and subcutaneous tissues (e.g., abscess, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, fasciitis)' for grade 2 and SIRS >=2 criteria for grade 3. The Table 3 citation is correct, and the guideline itself says 'the IDSA/IWGDF is incorporated into WIfI (see Table 3)'. Implementation warning the finding does not surface: the same document ALSO carries Table 4 'IDSA/IWGDF system', which grades the same construct on a different scale - Uninfected/Mild/Moderate/Severe = PEDIS 1-4, with a differently worded sign list ('purulence, or erythema, tenderness, warmth, or induration') - and Recommendation 3a directs use of 'the IDSA/IWGDF (2015 version) system', i.e. Table 4. A tool that stores a single 'infection grade' integer must state which scale it uses, or a Table 4 grade 1 (uninfected) will be read as a Table 3 grade 1 (local infection).

audit.assertion: Ulcer typology: neuropathic = LOPS no PAD; neuro-ischaemic = LOPS and PAD; ischaemic = PAD no LOPS (s4.1.1)
audit.reason: Practical Guidelines verbatim: 'the ulcer type can be described as neuropathic (LOPS, but no PAD), neuro-ischaemic (LOPS and PAD), or ischaemic (PAD, but no LOPS).' I confirmed by listing section headings that this line falls under '4.1.1 Classification of the foot ulcer', so the section citation is correct. Exact match on all three definitions.

audit.assertion: LOPS and PAD status must be established before any foot surgery (s3.1)
audit.reason: Practical Guidelines section 3.1 verbatim: 'Prior to any surgical procedure on the foot in a person with diabetes, the presence of LOPS and PAD status should be established in order to assess the suitability for and risks of the procedure.' Section attribution confirmed by heading list (3.1 IDENTIFYING THE PERSON WITH AN AT-RISK FOOT). Independently reinforced by PAD Guideline Recommendation 5 (Best Practice Statement) requiring PAD to be excluded before non-emergency invasive foot procedures.

audit.assertion: Absence of symptoms does not exclude diabetic foot disease; patients may have asymptomatic neuropathy, PAD, pre-ulcerative signs or an ulcer (s3.1)
audit.reason: Practical Guidelines section 3.1 verbatim: 'The absence of symptoms in a person with diabetes does not exclude foot disease; they may have asymptomatic neuropathy, PAD, pre-ulcerative signs, or even an ulcer.' Exact match including the enumeration. Correctly identified as the rationale for systematic rather than symptom-triggered screening, which is consistent with the annual-screening recommendation for IWGDF risk 0 in both the Practical and Prevention guidelines.

bundle.domain: Glycaemic targets, cardiovascular risk estimation, and the diabetes management ladder across resource tiers (ADA vs WHO/PEN-HEARTS vs KDIGO vs ESC/ISH), with attention to sub-Saharan African applicability

findings.assertion: ADA's default glycaemic goal for most non-pregnant adults is an A1C below 7%.
findings.value: A1C <7% (<53 mmol/mol)
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6, Rec 6.3a (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S132–S149; doi 10.2337/dc26-S006)
findings.sourceTitle: 6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 6.3a An A1C goal of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) is appropriate for many nonpregnant adults without severe hypoglycemia or hypoglycemia affecting health or quality of life.
findings.notes: Verified by direct string-grep of the retrieved PMC HTML, not only via summarisation. Evidence grade A. Note the wording is 'appropriate for many', not 'all' — ADA frames this as a default, not a universal rule.

findings.assertion: ADA permits a tighter A1C goal for people in good health with low treatment risk.
findings.value: A1C <6.5% (<48 mmol/mol)
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6, Rec 6.4
findings.sourceTitle: 6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 6.4 Lower A1C goals (e.g., <6.5% [<48 mmol/mol]) may be appropriate for individuals with diabetes with good health and function and low treatment risks (e.g., hypoglycemia) and burdens (see Fig. 6.1 ).
findings.notes: Grade B. Conditional ('may be appropriate') — must not be encoded as a hard target.

findings.assertion: ADA permits a looser A1C goal where health status is complex or life expectancy limited.
findings.value: A1C up to 8% (64 mmol/mol)
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6 (narrative accompanying Recs 6.4–6.5)
findings.sourceTitle: 6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Less stringent goals (e.g., A1C up to 8% [64 mmol/mol]) may be recommended for individuals with complex health status and/or limited life expectancy where benefits of more intensive treatment may not be realized
findings.notes: String-verified. This sentence is narrative text, not a numbered recommendation; the numbered recommendation (6.5) states the qualifying conditions without a number.

findings.assertion: ADA lists the qualifying conditions that justify a less stringent glycaemic goal.
findings.value: Qualitative criteria (no numeric threshold): cognitive/functional limitation, frailty, severe comorbidity, or harms exceeding benefits
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6, Rec 6.5
findings.sourceTitle: 6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 6.5 Less stringent glycemic goals may be appropriate for individuals with significant cognitive and/or functional limitations, frailty, or severe comorbidities or where the harms of treatment, including hypoglycemia, are greater than the benefits.
findings.notes: String-verified. These are the trigger conditions a decision-support rule would key on.

findings.assertion: ADA gives a preprandial capillary plasma glucose target range for non-pregnant adults.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6, Table 6.3
findings.sourceTitle: 6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Preprandial capillary plasma glucose 80–130 mg/dL * (4.4–7.2 mmol/L)
findings.notes: String-verified from Table 6.3. Table footnote: '*More or less stringent glycemic goals may be appropriate for certain individuals.'

findings.assertion: ADA gives a peak postprandial capillary plasma glucose target for non-pregnant adults.
findings.value: <180 mg/dL (<10.0 mmol/L)
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6, Table 6.3
findings.sourceTitle: 6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Peak postprandial capillary plasma glucose ‡ <180 mg/dL * (<10.0 mmol/L)
findings.notes: String-verified from Table 6.3. Peak postprandial is defined by ADA as measured 1–2 h after the start of the meal.

findings.assertion: ADA sets a continuous-glucose-monitoring time-in-range goal for most non-pregnant adults.
findings.value: >70% of time in 70–180 mg/dL (3.9–10.0 mmol/L)
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6, Rec 6.3b
findings.sourceTitle: 6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 6.3b A goal time in range of >70% in people using CGM is appropriate for many nonpregnant adults.
findings.notes: String-verified; grade B. The 70–180 mg/dL (3.9–10.0 mmol/L) range definition is stated elsewhere in the section, not inside Rec 6.3b itself. CGM is largely unavailable at a Mulago-tier resource level — this metric may be inapplicable in the target deployment.

findings.assertion: ADA sets time-below-range ceilings for people using CGM, with a tighter ceiling for older adults.
findings.value: <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L): <4% of time (or <1% for older adults); <54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L): <1% of time
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6, Rec 6.3c
findings.sourceTitle: 6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 6.3c A goal percent time <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) of <4% (or <1% for older adults) and a goal percent time <54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L) of <1% are recommended in people using CGM to prevent hypoglycemia. Deintensify or modify therapy if these goals are not met.
findings.notes: String-verified; grade B. Note the explicit deintensification instruction — this is an actionable safety trigger, not just a monitoring metric.

findings.assertion: ADA defines level 1 and level 2 hypoglycaemia by glucose concentration.
findings.value: Level 1: <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) and ≥54 mg/dL (≥3.0 mmol/L). Level 2: <54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L)
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6
findings.sourceTitle: 6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Level 1 hypoglycemia is defined as a measurable glucose concentration <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) and ≥54 mg/dL (≥3.0 mmol/L). […] Level 2 hypoglycemia (defined as a blood glucose concentration <54 mg/dL [<3.0 mmol/L]) is the threshold at which neuroglycopenic symptoms begin to occur and requires immediate action to resolve the hypoglycemic event.
findings.notes: Both sentences string-verified from the retrieved page (quote joins two sentences from the same section, separated by an ellipsis).

findings.assertion: ADA defines level 3 hypoglycaemia by clinical severity rather than by a glucose number.
findings.value: No numeric threshold — severe event requiring assistance, irrespective of glucose value
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6
findings.sourceTitle: 6. Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Level 3 hypoglycemia may be recognized or unrecognized and can progress to loss of consciousness, seizure, coma, or death.
findings.notes: The quoted sentence is string-verified. The fuller Table 6.4 wording ('a severe event characterised by altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance … irrespective of glucose level') came from the WebFetch summariser and was NOT independently string-verified — treat the table wording as provisional. Important for a decision-support tool: level 3 must not be gated on a glucose value.

findings.assertion: ADA sets a tighter A1C band for older adults who are healthy with intact cognition and function.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 13, Rec 13.7a (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1); doi 10.2337/dc26-S013)
findings.sourceTitle: 13. Older Adults: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 13.7a Older adults with diabetes with few and stable coexisting chronic illnesses, and intact cognitive and functional status, should have lower glycemic goals (such as A1C <7.0–7.5% [<53–58 mmol/mol]) and/or time in range [TIR] 70–180 mg/dL [3.9–10.0 mmol/L] of ≥70% and time below range ≤70 mg/dL [≤3.9 mmol/L] of ≤4%) if CGM is used.
findings.notes: String-verified; grade C.

findings.assertion: ADA sets a looser A1C goal for older adults with intermediate or complex health.
findings.value: A1C <8.0% (<64 mmol/mol); TIR ≥50%; TBR <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) of <1%
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 13, Rec 13.7b
findings.sourceTitle: 13. Older Adults: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Selection of glycemic goals should be individualized and should prioritize avoidance of hypoglycemia, with less stringent goals (such as A1C <8.0% [<64 mmol/mol] and/or TIR 70–180 mg/dL [3.9–10.0 mmol/L] of ≥50% and time below range <70 mg/dL [3.9 mmol/L] of <1%) for those with significant cognitive and/or functional limitations, frailty, severe comorbidities, and a less favorable risk-to-benef[it ratio]
findings.notes: String-verified. Quote truncated at the end of the retrieved run; the trailing word 'benefit ratio' is inferred and bracketed.

findings.assertion: For older adults in very complex or poor health, ADA advises against relying on A1C and gives glucose ranges instead.
findings.value: Fasting/preprandial 100–180 mg/dL (5.6–10.0 mmol/L); bedtime 110–200 mg/dL (6.1–11.1 mmol/L); BP <140/90 mmHg
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 13, Table 13.2 / Rec 13.7c
findings.sourceTitle: 13. Older Adults: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: Avoid reliance on A1C; glucose management decisions should be based on avoiding hypoglycemia and symptomatic hyperglycemia 100–180 mg/dL (5.6–10.0 mmol/L) 110–200 mg/dL (6.1–11.1 mmol/L) <140/90 mmHg Consider likelihood of benefit with statin
findings.notes: String-verified from Table 13.2; the quote is the flattened table row (target statement, fasting/preprandial range, bedtime range, BP goal, lipid stance). The intermediate/complex row reads '90–150 mg/dL (5.0–8.3 mmol/L)' fasting and '100–180 mg/dL (5.6–10.0 mmol/L)' bedtime with BP <130/80 mmHg.

findings.assertion: ADA sets the on-treatment blood pressure goal in diabetes, and encourages a lower systolic goal in high-risk people.
findings.value: <130/80 mmHg; SBP <120 mmHg encouraged if high cardiovascular or kidney risk
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 10, Rec 10.4 (Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl 1):S216–S245; doi 10.2337/dc26-S010)
findings.sourceTitle: 10. Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 10.4 If it can be safely attained, the on-treatment blood pressure goal is <130/80 mmHg; a systolic blood pressure goal <120 mmHg should be encouraged in individuals with high cardiovascular or kidney risk.
findings.notes: String-verified; grade A. The SBP <120 clause is new-ish and is the main point of divergence from WHO/ISH — see conflicts. It presupposes accurate, standardised BP measurement.

findings.assertion: ADA sets the blood pressure thresholds at which antihypertensive drug therapy is started, and when to start two agents.
findings.value: Initiate therapy at confirmed office BP ≥130/80 mmHg; start two drugs at ≥150/90 mmHg
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 10, Recs 10.6 and 10.7
findings.sourceTitle: 10. Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 10.6 In individuals with confirmed office-based blood pressure ≥130/80 mmHg, pharmacologic therapy should be initiated and titrated to achieve their individualized blood pressure goal. […] 10.7 Individuals with confirmed office-based blood pressure ≥150/90 mmHg should, in addition to lifestyle therapy, have prompt initiation and timely titration of two drugs
findings.notes: String-verified (two adjacent recommendations joined by an ellipsis).

findings.assertion: ADA applies the same blood pressure goal to type 1 diabetes as to type 2.
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 10 (narrative)
findings.sourceTitle: 10. Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: a similar blood pressure goal of <130/80 mmHg is recommended in people with type 1 diabetes. As discussed below, treatment should be individualized.
findings.notes: String-verified. Flagged in the ADA 2026 Summary of Revisions as a change for this edition.

findings.assertion: ADA recommends moderate-intensity statin for people with diabetes aged 40–75 without ASCVD.
findings.value: Moderate-intensity statin; no LDL numeric goal specified for this group
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 10, Rec 10.18
findings.sourceTitle: 10. Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 10.18 For people with diabetes aged 40–75 years without ASCVD, use moderate-intensity statin therapy in addition to lifestyle therapy. A
findings.notes: String-verified; grade A. Note ADA's baseline primary-prevention rule is intensity-based, not LDL-goal-based.

findings.assertion: ADA sets an LDL-cholesterol goal for higher-risk primary prevention in diabetes aged 40–75.
findings.value: LDL-C <70 mg/dL (<1.8 mmol/L), with ≥50% reduction from baseline, using high-intensity statin
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 10, Rec 10.20
findings.sourceTitle: 10. Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 10.20 For people with diabetes aged 40–75 years at higher cardiovascular risk, including those with one or more additional ASCVD risk factors, high-intensity statin therapy is recommended to reduce LDL cholesterol by ≥50% of baseline and to obtain an LDL cholesterol goal of <70 mg/dL (<1.8 mmol/L). A
findings.notes: String-verified; grade A. 'Higher risk' is defined by presence of one or more additional ASCVD risk factors rather than by a calculated percentage risk.

findings.assertion: ADA sets an LDL-cholesterol goal for secondary prevention in diabetes with established ASCVD.
findings.value: LDL-C <55 mg/dL (<1.4 mmol/L), with ≥50% reduction from baseline
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 10, Rec 10.27
findings.sourceTitle: 10. Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 10.27 For people with diabetes and ASCVD, treatment with high-intensity statin therapy is recommended to obtain an LDL cholesterol reduction of ≥50% from baseline and an LDL cholesterol goal of <55 mg/dL (<1.4 mmol/L). Addition of ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor with proven benefit in this population is recommended if this goal is not achi[eved]
findings.notes: String-verified; quote truncated at the retrieved run boundary. Ezetimibe/PCSK9 escalation is conditional on failing the goal on maximum tolerated statin.

findings.assertion: ADA's 2026 cardiovascular section does not name any specific 10-year cardiovascular risk calculator.
findings.value: No named model (negative finding): no PREVENT, no Pooled Cohort Equations, no ASCVD Risk Estimator, no SCORE2, no Framingham risk equation recommended
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 10
findings.sourceTitle: 10. Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: additional ASCVD risk factors, such as older age, hypertension, dyslipidemia, smoking, CKD, or obesity
findings.notes: Established by exhaustive case-insensitive string search of the full retrieved section text for 'PREVENT', 'Pooled Cohort', 'Risk Estimator', 'risk calculator', '10-year risk', 'SCORE2' and 'Framingham': zero hits for any risk tool as a recommended instrument (the only 'Framingham' hits are a cohort citation and a reference-list entry). ADA 2026 therefore stratifies by risk-factor counting, not by a calculated percentage — a significant design implication if MedSync intends to compute a risk score.

findings.assertion: ADA directs agent choice in type 2 diabetes by comorbidity (ASCVD, heart failure, CKD) independently of A1C, displacing a strictly metformin-first ladder.
findings.value: GLP-1 RA and/or SGLT2 inhibitor for established/high-risk ASCVD; SGLT2 inhibitor for heart failure; SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA for CKD with eGFR 20–60 mL/min/1.73 m² and/or albuminuria — all 'irrespective of A1C'
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9, Recs 9.7, 9.8, 9.10 (doi 10.2337/dc26-S009)
findings.sourceTitle: 9. Pharmacologic Approaches to Glycemic Treatment: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 9.7 In adults with type 2 diabetes and established or high risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, the treatment plan should include medications with demonstrated benefits to reduce cardiovascular events (e.g., glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist [GLP-1 RA] and/or sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 [SGLT2] inhibitor) for glycemic management and comprehensive cardiovascular risk reduction (irrespective of A1C)
findings.notes: Rec 9.7 wording came from the WebFetch summariser; the surrounding recommendation numbering (9.6, 9.14, 9.20, 9.21) was independently string-verified in the retrieved page, so the numbering is sound. The exact wording of 9.8 (heart failure) and 9.10 (CKD, eGFR 20–60) was NOT string-verified — see unverifiable. The 'irrespective of A1C' principle is the key divergence from WHO PEN/HEARTS-D.

findings.assertion: ADA sets an A1C distance-above-goal at which single-agent therapy is expected to be insufficient.
findings.value: A1C ≥1.5% (≥16 mmol/mol) above the individualised goal
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9 (narrative)
findings.sourceTitle: 9. Pharmacologic Approaches to Glycemic Treatment: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: When A1C is ≥1.5% above the individualized glycemic goal […] many individuals will require dual-combination therapy or a more potent glucose-lowering agent to achieve and maintain their goal A1C level
findings.notes: String-verified. The mmol/mol equivalent (≈16 mmol/mol for a 1.5 percentage-point difference) is my arithmetic conversion, NOT quoted from ADA — do not present it as sourced. Related Rec 9.6: 'Consider combination therapy in adults with type 2 diabetes for initial treatment to shorten time to attainment of individualized glycemic goals.' (string-verified).

findings.assertion: ADA gives explicit glycaemic thresholds and symptom criteria that trigger consideration of insulin in type 2 diabetes.
findings.value: A1C >10% (>86 mmol/mol) or blood glucose ≥300 mg/dL (≥16.7 mmol/L), or symptoms of hyperglycaemia
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9, Rec 9.20
findings.sourceTitle: 9. Pharmacologic Approaches to Glycemic Treatment: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 9.20 In adults with type 2 diabetes, initiation of insulin should be considered regardless of background glucose-lowering therapy or disease duration if symptoms of hyperglycemia are present or when A1C or blood glucose levels are very high (i.e., A1C >10% [>86 mmol/mol] or blood glucose ≥300 mg/dL [≥16.7 mmol/L])
findings.notes: String-verified. This is the clearest numeric escalation trigger in the ADA ladder and maps well onto a rules engine.

findings.assertion: ADA prefers GLP-1-based therapy over insulin for initial or add-on injectable therapy in the absence of severe hyperglycaemia.
findings.value: GLP-1-based therapy preferred to insulin (no threshold; conditional on absence of severe hyperglycaemia or hyperglycaemic crisis)
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9, Rec 9.21
findings.sourceTitle: 9. Pharmacologic Approaches to Glycemic Treatment: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 9.21 In adults with type 2 diabetes without severe hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis, GLP-1–based therapy is preferred to insulin for initial or add-on glucose-lowering therapy ( Fig. 9.4 ). A
findings.notes: String-verified; grade A. Directly opposed to the WHO HEARTS-D ladder for a resource-limited tier, where human insulin precedes newer agents on cost grounds. Requires an explicit MedSync policy decision.

findings.assertion: ADA specifies how often the medication plan should be reassessed.
findings.value: Every 3–6 months
findings.standardVersion: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9, Rec 9.14
findings.sourceTitle: 9. Pharmacologic Approaches to Glycemic Treatment: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
findings.quote: 9.14 Medication plan and medication-taking behavior should be reevaluated at regular intervals (e.g., every 3–6 months) and adjusted as needed to incorporate specific factors that affect choice of treatment and ensure achievement of individualized glycemic goals
findings.notes: String-verified.

findings.assertion: WHO's primary-care diabetes module sets a single default HbA1c aim for the majority of patients.
findings.value: HbA1c 7.0% (53 mmol/mol)
findings.standardVersion: HEARTS-D: Diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes, WHO 2020 (WHO/UCN/NCD/20.1)
findings.sourceTitle: HEARTS D: diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
findings.quote: The majority of patients can be expected to aim for an HbA1c of 7.0% (53 mmol/mol).
findings.notes: PDF downloaded from WHO IRIS and text-extracted locally; string-verified. IRIS landing page: https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/331710 (blocked to direct fetch; the bitstream URL above is what was actually retrieved). WHO states this as a flat aim, whereas ADA states '<7%' — a subtle but real difference in framing.

findings.assertion: WHO permits relaxing the HbA1c target under named clinical conditions.
findings.value: HbA1c <8% (<64 mmol/mol)
findings.standardVersion: HEARTS-D, WHO 2020
findings.sourceTitle: HEARTS D: diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
findings.quote: The HbA1c target can be relaxed (e.g. to <8% or <64 mmol/mol) in people with frequent severe hypoglycaemia, advanced complications or low life-expectancy.
findings.notes: String-verified. WHO also states the converse: 'Patients treated with diet, physical activity and metformin (very low risk of hypoglycaemia) should be encouraged to achieve a lower HbA1c target.' — i.e. WHO ties tightening to hypoglycaemia risk of the regimen, which is a cleaner rule than ADA's 'good health and function'.

findings.assertion: WHO gives explicit glucose surrogate targets for settings where HbA1c is unavailable or unreliable — the key adaptation for a resource-limited tier.
findings.value: Fasting plasma glucose ≤7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) and postprandial plasma glucose ≤9.0 mmol/L (160 mg/dL)
findings.standardVersion: HEARTS-D, WHO 2020
findings.sourceTitle: HEARTS D: diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
findings.quote: If HbA1c measurement is not available or there is concern over its validity, an FPG value of ≤7.0 mmol/L (126mg/dL) and a postprandial PG value of ≤9.0 mmol/L (160 mg/dL) can serve as surrogates.
findings.notes: String-verified. Note WHO's postprandial surrogate (≤160 mg/dL) is TIGHTER than ADA's peak postprandial target (<180 mg/dL) — worth flagging to clinicians. WHO also ranks monitoring modalities: FPG < FPG+2h postprandial < full glucose profile, with random plasma glucose least informative.

findings.assertion: WHO sets the blood pressure treatment threshold and target in people with diabetes at primary-care level.
findings.value: Treat when SBP ≥130 mmHg or DBP ≥80 mmHg; target <130/80 mmHg
findings.standardVersion: HEARTS-D, WHO 2020
findings.sourceTitle: HEARTS D: diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
findings.quote: Hypertension treatment is indicated in people with diabetes when systolic blood pressure ≥130 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥80 mmHg. […] Thiazide diuretics and ACE inhibitors are recommended to achieve a target blood pressure of <130/80 mmHg. If this is not achievable, refer to a higher level of care.
findings.notes: String-verified (two passages joined by an ellipsis). WHO names thiazide and ACE inhibitor as the drug classes and adds an explicit referral trigger when target is unattainable — directly usable as a referral rule.
