findings.assertion: WHO recommends statins for all people with type 2 diabetes aged 40 or over, but subordinates this to medicine-access constraints.
findings.value: Statin for all with type 2 diabetes aged ≥40 years; if not feasible, restrict to highest CVD risk (established CVD, nephropathy, or high risk on a CVD risk chart). No LDL numeric goal given.
findings.standardVersion: HEARTS-D, WHO 2020
findings.sourceTitle: HEARTS D: diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
findings.quote: Statins are recommended for all people with type 2 diabetes 40 years old or older, but only if this does not negatively impact access to glucose-lowering and blood pressure-lowering medication. […] If this is not feasible, use statins in patients at highest risk of CVD events (e.g. patients with CVD, patients with nephropathy and/or patients with a high risk on a CVD risk prediction chart).
findings.notes: String-verified (two passages joined). WHO gives NO LDL target at all — the whole strategy is fixed-benefit/age-based, not goal-based. The explicit rationing clause ('only if this does not negatively impact access to glucose-lowering and blood pressure-lowering medication') has no ADA analogue and should be surfaced to prescribers in a resource-limited deployment.

findings.assertion: WHO restricts antiplatelet therapy in diabetes to secondary prevention only.
findings.value: Acetylsalicylic acid 75–100 mg daily, secondary prevention only (survivors of a CVD event without major bleeding history)
findings.standardVersion: HEARTS-D, WHO 2020
findings.sourceTitle: HEARTS D: diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
findings.quote: Use of antiplatelet treatment is recommended only for secondary prevention of CVD events, even among patients with diabetes. The recommendation is for 75–100 mg of acetylsalicylic acid daily to be prescribed to all people with diabetes who have survived a CVD event and have no history of major bleeding.
findings.notes: String-verified. Included despite the 'no doses' instruction because the dose is inseparable from the recommendation as WHO states it; the load-bearing content is the secondary-prevention-only restriction.

findings.assertion: WHO's step 1 of the resource-limited glycaemic ladder is metformin, with gliclazide as the alternative first-line agent.
findings.value: Step 1: metformin (after diet and physical activity fail); second-generation sulfonylurea, preferably gliclazide, as first-line if metformin contraindicated or not tolerated
findings.standardVersion: HEARTS-D, WHO 2020 (protocol derived from WHO-PEN 2013)
findings.sourceTitle: HEARTS D: diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
findings.quote: Metformin does not cause weight gain or hypoglycaemia and is the recommended initial treatment for people who do not achieve the desired glycaemic control with diet and physical activity. […] A second-generation sulfonylurea (preferably gliclazide) can be used as initial (first-line) treatment when metformin is contraindicated or not tolerated. […] Other pharmacological agents have not been shown to be superior to metformin or sulfonylurea for glycaemic control and long-term outcomes as initial treatment.
findings.notes: String-verified (three consecutive bullets joined by ellipses). Metformin contraindications listed by WHO: eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m², severe reduced liver function, acute cardiac insufficiency, respiratory insufficiency, alcohol abuse, history of lactic acidosis. The Fig. 1 protocol is footnoted '* Derived from WHO-PEN 2013'.

findings.assertion: WHO's step 2 is adding a sulfonylurea to metformin, with a symptom-based shortcut to insulin.
findings.value: Step 2: add second-generation sulfonylurea (preferably gliclazide) to metformin; if symptomatic hyperglycaemia, give a sulfonylurea or refer for insulin
findings.standardVersion: HEARTS-D, WHO 2020
findings.sourceTitle: HEARTS D: diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
findings.quote: Add a second-generation sulfonylurea (preferably gliclazide) to metformin in patients with inadequately controlled glycaemia on metformin, along with diet and physical activity. […] In hyperglycaemic patients with symptoms, give a sulfonylurea or refer for insulin treatment.
findings.notes: String-verified. WHO separately restricts glibenclamide: not recommended in people aged ≥60 years, severe liver disease, where hypoglycaemia is a concern (falls risk, impaired awareness, living alone), or people who drive/operate machinery for work — a directly encodable safety rule.

findings.assertion: WHO's step 3 is human insulin, with DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors and thiazolidinediones explicitly demoted below insulin on cost grounds.
findings.value: Step 3: refer for insulin or add human insulin to oral medication. DPP-4 inhibitor, SGLT2 inhibitor or TZD only if insulin is unsuitable, and 'not recommended for routine use due to high cost'
findings.standardVersion: HEARTS-D, WHO 2020
findings.sourceTitle: HEARTS D: diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
findings.quote: Refer for insulin treatment or add human insulin to oral medication (Annex 1). […] If insulin is unsuitable, a DPP-4 inhibitor, SGLT-2 inhibitor or a thiazolidinedione (TZD) may be added, but these are not recommended for routine use due to high cost and, with the exception of SGLT-2 inhibitors, uncertain benefit.
findings.notes: String-verified (footnote markers removed from the quote). WHO defines 'insulin unsuitable' as: more costly than oral agents, or circumstances making use difficult (e.g. people living alone and dependent on others to inject). This is the sharpest divergence from ADA 2026, which places GLP-1 RA/SGLT2i ahead of insulin. Note WHO singles out SGLT2 inhibitors as the exception on benefit — only cost holds them back.

findings.assertion: WHO advises against routine use of insulin analogues in favour of human insulin.
findings.value: Human insulin preferred; insulin analogues not recommended for routine use
findings.standardVersion: HEARTS-D, WHO 2020 (footnote to the intensification section)
findings.sourceTitle: HEARTS D: diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
findings.quote: Insulin analogues are not recommended for routine use as they are substantially more costly than human insulin and there is considerable uncertainty over their benefits, especially in people with type 2 diabetes.
findings.notes: String-verified. HEARTS-D cross-references the WHO 2018 'Guidelines on second- and third-line medicines and type of insulin for the control of blood glucose levels in non-pregnant adults with diabetes mellitus', which I did not retrieve separately.

findings.assertion: WHO sets blood pressure thresholds for initiating antihypertensive drugs, with a lower threshold for people with diabetes.
findings.value: General: SBP ≥140 mmHg or DBP ≥90 mmHg. Diabetes, CKD or high CV risk without CVD: SBP 130–139 mmHg. Existing CVD: SBP 130–139 mmHg.
findings.standardVersion: WHO Guideline for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults, 2021
findings.sourceTitle: Recommendations — Guideline for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults (WHO, 2021)
findings.quote: WHO suggests pharmacological antihypertensive treatment of individuals without cardiovascular disease but with high cardiovascular risk, diabetes mellitus, or chronic kidney disease, and systolic blood pressure of 130–139 mmHg. Strong recommendation, moderate- to high-certainty evidence
findings.notes: String-verified by local regex extraction of the NCBI Bookshelf page text, including the strength label immediately following the recommendation. Note the internal oddity in the WHO document itself: the verb is 'suggests' yet the label reads 'Strong recommendation' — quoted faithfully.

findings.assertion: WHO sets blood pressure treatment targets, with a lower systolic target for people with diabetes but at a weaker recommendation strength.
findings.value: No comorbidity: <140/90 mmHg (strong). Known CVD: SBP <130 mmHg (strong). High CV risk, diabetes, or CKD: SBP <130 mmHg (conditional).
findings.standardVersion: WHO Guideline for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults, 2021
findings.sourceTitle: Recommendations — Guideline for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults (WHO, 2021)
findings.quote: WHO recommends a target blood pressure treatment goal of <140/90 mmHg in all patients with hypertension without comorbidities. Strong recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence […] WHO suggests a target systolic blood pressure treatment goal of <130 mmHg in high-risk patients with hypertension (those with high CVD risk, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease). Conditional recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence
findings.notes: String-verified with strength labels. Critically: WHO gives NO diastolic target for the diabetes group — systolic only. ADA gives <130/80 (systolic and diastolic). A tool that enforces a diastolic component is going beyond WHO.

findings.assertion: WHO explicitly subordinates cardiovascular risk assessment to timely treatment initiation.
findings.value: Risk assessment at or after treatment initiation, only where feasible and non-delaying (conditional, low-certainty)
findings.standardVersion: WHO Guideline for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults, 2021
findings.sourceTitle: Recommendations — Guideline for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults (WHO, 2021)
findings.quote: WHO suggests cardiovascular risk assessment at or after the initiation of pharmacological treatment for hypertension, but only where this is feasible and does not delay treatment. Conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence
findings.notes: String-verified. Strong design signal for MedSync: a CV risk calculator must never be a blocking step in the hypertension workflow.

findings.assertion: The WHO cardiovascular risk charts provide regionally-specific 10-year risk models, in laboratory-based and non-laboratory-based variants.
findings.value: 10-year risk of fatal and non-fatal CVD (MI and stroke), ages 40–80 years, across 21 GBD regions. Laboratory model: age, smoking, SBP, diabetes history, total cholesterol. Non-laboratory model: age, smoking, SBP, BMI.
findings.standardVersion: WHO CVD Risk Chart Working Group, Lancet Global Health 2019;7(10):e1332–e1345 (doi 10.1016/S2214-109X(19)30318-3)
findings.sourceTitle: World Health Organization cardiovascular disease risk charts: revised models to estimate risk in 21 global regions
findings.quote: we have derived, validated, and illustrated new WHO risk prediction models to estimate cardiovascular disease risk in 21 Global Burden of Disease regions
findings.notes: Retrieved via WebFetch of the PMC article; the predictor lists and the 40–80 age range were read from that retrieval but were NOT independently string-verified by me. The non-laboratory variant is the operationally important one for Ugandan primary care (no lipid panel needed). The specific names of the sub-Saharan Africa sub-regions were not surfaced in the retrieved text — see unverifiable.

findings.assertion: WHO states that the cohort data needed to derive risk models for low- and middle-income countries do not exist, and that recalibration was used instead of local derivation.
findings.value: Derived from 85 cohorts mostly in high-income countries; recalibrated using GBD and NCD-RisC aggregate data rather than local cohorts
findings.standardVersion: WHO CVD Risk Chart Working Group, Lancet Global Health 2019
findings.sourceTitle: World Health Organization cardiovascular disease risk charts: revised models to estimate risk in 21 global regions
findings.quote: we derived risk prediction models from 85 cohorts mostly from high-income countries in the ERFC. Ideally, however, the derivation of risk models for low-income and middle-income countries would involve nationally representative, large-scale prospective cohort data from several of these countries...Unfortunately, however, such data do not yet exist for most low-income and middle-income countries.
findings.notes: Retrieved via WebFetch of the PMC article; not independently string-verified — treat the quote as high-confidence but re-check before it is displayed verbatim to clinicians. This is the single most important caveat for deploying any risk score in Uganda: even WHO's own regionally-labelled African charts are recalibrations of high-income-country cohorts, not African-derived models.

findings.assertion: WHO's 2025 Essential Medicines List added GLP-1 receptor agonists and a dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist, but only for a narrowly defined subgroup.
findings.value: Semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide and tirzepatide added — restricted to adults with type 2 diabetes with established cardiovascular disease or chronic kidney disease AND obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²)
findings.standardVersion: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, 24th list, 2025 (announced 5 September 2025)
findings.sourceTitle: WHO updates list of essential medicines to include key cancer, diabetes treatments
findings.quote: GLP-1 receptor agonists – semaglutide, dulaglutide and liraglutide – and the GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) dual receptor agonist (tirzepatide) have been added to the EML. They are used as glucose lowering therapy for adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus with established cardiovascular disease or chronic kidney disease and obesity (defined as body mass index (BMI) ≥ 30kg/m 2 ).
findings.notes: Fetched by curl and read from the extracted page text — string-verified. This is the WHO news release, NOT the EML document itself (the 24th list, section 18.5, was not retrieved). The BMI ≥30 criterion is a much narrower gate than ADA's comorbidity-driven GLP-1 recommendation and materially changes the ladder for a WHO-aligned formulary.

findings.assertion: KDIGO recommends an individualised HbA1c target expressed as a range rather than a single default, for people with diabetes and CKD not on dialysis.
findings.value: HbA1c <6.5% to <8.0% (<48 to <64 mmol/mol)
findings.standardVersion: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease, Rec 2.2.1 (1C)
findings.sourceTitle: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
findings.quote: Recommendation 2.2.1: We recommend an individualized HbA1c target ranging from <6.5% to <8.0% in patients with diabetes and CKD not treated with dialysis
findings.notes: PDF downloaded from kdigo.org and text-extracted locally; string-verified. The mmol/mol conversions are mine, not quoted. KDIGO adds Practice Point 2.1.2: accuracy and precision of HbA1c declines in advanced CKD (G4–G5) — clinically important where HbA1c is the only available metric.

findings.assertion: KDIGO's systolic blood pressure target in CKD is lower than every other body reviewed, and is conditional on standardised office measurement.
findings.value: SBP <120 mmHg, when tolerated, using standardized office BP measurement (2B — suggestion, moderate quality)
findings.standardVersion: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Blood Pressure in Chronic Kidney Disease, Rec 3.1.1
findings.sourceTitle: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Blood Pressure in Chronic Kidney Disease
findings.quote: Recommendation 3.1.1: We suggest that adults with high BP and CKD be treated with a target systolic blood pressure (SBP) of <120 mm Hg, when tolerated, using standardized office BP measurement (2B). Practice Point 3.1.1: It is potentially hazardous to apply the recommended SBP target of <120 mm Hg to BP mea[surements obtained in a non-standardized manner]
findings.notes: PDF downloaded and text-extracted locally; string-verified. Practice Point 3.1.1 is a safety-critical caveat: KDIGO itself calls it 'potentially hazardous' to apply <120 mmHg to non-standardised measurements. In a busy Ugandan outpatient setting, non-standardised measurement is the norm — this target should almost certainly NOT be the default in MedSync. Quote truncated at the retrieved run boundary; bracketed completion is inferred.

findings.assertion: KDIGO makes SGLT2 inhibitors a first-line recommendation in type 2 diabetes with CKD, independent of glycaemic need.
findings.value: SGLT2 inhibitor for T2D + CKD with eGFR ≥20 mL/min/1.73 m² (1A); continue even if eGFR later falls below 20
findings.standardVersion: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes Management in CKD, Rec 1.3.1 and Practice Points 1.3.1, 1.3.6
findings.sourceTitle: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
findings.quote: Recommendation 1.3.1: We recommend treating patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D), CKD, and an eGFR≥20 ml/min per 1.73 m2 with an SGLT2i (1A). Practice Point 1.3.1: The recommendation for SGLT2i is for kidney and cardiovascular protection and SGLT2i have been shown to have safety and benefit in CKD patients, even for those without T2D.
findings.notes: String-verified from the locally extracted PDF (the '≥' renders as '‡' in raw extraction; corrected here). Note the eGFR threshold difference from ADA Rec 9.10 (eGFR 20–60) — KDIGO has no upper bound.

findings.assertion: KDIGO places GLP-1 receptor agonists as the next step after metformin and SGLT2 inhibitor in T2D with CKD.
findings.value: Long-acting GLP-1 RA when individualised glycaemic targets are unmet despite metformin + SGLT2i, or when those cannot be used (1B)
findings.standardVersion: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes Management in CKD, Rec 4.2.1
findings.sourceTitle: KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
findings.quote: Recommendation 4.2.1: In patients with T2D and CKD who have not achieved individualized glycemic targets despite use of metformin and SGLT2i treatment, or who are unable to use those medications, we recommend a long-acting GLP-1 RA (1B).
findings.notes: String-verified. KDIGO also states metformin may be given when eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m², and Practice Point 4.2.3: 'GLP-1 RA should not be used in combination with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors.' — an encodable interaction rule.

findings.assertion: KDIGO recommends a statin for every patient with diabetes and CKD, without an LDL goal.
findings.value: Statin for all patients with T1D or T2D and CKD; no LDL-C target specified
findings.standardVersion: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes Management in CKD, Executive Summary (comprehensive-care narrative)
findings.sourceTitle: Executive summary of the KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease
findings.quote: A statin is recommended for all patients with T1D or T2D and CKD.
findings.notes: PDF downloaded and text-extracted locally; string-verified. Like WHO and unlike ADA, KDIGO here is fixed-therapy rather than LDL-goal based.

findings.assertion: ESC's 2024 hypertension guideline sets a systolic target band that is lower than ADA's and lower than WHO's.
findings.value: Target systolic BP 120–129 mmHg for adults receiving BP-lowering medication (when tolerated)
findings.standardVersion: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of elevated blood pressure and hypertension (Eur Heart J 2024;45(38):3912; doi 10.1093/eurheartj/ehae178)
findings.sourceTitle: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of elevated blood pressure and hypertension
findings.quote: a target systolic BP of 120–129 mmHg among adults receiving BP-lowering medications
findings.notes: Retrieved via WebFetch of the OUP full-text page; NOT independently string-verified (curl to OUP is blocked). ESC qualifies this with tolerability and lists more lenient targets for age ≥85, symptomatic orthostatic hypotension, moderate-to-severe frailty, or limited life expectancy. Note this is a BAND (a floor of 120 as well as a ceiling of 129), unlike ADA's open-ended '<130/80'.

findings.assertion: ESC 2024 introduces an 'elevated blood pressure' category between normal and hypertension.
findings.value: Elevated BP: office SBP 120–139 mmHg or DBP 70–89 mmHg. Hypertension: office SBP ≥140 mmHg or DBP ≥90 mmHg.
findings.standardVersion: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of elevated blood pressure and hypertension
findings.sourceTitle: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of elevated blood pressure and hypertension
findings.quote: office systolic BP of 120–139 mmHg or diastolic BP of 70–89 mmHg
findings.notes: Retrieved via WebFetch of the OUP page; not independently string-verified. Relevant to MedSync's BP classification vocabulary — ESC's category boundaries differ from the ones ADA and WHO use.

findings.assertion: The 2023 ESC diabetes guideline endorses SCORE2-Diabetes as its type-2-diabetes-specific 10-year risk score, restricted to patients without overt ASCVD or severe target-organ damage.
findings.value: SCORE2-Diabetes, for T2D patients without ASCVD or severe target-organ damage; stratifies low / moderate / high / very high risk
findings.standardVersion: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiovascular disease in patients with diabetes (Eur Heart J 2023;44(39):4043)
findings.sourceTitle: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiovascular disease in patients with diabetes
findings.quote: a novel, dedicated, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM)-specific, 10-year CVD risk score […] serves as a guide for clinical decision-making in patients with T2DM at low, moderate, high, or very high risk, but without clinically overt ASCVD or severe TOD.
findings.notes: Retrieved via WebFetch of the OUP page; not independently string-verified. Only the front matter of this article was retrievable — the numeric BP and LDL recommendation tables were NOT obtainable (see unverifiable). Contrast with ADA 2026, which names no risk score at all.

findings.assertion: SCORE2-Diabetes is derived and calibrated exclusively for European populations, in four European risk regions.
findings.value: 10-year risk of non-fatal MI, stroke, or CVD mortality; type 2 diabetes, aged over 40, without previous CVD; recalibrated to four European risk regions (low, moderate, high, very-high)
findings.standardVersion: SCORE2-Diabetes working group, Eur Heart J 2023;44:2544–2556 (doi 10.1093/eurheartj/ehad260)
findings.sourceTitle: SCORE2-Diabetes: 10-year cardiovascular risk estimation in type 2 diabetes in Europe
findings.quote: to predict 10-year risk of CVD in individuals with type 2 diabetes in Europe
findings.notes: Retrieved via WebFetch of the PMC article; not independently string-verified. Predictors: conventional risk factors plus age at diabetes diagnosis, HbA1c, and creatinine-based eGFR. Derivation datasets were English/Welsh/Scottish, French, German and Italian; validation in Sweden, Spain, Croatia and Malta. NO African derivation or validation cohort exists — SCORE2-Diabetes must not be applied to a Ugandan population without explicit CSO sign-off.

findings.assertion: ISH uniquely splits its blood pressure targets into an 'essential' minimum standard and an 'optimal' standard, explicitly to serve low-resource settings.
findings.value: Optimal: <65 years <130/80 mmHg; ≥65 years <140/90 mmHg. Essential: reduce BP by at least 20/10 mmHg, ideally to <140/90 mmHg. Drug treatment threshold ≥140/90 mmHg (raised to ≥160/100 mmHg for those at lowest risk).
findings.standardVersion: 2020 International Society of Hypertension Global Hypertension Practice Guidelines (Hypertension 2020;75:1334–1357; doi 10.1161/HYPERTENSIONAHA.120.15026)
findings.sourceTitle: 2020 ISH Global Hypertension Practice Guidelines — official ISH guideline presentation slide deck
findings.quote: Drug Treatment Threshold ≥140/90 mmHg (raising to ≥160/100 mmHg for those at lowest risk) […] Drug Treatment Target Optimal: <65 years: <130/80 mmHg ≥65 years: <140/90 mmHg […] Essential: Reduce BP by at 20/10mmHg and ideally to <140/90 and individualize in the elderly based on frailty
findings.notes: PDF downloaded from ish-world.com and text-extracted locally; string-verified. IMPORTANT SOURCE CAVEAT: this is ISH's own official slide deck, NOT the guideline article text (both the Hypertension and J Hypertens full texts are paywalled — 403 and 402 respectively). The deck contains a typo, 'Reduce BP by at 20/10mmHg', which reads elsewhere in the same deck as '≥20/10 mmHg'; quoted as printed. The ISH diabetes-SPECIFIC comorbidity target was not present in the deck — see unverifiable. The essential/optimal split is the most directly transferable framing for a Ugandan deployment.

findings.assertion: ISH 2020 deliberately does not specify which cardiovascular risk assessment tool to use.
findings.value: No named risk tool (negative finding)
findings.standardVersion: 2020 ISH Global Hypertension Practice Guidelines
findings.sourceTitle: 2020 ISH Global Hypertension Practice Guidelines — official ISH guideline presentation slide deck
findings.quote: Cardiovascular Risk Assessment High Risk: CV disease, CKD3, Diabetes, HMOD CV risk assessment in all others […] Same as ESC-ESH CV risk assessment tool not specified
findings.notes: String-verified from the locally extracted deck (an ISH-vs-ESC/ESH comparison table; the quote flattens the ESC-ESH column then the ISH column). Note that ISH, like ESC/ESH, treats diabetes itself as automatically conferring high risk — which removes the need for a calculator in exactly the population MedSync targets.

findings.assertion: Framingham, SCORE2 and the WHO model classify substantially different proportions of the same sub-Saharan African population as moderate-to-high risk.
findings.value: Moderate-to-high risk in sub-Saharan Africa: WHO 16.30% (95% CI 15.78–16.83); SCORE2 22.69% (95% CI 22.09–23.28); Framingham 33.85% (95% CI 33.18–34.52)
findings.standardVersion: Liu Y et al., Journal of Global Health 2025;15:04323 (peer-reviewed study, not a guideline)
findings.sourceTitle: Regional variations in cardiovascular risk predictions: a comparative analysis of Framingham, SCORE2, and WHO models across 53 countries
findings.quote: These models were primarily developed using data from European and North American populations, leading to limited representation of other regions.
findings.notes: Retrieved via WebFetch; the percentages were read from that retrieval but NOT independently string-verified — verify before citing the numbers to clinicians. This is supporting evidence, not a standard: it quantifies how much the choice of model changes who gets treated in sub-Saharan Africa (a roughly two-fold spread). Combined with the WHO derivation caveat, it argues strongly against silently defaulting MedSync to any one risk model.

conflicts.assertion: Blood pressure target for an adult with diabetes
positions: ADA 2026 (Rec 10.4): on-treatment goal <130/80 mmHg if safely attainable, and 'a systolic blood pressure goal <120 mmHg should be encouraged in individuals with high cardiovascular or kidney risk' (grade A). Initiate drugs at confirmed office BP ≥130/80 mmHg.

WHO 2021 hypertension guideline: SBP <130 mmHg for high-risk patients including diabetes — CONDITIONAL recommendation, moderate certainty. No diastolic target given for this group. Initiation at SBP 130–139 mmHg.
WHO HEARTS-D 2020 (primary care): treat at SBP ≥130 or DBP ≥80 mmHg; target <130/80 mmHg; refer to higher-level care if not achievable.

ESC 2024 hypertension guideline: target systolic 120–129 mmHg for adults on BP-lowering medication when tolerated — a band with a floor, not an open-ended ceiling; more lenient targets for age ≥85, orthostatic hypotension, moderate-to-severe frailty, or limited life expectancy.

ISH 2020: OPTIMAL <130/80 mmHg if aged <65, <140/90 mmHg if aged ≥65. ESSENTIAL (minimum standard where resources are limited): reduce BP by ≥20/10 mmHg and ideally to <140/90 mmHg. Drug threshold ≥140/90 mmHg.

KDIGO 2021 (diabetes with CKD): SBP <120 mmHg when tolerated, but only using standardized office BP measurement (2B), and KDIGO itself calls it 'potentially hazardous' to apply this target to non-standardised measurements.
ADA 2026 (Rec 13.9, older adults): <130/80 mmHg for most, but a relaxed goal of <140/90 mmHg for poor health, limited life expectancy, or high risk of treatment adverse effects.
conflicts.recommendation: Do not pick a single global number. Implement <130/80 mmHg as the default operational target for diabetes — it is the value shared by ADA, WHO HEARTS-D and ISH's 'optimal' tier, and it is what a Mulago-tier service can realistically pursue. Then layer two explicit modifiers: (1) an ISH-style 'essential' fallback where a patient cannot reach 130/80 — record a ≥20/10 mmHg reduction with an interim ceiling of <140/90 as a legitimate, guideline-backed outcome rather than a failure, since this is the only framing designed for resource-limited care; (2) an age/frailty relaxation to <140/90 mmHg mirroring ADA 13.9 and ISH's ≥65 tier. Explicitly EXCLUDE the sub-120 systolic targets (ADA's high-risk encouragement, ESC's 120–129 band, KDIGO's <120) from any automated prompt unless the deployment can guarantee standardised BP measurement — KDIGO's own hazard warning makes this a patient-safety issue, not a preference. Requires CSO sign-off on the fallback thresholds before release.

conflicts.assertion: Whether the diabetes management ladder is comorbidity-driven or cost-driven, and where insulin sits in it
positions: ADA 2026 Section 9: metformin is described as the agent that 'historically has been the first-line treatment' for uncomplicated T2D, but agent choice is comorbidity-led — GLP-1 RA and/or SGLT2 inhibitor for ASCVD (Rec 9.7), SGLT2 inhibitor for heart failure (9.8), SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA for CKD (9.10), each 'irrespective of A1C'. Rec 9.21: 'GLP-1–based therapy is preferred to insulin for initial or add-on glucose-lowering therapy' (grade A). Insulin is a rescue for A1C >10% (>86 mmol/mol), glucose ≥300 mg/dL (≥16.7 mmol/L) or symptoms (9.20).

WHO HEARTS-D 2020: strict sequential ladder — diet/activity → metformin (gliclazide if metformin contraindicated) → add gliclazide → human insulin. DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors and TZDs sit BELOW insulin and are 'not recommended for routine use due to high cost and, with the exception of SGLT-2 inhibitors, uncertain benefit'. Insulin analogues 'not recommended for routine use'. No comorbidity-driven branch at all.

KDIGO 2022 (T2D with CKD): metformin PLUS an SGLT2 inhibitor as first-line (SGLT2i recommended at eGFR ≥20 mL/min/1.73 m², grade 1A), with a long-acting GLP-1 RA as the next step (4.2.1) — i.e. agrees with ADA's comorbidity-first logic, not WHO's cost-first logic.

WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, 24th list (2025): GLP-1 RAs and tirzepatide are now listed, but only for T2D with established CVD or CKD AND obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²) — a far narrower gate than either ADA or KDIGO applies.
conflicts.recommendation: Treat this as two distinct, explicitly labelled care pathways rather than one ladder with exceptions — the divergence is about resource tier, not about disagreement over evidence. Make WHO HEARTS-D the default pathway for the Ugandan/Mulago deployment (it is the protocol Ugandan primary care is built around, and it is the only one whose escalation steps are all achievable on a national formulary), and expose the ADA/KDIGO comorbidity-driven pathway as an overlay that activates only when the specific agent is actually on the local formulary and affordable for that patient. Critically, do NOT let the ADA rule 'GLP-1 preferred to insulin' fire in a WHO-tier context — that inversion is the single highest-risk mismatch in this domain, because it would recommend an agent the patient cannot obtain while deferring one they can. Use the WHO EML BMI ≥30 + CVD/CKD criteria as the gate for surfacing GLP-1 RAs at all. CSO must sign off on which pathway is default and on the formulary gating logic.

conflicts.assertion: Which cardiovascular risk estimation model to use, and whether to use one at all
positions: ADA 2026 Section 10: names NO risk calculator. Verified by exhaustive string search — no PREVENT, no Pooled Cohort Equations, no ASCVD Risk Estimator, no SCORE2, no Framingham equation. Statin intensity is decided by age band plus presence of 'one or more additional ASCVD risk factors'.
ISH 2020: 'CV risk assessment tool not specified'. Diabetes itself is treated as automatically conferring high risk, alongside CVD, CKD stage 3 and hypertension-mediated organ damage.

WHO 2021 hypertension guideline: risk assessment 'at or after the initiation of pharmacological treatment … but only where this is feasible and does not delay treatment' — conditional, low-certainty. Risk scoring must not block treatment.

WHO CVD risk charts (2019): 21 GBD-region models including African regions, in laboratory-based (age, smoking, SBP, diabetes, total cholesterol) and non-laboratory-based (age, smoking, SBP, BMI) variants, ages 40–80, for 10-year fatal and non-fatal MI/stroke. But WHO states the models were derived from '85 cohorts mostly from high-income countries' and that nationally representative cohort data 'do not yet exist for most low-income and middle-income countries' — the African charts are recalibrations, not African-derived models.

ESC 2023 diabetes guideline: recommends SCORE2-Diabetes, which is explicitly 'to predict 10-year risk of CVD in individuals with type 2 diabetes in Europe', recalibrated to four EUROPEAN risk regions, derived in UK/French/German/Italian data and validated in Sweden, Spain, Croatia and Malta. No African cohort.

Independent comparison (J Glob Health 2025): applied to sub-Saharan African populations, the three major models classify 16.3% (WHO), 22.7% (SCORE2) and 33.9% (Framingham) as moderate-to-high risk — roughly a two-fold spread on the same people.
conflicts.recommendation: Do not compute or display a percentage CV risk as a primary driver of treatment decisions in this deployment. Two of the four standard-setting bodies reviewed (ADA, ISH) deliberately name no tool, WHO explicitly forbids risk scoring from delaying treatment, and the two models that ARE named have no African derivation cohort — SCORE2-Diabetes is Europe-only by its authors' own statement, and even WHO's African charts are recalibrations of high-income-country data. Follow ISH and ESC/ESH instead: treat diabetes itself as conferring high risk, and drive statin and BP decisions off the ADA-style risk-factor count (age band + additional ASCVD risk factors) plus WHO HEARTS-D's age ≥40 statin rule. If a score is wanted for triage or reporting, use ONLY the WHO non-laboratory chart for the correct African sub-region (it needs no lipid panel, which suits the setting), label it visibly as a recalibrated estimate not validated in Ugandan cohorts, and never let it gate treatment initiation. SCORE2/SCORE2-Diabetes should be blocked outright for this population. Needs CSO sign-off.

conflicts.assertion: Lipid management strategy: LDL-cholesterol goal-based versus fixed-therapy by age and risk
positions: ADA 2026: goal-based and tiered. Age 40–75 without ASCVD, moderate-intensity statin, no numeric LDL goal (10.18). Higher risk (one or more additional ASCVD risk factors): high-intensity statin, ≥50% LDL reduction and LDL-C <70 mg/dL (<1.8 mmol/L) (10.20). Established ASCVD: ≥50% reduction and LDL-C <55 mg/dL (<1.4 mmol/L), adding ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor if unmet (10.27). Age 20–39 with risk factors: statin may be reasonable (10.19).

WHO HEARTS-D 2020: fixed-therapy and age-based, with NO LDL target anywhere. Statin for all with T2D aged ≥40 — but explicitly 'only if this does not negatively impact access to glucose-lowering and blood pressure-lowering medication', and if not feasible, restricted to those at highest risk (established CVD, nephropathy, or high risk on a CVD risk chart).
KDIGO 2022: fixed-therapy — 'A statin is recommended for all patients with T1D or T2D and CKD', with no LDL goal.

ADA 2026 Section 13 (older adults): 'Statin, unless contraindicated or not tolerated' for healthy and intermediate/complex health; for very complex/poor health, only 'Consider likelihood of benefit with statin'.
ESC 2023 diabetes guideline: states LDL-C targets by cardiovascular risk category (its Figure 10), but the numeric values could not be retrieved — see unverifiable.
conflicts.recommendation: Implement the WHO/KDIGO fixed-therapy rule as the primary decision logic — statin for every patient with type 2 diabetes aged ≥40, and for every patient with diabetes and CKD regardless of age — because it needs no lipid panel and is therefore executable at every MedSync site. Carry ADA's LDL goals (<70 mg/dL / <1.8 mmol/L for higher-risk primary prevention; <55 mg/dL / <1.4 mmol/L with established ASCVD) as a secondary, optional layer that activates only where a lipid profile actually exists, and never let an absent LDL result block statin initiation. Surface WHO's rationing caveat verbatim to prescribers: WHO subordinates the statin to glucose- and BP-lowering medicines when access is constrained, which no other body does, and clinicians in this setting need to see that trade-off stated rather than inferred. Do not encode ezetimibe/PCSK9 escalation unless those agents are on the local formulary. CSO sign-off needed on the age-based default.

conflicts.assertion: How the general adult HbA1c target is expressed, and how it is individualised
positions: ADA 2026 (6.3a): '<7% (<53 mmol/mol) is appropriate for many nonpregnant adults'. Tighter <6.5% (<48 mmol/mol) for good health and low treatment risk (6.4); looser 'up to 8% (64 mmol/mol)' for complex health status or limited life expectancy.

WHO HEARTS-D 2020: 'The majority of patients can be expected to aim for an HbA1c of 7.0% (53 mmol/mol)' — a flat value, not a '<' ceiling. Relax to <8% (<64 mmol/mol) for frequent severe hypoglycaemia, advanced complications or low life expectancy. Tighten for patients on diet, activity and metformin only, i.e. individualisation keyed to the hypoglycaemia risk of the REGIMEN.
KDIGO 2022 (2.2.1): no default at all — 'an individualized HbA1c target ranging from <6.5% to <8.0%' for diabetes with CKD, plus the warning that HbA1c accuracy and precision decline in CKD G4–G5.

ADA 2026 Section 13 (older adults): stratified by health status — healthy <7.0–7.5% (<53–58 mmol/mol); intermediate/complex <8.0% (<64 mmol/mol); very complex/poor health, 'Avoid reliance on A1C' entirely, managing instead to fasting 100–180 mg/dL (5.6–10.0 mmol/L) and bedtime 110–200 mg/dL (6.1–11.1 mmol/L).
conflicts.recommendation: Adopt <7.0% (<53 mmol/mol) as the displayed default — ADA and WHO agree on the number even though ADA writes it as a ceiling and WHO as an aim — but do not present it as a fixed target anywhere in the UI. Encode the three named relaxation triggers, which all four bodies broadly share: frequent or severe hypoglycaemia, advanced complications or limited life expectancy, and significant frailty or cognitive/functional limitation; each should relax the target to <8.0% (<64 mmol/mol). Prefer WHO's individualisation logic over ADA's for this deployment: WHO keys tightening to whether the regimen itself carries hypoglycaemia risk (diet/activity/metformin only), which is objective and computable from the prescription, whereas ADA's 'good health and function' is not. Two hard requirements: (1) where CKD is present, switch to KDIGO's <6.5%–<8.0% range and flag that HbA1c is unreliable at G4–G5; (2) implement ADA's 'avoid reliance on A1C' state for very complex/poor health — the tool must be able to drop A1C as the governing metric entirely and manage to glucose ranges instead, rather than showing an unmet target. Since HbA1c is frequently unavailable at the target sites, WHO's surrogates (FPG ≤7.0 mmol/L / 126 mg/dL, postprandial ≤9.0 mmol/L / 160 mg/dL) must be first-class, not a fallback — note WHO's postprandial surrogate is tighter than ADA's <180 mg/dL peak postprandial target, and CSO should rule on which to display.

unverifiable: ESC 2023 diabetes guideline — the actual BLOOD PRESSURE target numbers for patients with diabetes (Recommendation Table 10) could not be retrieved. The Oxford Academic full-text page returns only front matter to WebFetch and 403s to curl; PMC and Europe PMC have no open copy. Widely-cited values (SBP target 130 mmHg, <130 if tolerated but not <120; 130–139 mmHg if aged >65) are from my memory ONLY and were deliberately excluded from findings. This is a real gap in the ADA/ESC/ISH BP comparison the task asked for — the ESC position in the BP conflict rests on the 2024 hypertension guideline instead.

ESC 2023 diabetes guideline — the LDL-cholesterol goals by cardiovascular risk category (its Figure 10) in mmol/L and mg/dL. The figure is referenced in the retrievable text but its numeric values are not. No ESC LDL target is asserted anywhere in the findings.

ESC 2024 hypertension guideline — the diabetes-SPECIFIC recommendation (section 9.6). Only the general 120–129 mmHg systolic target was retrievable, and even that was via summarisation of the OUP page rather than direct string verification.

ISH 2020 — the diabetes-specific comorbidity blood pressure target. Both full texts are paywalled (ahajournals 403, journals.lww.com 402). The essential/optimal targets recorded come from ISH's own official slide deck, which is an ISH-published summary, NOT the guideline article. The commonly quoted 'BP lowered if ≥140/90 and treated to <130/80 (<140/80 in elderly) in diabetes' appeared only in a search-result summary and is NOT sourced.

IDF — no International Diabetes Federation position was retrieved at all. No IDF glycaemic, BP or lipid target, and no IDF stance on risk models, appears in the findings. The task's schema lists IDF as an expected standard; this is an outright gap.

ADA 2026 Section 9 — the exact wording of Rec 9.8 (heart failure/SGLT2 inhibitor) and Rec 9.10 (CKD, eGFR 20–60 mL/min/1.73 m² and/or albuminuria) was obtained via the WebFetch summariser and NOT independently string-verified against the retrieved page, unlike Recs 9.6, 9.14, 9.20 and 9.21 which were. The eGFR range in 9.10 in particular should be re-checked before encoding.

ADA 2026 Section 6, Table 6.4 — the full definitional wording of level 3 hypoglycaemia ('a severe event characterised by altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance for treatment, irrespective of glucose level') came from the summariser; only the narrative sentence about progression to loss of consciousness/seizure/coma/death was string-verified.

WHO CVD risk charts (Lancet Glob Health 2019) — the NAMES of the sub-Saharan Africa regional variants among the 21 GBD regions were not surfaced by the retrieval (the paper points to appendix 1 p 39, which was not fetched). I cannot state which specific African sub-region charts exist or which one applies to Uganda. The predictor variable lists and the 40–80 age range were read from the retrieval but not independently string-verified.

WHO Model List of Essential Medicines — the EML document itself (24th list, 2025, section 18.5 'Insulins and other medicines used for diabetes') was NOT retrieved. Only the WHO news release announcing the update was. Therefore: which insulins are listed, whether and under what conditions SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin/canagliflozin/dapagliflozin) appear, and the status of gliclazide and metformin on the current list are all unconfirmed against the primary document. Search-result claims about SGLT2 inhibitor listing were deliberately not recorded as findings.

WHO PEN (Package of Essential Noncommunicable Disease Interventions) — the PEN protocol document itself was not fetched. The resource-limited ladder recorded comes from WHO HEARTS-D 2020, whose glucose protocol is footnoted 'Derived from WHO-PEN 2013'. PEN-specific thresholds that differ from HEARTS-D, if any, are unknown.

WHO 2018 'Guidelines on second- and third-line medicines and type of insulin for the control of blood glucose levels in non-pregnant adults with diabetes mellitus' — cross-referenced by HEARTS-D but not retrieved. Its specific escalation criteria are unconfirmed.

Uganda national diabetes or NCD clinical guidelines — not searched for and not retrieved. Any claim that the WHO HEARTS-D ladder matches current Ugandan Ministry of Health protocol is an assumption on my part, not a sourced finding, and should be checked locally before it drives defaults.

Whether the WHO/ISH risk charts, or any CV risk model, have been externally validated against hard cardiovascular OUTCOMES in a Ugandan or East African cohort. The J Glob Health 2025 comparison shows models disagree with each other in sub-Saharan Africa, which is not the same as showing any of them is right; and its specific percentages were read via summarisation, not string-verified.

ADA 2026 evidence grades — grades (A/B/C/E) were captured where they appeared adjacent to the recommendation text in the retrieved HTML, but the grading letter is rendered separately from the sentence and the association could be off by one recommendation in places. Re-check grades before displaying them as ADA's.

ETDRS, ICDR and IWGDF standards — no retinopathy grading, diabetic retinopathy severity scale, or diabetic foot risk stratification content was sought or retrieved. These appear in the task's standard enumeration but fall outside the glycaemic/CV/management-ladder scope I covered; there are no findings for them.

All mmol/mol equivalents I supplied for A1C percentage DIFFERENCES (notably the ≈16 mmol/mol paired with ADA's 'A1C ≥1.5% above goal') are my own arithmetic conversions, not values quoted from any source. Absolute A1C values in mmol/mol are quoted from the sources; difference conversions are not.

audit.assertion: ADA's default glycaemic goal for most non-pregnant adults is an A1C below 7%.
audit.reason: Fetched raw HTML of PMC12690178 and string-matched. Rec 6.3a verbatim: 'An A1C goal of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) is appropriate for many nonpregnant adults without severe hypoglycemia or hypoglycemia affecting health or quality of life. A'. Citation block on the same page reads 'Diabetes Care . 2025 Dec 8;49(Suppl 1):S132–S149. doi: 10.2337/dc26-S006', matching the stated section, volume, pages and DOI exactly.

audit.assertion: ADA permits a tighter A1C goal for people in good health with low treatment risk.
audit.reason: Rec 6.4 verbatim in PMC12690178: 'Lower A1C goals (e.g., <6.5% [<48 mmol/mol]) may be appropriate for individuals with diabetes with good health and function and low treatment risks (e.g., hypoglycemia) and burdens (see Fig. 6.1). B'. Both value and mmol/mol conversion are literally present.

audit.assertion: ADA permits a looser A1C goal where health status is complex or life expectancy limited.
audit.reason: Section 6 narrative verbatim: 'Less stringent goals (e.g., A1C up to 8% [64 mmol/mol]) may be recommended for individuals with complex health status and/or limited life expectancy where benefits of more intensive treatment may not be realized or if the expected risks and burdens of treatment outweigh the potential benefits.' The 'narrative accompanying Recs 6.4–6.5' attribution is accurate — the number is in prose, not in a numbered rec.

audit.assertion: ADA lists the qualifying conditions that justify a less stringent glycaemic goal.
audit.reason: Rec 6.5 verbatim: 'Less stringent glycemic goals may be appropriate for individuals with significant cognitive and/or functional limitations, frailty, or severe comorbidities or where the harms of treatment, including hypoglycemia, are greater than the benefits. B'. All four criteria in the finding, including 'harms exceeding benefits', are present in the rec text.

audit.assertion: ADA gives a preprandial capillary plasma glucose target range for non-pregnant adults.
audit.reason: Table 6.3 ('Summary of glycemic goals for many nonpregnant adults with diabetes') verbatim: 'Preprandial capillary plasma glucose 80–130 mg/dL* (4.4–7.2 mmol/L)'. Both units as stated, correct table number.

audit.assertion: ADA gives a peak postprandial capillary plasma glucose target for non-pregnant adults.
audit.reason: Table 6.3 verbatim: 'Peak postprandial capillary plasma glucose‡ <180 mg/dL* (<10.0 mmol/L)'. Correct in both units.

audit.assertion: ADA sets a continuous-glucose-monitoring time-in-range goal for most non-pregnant adults.
audit.reason: Rec 6.3b verbatim: 'A goal time in range of >70% in people using CGM is appropriate for many nonpregnant adults. B'. Caveat, not an error: the '70–180 mg/dL (3.9–10.0 mmol/L)' range is NOT inside Rec 6.3b's own sentence — it is defined in Table 6.2 of the same section ('TIR 70–180 mg/dL (3.9–10.0 mmol/L) Percent of time in range >70% (most adults)'). The composite value is correct but is assembled from rec + table.

audit.assertion: ADA sets time-below-range ceilings for people using CGM, with a tighter ceiling for older adults.
audit.reason: Rec 6.3c verbatim: 'A goal percent time <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) of <4% (or <1% for older adults) and a goal percent time <54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L) of <1% are recommended in people using CGM to prevent hypoglycemia. Deintensify or modify therapy if these goals are not met. B'. Exact match including the older-adult parenthetical.

audit.assertion: ADA defines level 1 and level 2 hypoglycaemia by glucose concentration.
audit.reason: Table 6.4 ('Classification of hypoglycemia') verbatim: 'Level 1 Glucose <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) and ≥54 mg/dL (≥3.0 mmol/L) Level 2 Glucose <54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L)'. Corroborated by the narrative. The finding cites 'Section 6' generically; the precise locus is Table 6.4.

audit.assertion: ADA defines level 3 hypoglycaemia by clinical severity rather than by a glucose number.
audit.reason: Table 6.4 verbatim: 'Level 3 A severe event characterized by altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance for treatment of hypoglycemia, irrespective of glucose level'. The 'no numeric threshold' framing is correct.

audit.assertion: ADA sets a tighter A1C band for older adults who are healthy with intact cognition and function.
audit.reason: PMC12690186 fetched raw; header confirms '49(Suppl 1):S277–S296. doi: 10.2337/dc26-S013', i.e. Section 13 as claimed. Rec 13.7a verbatim: '...should have lower glycemic goals (such as A1C <7.0–7.5% [<53–58 mmol/mol]) and/or time in range [TIR] 70–180 mg/dL [3.9–10.0 mmol/L] of ≥70% and time below range ≤70 mg/dL [≤3.9 mmol/L] of ≤4%) if CGM is used. C'. Every number matches, including the ≤ (not <) in the TBR clause.

audit.assertion: ADA sets a looser A1C goal for older adults with intermediate or complex health.
audit.reason: Rec 13.7b verbatim: '...less stringent goals (such as A1C <8.0% [<64 mmol/mol] and/or TIR 70–180 mg/dL [3.9–10.0 mmol/L] of ≥50% and time below range <70 mg/dL [3.9 mmol/L] of <1%)...'. Exact match.

audit.assertion: For older adults in very complex or poor health, ADA advises against relying on A1C and gives glucose ranges instead.
audit.reason: Table 13.2 'Very complex/poor health' row verbatim: 'Avoid reliance on A1C; glucose management decisions should be based on avoiding hypoglycemia and symptomatic hyperglycemia | 100–180 mg/dL (5.6–10.0 mmol/L) | 110–200 mg/dL (6.1–11.1 mmol/L) | <140/90 mmHg | Consider likelihood of benefit with statin'. Numbers and both unit sets match. Note the numbers live only in Table 13.2; Rec 13.7c itself carries no figures, which the finding's dual attribution states correctly.

audit.assertion: ADA sets the on-treatment blood pressure goal in diabetes, and encourages a lower systolic goal in high-risk people.
audit.reason: PMC12690187 header confirms '10. Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 ... 49(Suppl 1):S216–S245. doi: 10.2337/dc26-S010'; CrossRef independently returns the same volume/pages for that DOI. Rec 10.4 verbatim: 'If it can be safely attained, the on-treatment blood pressure goal is <130/80 mmHg; a systolic blood pressure goal <120 mmHg should be encouraged in individuals with high cardiovascular or kidney risk. A'.

audit.assertion: ADA sets the blood pressure thresholds at which antihypertensive drug therapy is started, and when to start two agents.
audit.reason: Rec 10.6 verbatim: 'In individuals with confirmed office-based blood pressure ≥130/80 mmHg, pharmacologic therapy should be initiated and titrated to achieve their individualized blood pressure goal. A'. Rec 10.7 verbatim: 'Individuals with confirmed office-based blood pressure ≥150/90 mmHg should ... have prompt initiation and timely titration of two drugs or a single-pill combination...'. Both thresholds and the 'confirmed office-based' qualifier are exact.

audit.assertion: ADA applies the same blood pressure goal to type 1 diabetes as to type 2.
audit.reason: Section 10 narrative verbatim: 'Notably, there is an absence of high-quality data available to guide blood pressure goals in people with type 1 diabetes, but a similar blood pressure goal of <130/80 mmHg is recommended in people with type 1 diabetes.' Attribution to the narrative (not a numbered rec) is correct.

audit.assertion: ADA recommends moderate-intensity statin for people with diabetes aged 40–75 without ASCVD.
audit.reason: Rec 10.18 verbatim: 'For people with diabetes aged 40–75 years without ASCVD, use moderate-intensity statin therapy in addition to lifestyle therapy. A'. No LDL number appears in this rec, so the 'no LDL numeric goal specified for this group' qualifier is accurate.

audit.assertion: ADA sets an LDL-cholesterol goal for higher-risk primary prevention in diabetes aged 40–75.
audit.reason: Rec 10.20 verbatim: 'For people with diabetes aged 40–75 years at higher cardiovascular risk, including those with one or more additional ASCVD risk factors, high-intensity statin therapy is recommended to reduce LDL cholesterol by ≥50% of baseline and to obtain an LDL cholesterol goal of <70 mg/dL (<1.8 mmol/L). A'. Both units and the ≥50% reduction match.

audit.assertion: ADA sets an LDL-cholesterol goal for secondary prevention in diabetes with established ASCVD.
audit.reason: Rec 10.27 verbatim: 'For people with diabetes and ASCVD, treatment with high-intensity statin therapy is recommended to obtain an LDL cholesterol reduction of ≥50% from baseline and an LDL cholesterol goal of <55 mg/dL (<1.4 mmol/L). Addition of ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor with proven benefit in this population is recommended if this goal is not achieved on maximum tolerated statin therapy. B'. Exact match in both units.

audit.assertion: ADA's 2026 cardiovascular section does not name any specific 10-year cardiovascular risk calculator.
audit.reason: I tried hardest to refute this one, since a sweeping negative is the easiest thing to get wrong. Case-insensitive search of the complete Section 10 text (216,731 chars incl. references): 'PREVENT' 0 hits, 'Pooled Cohort' 0, 'risk calculator' 0, 'Risk Estimator' 0, 'SCORE2' 0, 'QRISK' 0, 'risk equation' 0, 'risk estimat*' 0, 'PCE' 0. 'Framingham' appears twice — once as 'the Framingham cohort' in the heart-failure narrative and once in a reference title (Murabito et al., Circulation 1997) — never as a recommended equation. Negative finding stands.

audit.assertion: ADA directs agent choice in type 2 diabetes by comorbidity (ASCVD, heart failure, CKD) independently of A1C, displacing a strictly metformin-first ladder.
audit.reason: PMC12690185 header confirms Section 9, '49(Suppl 1):S183–S215. doi: 10.2337/dc26-S009'. Rec 9.7 ('...GLP-1 RA and/or SGLT2 inhibitor ... (irrespective of A1C)'), Rec 9.8 ('...an SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended for both glycemic management and prevention of HF hospitalizations (irrespective of A1C)'), Rec 9.10 ('...CKD (with confirmed eGFR 20–60 mL/min/1.73 m2 and/or albuminuria), an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA ... (irrespective of A1C)') all verbatim. The eGFR band 20–60 is exact. Worth carrying forward: 9.10 adds 'The glycemic benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors are reduced at eGFR <45 mL/min/1.73 m2.'

audit.assertion: ADA sets an A1C distance-above-goal at which single-agent therapy is expected to be insufficient.
audit.reason: Section 9 narrative verbatim: 'When A1C is ≥1.5% above the individualized glycemic goal ... many individuals will require dual-combination therapy or a more potent glucose-lowering agent to achieve and maintain their goal A1C level.' Caveat: the parenthetical '(≥16 mmol/mol)' is NOT in the source — ADA states the delta only in DCCT %. The conversion is arithmetically defensible (1.5 × 10.93 ≈ 16.4) but is the sourcing agent's own, so it should not be presented as quoted from ADA.
audit.correctedValue: A1C ≥1.5% above the individualised goal (source states the delta in % only; the ≥16 mmol/mol equivalent is a derived conversion, not ADA text)

audit.assertion: ADA gives explicit glycaemic thresholds and symptom criteria that trigger consideration of insulin in type 2 diabetes.
audit.reason: Rec 9.20 verbatim: 'In adults with type 2 diabetes, initiation of insulin should be considered regardless of background glucose-lowering therapy or disease duration if symptoms of hyperglycemia are present or when A1C or blood glucose levels are very high (i.e., A1C >10% [>86 mmol/mol] or blood glucose ≥300 mg/dL [≥16.7 mmol/L]). E'. All three criteria and both unit sets match exactly.

audit.assertion: ADA prefers GLP-1-based therapy over insulin for initial or add-on injectable therapy in the absence of severe hyperglycaemia.
audit.reason: Rec 9.21 verbatim: 'In adults with type 2 diabetes without severe hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis, GLP-1–based therapy is preferred to insulin for initial or add-on glucose-lowering therapy (Fig. 9.4). A'. The conditional framing in the finding matches the rec's own wording.

audit.assertion: ADA specifies how often the medication plan should be reassessed.
audit.reason: Rec 9.14 verbatim: 'Medication plan and medication-taking behavior should be reevaluated at regular intervals (e.g., every 3–6 months) and adjusted as needed ... E'. Interval matches.

audit.assertion: WHO's primary-care diabetes module sets a single default HbA1c aim for the majority of patients.
audit.reason: Downloaded the IRIS bitstream (HTTP 200, application/pdf, 35pp) and extracted text: cover page reads 'Diagnosis and Management of Type 2 Diabetes ... WHO/UCN/NCD/20.1 © World Health Organization 2020', matching the stated document and reference number. Body verbatim: 'The majority of patients can be expected to aim for an HbA1c of 7.0% (53 mmol/mol).' Repeated in the monitoring section as '≤7.0% (53 mmol/mol)'.

audit.assertion: WHO permits relaxing the HbA1c target under named clinical conditions.
audit.reason: Verbatim: 'The HbA1c target can be relaxed (e.g. to <8% or <64 mmol/mol) in people with frequent severe hypoglycaemia, advanced complications or low life-expectancy.' Value and both units present in the source.

audit.assertion: WHO gives explicit glucose surrogate targets for settings where HbA1c is unavailable or unreliable.
audit.reason: Verbatim, appearing twice: 'If HbA1c measurement is not available or there is concern over its validity, an FPG value of ≤7.0 mmol/L (126mg/dL) and a postprandial PG value of ≤9.0 mmol/L (160 mg/dL) can serve as surrogates.' Both thresholds and both unit sets are exact. (Note the source's own mg/dL rounding: 9.0 mmol/L is given as 160 mg/dL, not 162.)

audit.assertion: WHO sets the blood pressure treatment threshold and target in people with diabetes at primary-care level.
audit.reason: Threshold verbatim: 'Hypertension treatment is indicated in people with diabetes when systolic blood pressure ≥130 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥80 mmHg.' Target verbatim: 'Thiazide diuretics and ACE inhibitors are recommended to achieve a target blood pressure of <130/80 mmHg.' Both exact. Flagging for the finding set as a whole: this conflicts with WHO's own 2021 hypertension guideline (finding 37, conditional SBP <130 for diabetes), an intra-WHO disagreement not recorded in any conflicts field.

audit.assertion: WHO recommends statins for all people with type 2 diabetes aged 40 or over, but subordinates this to medicine-access constraints.
audit.reason: Two verbatim passages: 'Statins are recommended for all people with type 2 diabetes 40 years old or older, but only if this does not negatively impact access to glucose-lowering and blood pressure-lowering medication' and 'Statins are recommended for all patients of 40 years of age and older with diabetes. If this is not feasible, use statins in patients at highest risk of CVD events (e.g. patients with CVD, patients with nephropathy and/or patients with a high risk on a CVD risk prediction chart).' The 'no LDL numeric goal' claim is supported: 'LDL' has 0 occurrences in the whole document.

audit.assertion: WHO restricts antiplatelet therapy in diabetes to secondary prevention only.
audit.reason: Verbatim: 'Use of antiplatelet treatment is recommended only for secondary prevention of CVD events, even among patients with diabetes. The recommendation is for 75–100 mg of acetylsalicylic acid daily to be prescribed to all people with diabetes who have survived a CVD event and have no history of major bleeding.' Dose, restriction and the no-major-bleeding qualifier all match. (The word 'aspirin' has 0 hits — WHO uses INN 'acetylsalicylic acid' — which the finding correctly reproduces.)

audit.assertion: WHO's step 1 of the resource-limited glycaemic ladder is metformin, with gliclazide as the alternative first-line agent.
audit.reason: Under 'Initial treatment', verbatim: 'Metformin ... is the recommended initial treatment for people who do not achieve the desired glycaemic control with diet and physical activity' and 'A second-generation sulfonylurea (preferably gliclazide) can be used as initial (first-line) treatment when metformin is contraindicated or not tolerated.' Substance exact. Presentational caveat: WHO does not label these 'Step 1/2/3' — the document uses 'Initial treatment' / 'Intensification of treatment when metformin alone fails' / 'Intensification when metformin and sulfonylurea fail'; the step numbering is the sourcing agent's framing. The WHO-PEN 2013 provenance is genuine: Fig. 1 carries the footnote '*Derived from WHO-PEN 2013'.

audit.assertion: WHO's step 2 is adding a sulfonylurea to metformin, with a symptom-based shortcut to insulin.
audit.reason: Verbatim under 'Intensification of treatment when metformin alone fails to control glycaemia': 'Add a second-generation sulfonylurea (preferably gliclazide) to metformin in patients with inadequately controlled glycaemia on metformin, along with diet and physical activity. • In hyperglycaemic patients with symptoms, give a sulfonylurea or refer for insulin treatment.' Both clauses exact; 'Step 2' is again the agent's label, not WHO's.

audit.assertion: WHO's step 3 is human insulin, with DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors and thiazolidinediones explicitly demoted below insulin on cost grounds.
audit.reason: Verbatim: 'Refer for insulin treatment or add human insulin to oral medication (Annex 1). • If insulin is unsuitable, a DPP-4 inhibitor, SGLT-2 inhibitor or a thiazolidinedione (TZD) may be added, but these are not recommended for routine use due to high cost and, with the exception of SGLT-2 inhibitors, uncertain benefit.' The quoted phrase 'not recommended for routine use due to high cost' is a literal match. The finding omits WHO's own carve-out that SGLT2 inhibitors are excepted from the 'uncertain benefit' judgement — worth keeping.

audit.assertion: WHO advises against routine use of insulin analogues in favour of human insulin.
audit.reason: Footnote 1 to the intensification section, verbatim: 'Insulin analogues are not recommended for routine use as they are substantially more costly than human insulin and there is considerable uncertainty over their benefits, especially in people with type 2 diabetes.' The finding's attribution to a footnote is precisely right.

audit.assertion: WHO sets blood pressure thresholds for initiating antihypertensive drugs, with a lower threshold for people with diabetes.
audit.reason: Fetched NBK573627 (the Recommendations chapter of the 2021 WHO guideline). Recommendation 1 verbatim: 'WHO recommends initiation of pharmacological antihypertensive treatment of individuals with a confirmed diagnosis of hypertension and systolic blood pressure of ≥140 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure of ≥90 mmHg... WHO recommends pharmacological antihypertensive treatment of individuals with existing cardiovascular disease and systolic blood pressure of 130–139 mmHg... WHO suggests pharmacological antihypertensive treatment of individuals without cardiovascular disease but with high cardiovascular risk, diabetes mellitus, or chronic kidney disease, and systolic blood pressure of 130–139 mmHg.' All three thresholds exact.

audit.assertion: WHO sets blood pressure treatment targets, with a lower systolic target for people with diabetes but at a weaker recommendation strength.
audit.reason: Recommendation 6 verbatim: '<140/90 mmHg in all patients with hypertension without comorbidities. Strong recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence'; 'target systolic ... <130 mmHg in patients with hypertension and known cardiovascular disease (CVD). Strong recommendation'; 'WHO suggests a target systolic blood pressure treatment goal of <130 mmHg in high-risk patients with hypertension (those with high CVD risk, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease). Conditional recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence'. Values AND the strong/conditional split are exact — this is the finding I most expected to be garbled, and it is not.

audit.assertion: WHO explicitly subordinates cardiovascular risk assessment to timely treatment initiation.
audit.reason: Recommendation 3 verbatim: 'WHO suggests cardiovascular risk assessment at or after the initiation of pharmacological treatment for hypertension, but only where this is feasible and does not delay treatment. Conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence.' Both the substance and the (conditional, low-certainty) grading match word for word.

audit.assertion: The WHO cardiovascular risk charts provide regionally-specific 10-year risk models, in laboratory-based and non-laboratory-based variants.
audit.reason: PMC7025029 header: 'Lancet Glob Health. 2019 Sep 2;7(10):e1332–e1345. doi: 10.1016/S2214-109X(19)30318-3' — journal, year, volume, issue, pages and DOI all match. Abstract verbatim: 'we derived 10-year risk prediction models for fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular disease (ie, myocardial infarction and stroke)... Models included information on age, smoking status, systolic blood pressure, history of diabetes, and total cholesterol. For derivation, we included participants aged 40–80 years...' and 'recalibrated models using ... 21 global regions'. Non-lab BMI variant confirmed: 'pragmatic risk models (eg, those that include information on body-mass index [BMI] instead of serum lipid values)'.

audit.assertion: WHO states that the cohort data needed to derive risk models for low- and middle-income countries do not exist, and that recalibration was used instead of local derivation.
audit.reason: Discussion verbatim: 'We derived risk prediction models from 85 cohorts mostly from high-income countries in the ERFC. Ideally, however, the derivation of risk models for low-income and middle-income countries would involve nationally representative, large-scale prospective cohort data ... Unfortunately, however, such data do not yet exist for most low-income and middle-income countries. Therefore, to inform recalibration, we used data from the GBD study and the NCD-RisC'. The VALUE payload matches exactly. Minor overstatement in the assertion sentence only: the paper says 'do not YET exist for MOST' LMICs, not flatly 'do not exist'.
audit.correctedValue: Derived from 85 cohorts mostly in high-income countries; the paper states such cohort data 'do not yet exist for most low-income and middle-income countries', so recalibration used GBD and NCD-RisC aggregate data rather than local cohorts

audit.assertion: WHO's 2025 Essential Medicines List added GLP-1 receptor agonists and a dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist, but only for a narrowly defined subgroup.
audit.reason: Fetched the WHO news page directly (HTTP 200) and string-matched. Verbatim: 'GLP-1 receptor agonists – semaglutide, dulaglutide and liraglutide – and the GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) dual receptor agonist (tirzepatide) have been added to the EML. They are used as glucose lowering therapy for adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus with established cardiovascular disease or chronic kidney disease and obesity (defined as body mass index (BMI) ≥ 30kg/m2).' The '24th list' claim is also literal: 'The revisions mark the 24th edition of WHO EML and 10th edition of EMLc', dated 5 September 2025. All four drug names, both comorbidity arms and the BMI cut-off verified.

audit.assertion: KDIGO recommends an individualised HbA1c target expressed as a range rather than a single default, for people with diabetes and CKD not on dialysis.
audit.reason: Downloaded the 128-page KDIGO 2022 diabetes guideline PDF from the stated kdigo.org URL (HTTP 200). Recommendation 2.2.1 verbatim, appearing twice: 'We recommend an individualized HbA1c target ranging from <6.5% to <8.0% in patients with diabetes and CKD not treated with dialysis (Figure 14) (1C).' Range and the 1C grade are exact. Caveat: the '<48 to <64 mmol/mol' conversions are the sourcing agent's arithmetic (correct), not KDIGO's stated units in that recommendation.

audit.assertion: KDIGO's systolic blood pressure target in CKD is lower than every other body reviewed, and is conditional on standardised office measurement.
audit.reason: I specifically probed this URL because the '/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/' path segment on a 2021 document looks like the signature of a fabricated link. It is genuine: HTTP 200, 4.65 MB PDF, 92 pages, cover reads 'SUPPLEMENT TO VOLUME 99 | ISSUE 3S | MARCH 2021 ... KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Blood Pressure in Chronic Kidney Disease'. Recommendation 3.1.1 verbatim: 'We suggest that adults with high BP and CKD be treated with a target systolic blood pressure (SBP) of <120 mm Hg, when tolerated, using standardized office BP measurement (2B).' Value, conditionality and 2B grade exact.

audit.assertion: KDIGO makes SGLT2 inhibitors a first-line recommendation in type 2 diabetes with CKD, independent of glycaemic need.
audit.reason: Recommendation 1.3.1 verbatim: 'We recommend treating patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D), CKD, and an eGFR ≥20 ml/min per 1.73 m2 with an SGLT2i (1A).' Practice Point 1.3.1 supports the 'independent of glycaemic need' framing: 'The recommendation for SGLT2i is for kidney and cardiovascular protection...'. Practice Point 1.3.6 verbatim: 'Once an SGLT2i is initiated, it is reasonable to continue an SGLT2i even if the eGFR falls below 20 ml/min per 1.73 m2, unless it is not tolerated or kidney replacement therapy is initiated.' All three loci cited by the finding exist and say what is claimed.

audit.assertion: KDIGO places GLP-1 receptor agonists as the next step after metformin and SGLT2 inhibitor in T2D with CKD.
audit.reason: Recommendation 4.2.1 verbatim: 'In patients with T2D and CKD who have not achieved individualized glycemic targets despite use of metformin and SGLT2i treatment, or who are unable to use those medications, we recommend a long-acting GLP-1 RA (1B).' Sequencing, the 'or unable to use' branch and the 1B grade all match.

audit.assertion: KDIGO recommends a statin for every patient with diabetes and CKD, without an LDL goal.
audit.reason: Fetched the separate Executive Summary PDF at the stated URL (HTTP 200, 10pp, Rossing et al.). Verbatim: 'A statin is recommended for all patients with T1D or T2D and CKD.' Figure 1 ('Kidney–heart risk factor management') lists 'Lipid management: Statin' and the care-bundle figure specifies 'Moderate- or high-intensity statin'. The 'no LDL-C target' claim holds: 'LDL' has 0 occurrences in the Executive Summary, and in the full guideline 'LDL' never appears attached to a numeric goal.

audit.assertion: ESC's 2024 hypertension guideline sets a systolic target band that is lower than ADA's and lower than WHO's.
audit.reason: Retrieved the OUP full-text page (curl is 403 there; WebFetch reaches it). Article confirmed as '2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of elevated blood pressure and hypertension', Eur Heart J 2024;45(38):3912–4018, doi 10.1093/eurheartj/ehae178 — independently corroborated via the CrossRef API for that DOI (same title, volume 45, issue 38, pages 3912-4018). Target quoted from the page: 'a target systolic BP of 120–129 mmHg among adults receiving BP-lowering medications'. Corroborated a second time by the ACC 'Ten Points to Remember' summary of this guideline.

audit.assertion: ESC 2024 introduces an 'elevated blood pressure' category between normal and hypertension.
audit.reason: From the OUP page: non-elevated BP <120/70; elevated BP 120–139 systolic OR 70–89 diastolic; hypertension ≥140 systolic OR ≥90 diastolic. Independently corroborated by the ACC key-points summary and the ESC's own press release ('a novel elevated blood pressure category'). Both boundary values in the finding are right.

audit.assertion: The 2023 ESC diabetes guideline endorses SCORE2-Diabetes as its type-2-diabetes-specific 10-year risk score, restricted to patients without overt ASCVD or severe target-organ damage.
audit.reason: Article confirmed as Eur Heart J 2023;44(39):4043 (CrossRef for doi 10.1093/eurheartj/ehad192 returns the same title, volume 44, issue 39, pages 4043-4140). Guideline text: 'SCORE2-Diabetes serves as a guide for clinical decision-making in patients with T2DM at low, moderate, high, or very high risk, but without clinically overt ASCVD or severe TOD.' Independently corroborated by the ACC key-points summary, which adds detail the finding omits and which may be worth capturing: the recommendation is Class I Level B, applies to T2DM aged over 40, and the bands are low <5%, moderate 5–<10%, high 10–<20%.

audit.assertion: SCORE2-Diabetes is derived and calibrated exclusively for European populations, in four European risk regions.
audit.reason: Value payload confirmed verbatim from PMC10361012: 'to estimate the 10-year risk of non-fatal myocardial infarction, stroke, or any CVD mortality in individuals with diabetes but without previous CVD, aged over 40 years, in four different European risk regions'; 'Models were recalibrated to CVD incidence in four European risk regions'. Citation exact — PMC header 'Eur Heart J. 2023 May 29;44(28):2544–2556. doi: 10.1093/eurheartj/ehad260', matching CrossRef (note the finding gives no issue number; it is issue 28). One refutation on the assertion's framing: 'exclusively' European is contradicted by the Methods, which state derivation used data 'across seven countries (England, Wales, Scotland, France, Germany, Italy, and the USA)'. Only the recalibration is European-exclusive.
audit.correctedValue: 10-year risk of non-fatal MI, stroke, or CVD mortality; type 2 diabetes, aged over 40, without previous CVD. Derivation data spanned seven countries including the USA; RECALIBRATION is to four European risk regions (low, moderate, high, very-high) — 'derived exclusively for European populations' overstates it

audit.assertion: ISH uniquely splits its blood pressure targets into an 'essential' minimum standard and an 'optimal' standard, explicitly to serve low-resource settings.
audit.reason: Downloaded the ish-world.com slide deck (HTTP 200, 105 slides, '2020 ISH Global Hypertension Practice Guidelines 6th May 2020'). Verbatim: 'Drug Treatment Threshold ≥140/90 mmHg (raising to ≥160/100 mmHg for those at lowest risk)' and 'Drug Treatment Target Optimal: <65 years: <130/80 mmHg  ≥65 years: <140/90 mmHg : reduce BP by ≥20/10 mmHg'; the comparison table repeats 'Essential: Reduce BP by at 20/10mmHg and ideally to <140/90'. Every number matches. I separately verified the journal citation via PubMed eSummary (PMID 32370572): Hypertension 2020 Jun;75(6):1334-1357, doi 10.1161/HYPERTENSIONAHA.120.15026 — exactly as cited.

audit.assertion: ISH 2020 deliberately does not specify which cardiovascular risk assessment tool to use.
audit.reason: Strongest possible support for a negative finding: the deck's own 'ISH vs European Guidelines' comparison table states literally, in the ISH 2020 column under 'Cardiovascular Risk Assessment', 'CV risk assessment tool not specified'. Corroborated by absence: across the full deck 'score' 0 hits, 'Framingham' 0, 'chart' 0, 'calculator' 0, '10-year' 0. Evidence-tier caveat only: the source is ISH's own summary slide deck rather than the peer-reviewed guideline text (ahajournals.org returns 403 to both curl and WebFetch), so this is verified against a first-party summary, not the full guideline.

audit.assertion: Framingham, SCORE2 and the WHO model classify substantially different proportions of the same sub-Saharan African population as moderate-to-high risk.
audit.reason: jogh.org returns 403 to curl, so I located the open-access copy via the Europe PMC API (PMC12714358, PMID 41411530) and matched strings there. Abstract verbatim: 'sub-Saharan Africa (WHO: 16.30%; 95% CI = 15.78–16.83; SCORE2: 22.69%; 95% CI = 22.09–23.28; Framingham: 33.85%; 95% CI = 33.18–34.52)'. All three point estimates and all six CI bounds match to the decimal, and are reproduced in the results table. CrossRef for doi 10.7189/jogh.15.04323 confirms 'Regional variations in cardiovascular risk predictions: a comparative analysis of Framingham, SCORE2, and WHO models across 53 countries', Journal of Global Health, vol 15, 2025. The finding's own framing of it as a peer-reviewed study rather than a guideline is correct; population is adults aged 40–69 without prior CVD.
audit.correctedSource: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12714358/ (open-access mirror; the cited jogh.org URL is genuine but returns 403 to non-browser clients)
